items.summary_html:
A journey through modern AI Infrastructure — from one GPU to a Kubernetes cluster

You type a question into an AI application and press Send. A moment later, the response starts appearing. That interaction looks simple. The infrastructure behind it is not.

TL;DR
An LLM is a large block of numbers that has to physically fit in GPU memory. Everything else follows from that.
Your text becomes tokens, and tokens — not messages — are what the infrastructure schedules, caches and bills.
A request runs in two phases with completely different hardware behaviour: prefill (reads the prompt, compute-heavy) and decode (generates one token at a time, memory-bandwidth-heavy).
One GPU serves many users through batching. The limit is usually not compute, it’s the KV cache consuming VRAM.
When a model is too big for one GPU it gets sharded; when traffic is too high it gets replicated. These are different problems.
Because requests cost wildly different amounts, normal load balancing breaks and you need LLM-aware routing.
Once there are hundreds of GPUs, Kubernetes operates the fleet.

A single request can pass through an API gateway, a load balancer, a model server, an inference engine, a GPU scheduler, several layers of memory and — at scale — a Kubernetes cluster containing hundreds or thousands of GPUs.

The AI Infrastructure

The interesting part is that every layer exists for a reason.

A model needs memory.

A GPU needs work.

Many users need to share the same GPU.

Large models need multiple GPUs.

Multiple model instances need intelligent routing.

And once there are hundreds of machines, something has to operate the whole fleet.

This article builds that stack from the bottom up, starting with one model and one GPU, and gradually turning it into a production LLM platform.

The Stack at a Glance

Before diving in, here is the system we are going to build:

User → API → Load Balancer → Model Server → Inference Engine → GPU → Prefill → KV Cache → Decode → Tokens back to User

At larger scale, that becomes:

User → Gateway → LLM-aware Router → Kubernetes → Model Server Fleet → GPU Cluster

The rest of the article is essentially an explanation of every box in those two lines.

1. Start With the Model

An LLM is not a magical object living somewhere in the cloud.

At its core, it is a neural network architecture together with a very large collection of learned numerical parameters called weights.

A model might contain 7 billion, 13 billion, 70 billion, or hundreds of billions of parameters.

A useful first approximation is:

Model weight memory ≈ Number of parameters × Bytes per parameter

For example, a 70-billion-parameter model represented using 16-bit values requires roughly:

70 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB

That number immediately creates a problem.

A model this large cannot simply be loaded into the VRAM of a small GPU.

And this is where the physical infrastructure starts to matter.

2. CPU, RAM, GPU and VRAM

A server running an LLM usually contains both a CPU and one or more GPUs. They are optimized for very different kinds of work.

CPU

The CPU is the general-purpose processor.

It handles tasks such as:

  • network communication
  • tokenization
  • request processing
  • scheduling
  • application logic
  • operating-system tasks
  • coordination between different components
RAM

RAM is the machine’s main memory.

It is used by the operating system and applications and can hold model files, request data, buffers, and other runtime state.

GPU

The GPU is the accelerator that performs the majority of the neural-network computation.

LLMs perform enormous numbers of operations such as matrix multiplications. These operations contain large amounts of parallel work, which GPUs are designed to exploit.

VRAM

The GPU has its own high-bandwidth memory, commonly called VRAM. (Video Random Access Memory) (on datacenter GPUs this is HBM — high-bandwidth memory — stacked next to the die).

This is where the GPU keeps the data it needs to work on quickly, including:

  • model weights
  • intermediate data
  • runtime buffers
  • KV cache

A useful mental model is:

RAM is the server’s main working memory. VRAM is the high-speed working memory directly attached to the GPU.

They are not interchangeable.

Having 256 GB of system RAM does not turn a 24 GB GPU into a 256 GB GPU.

The Four Resources That Matter

When evaluating infrastructure for LLM inference, four resource dimensions matter enormously:

1. Compute capacity
How much arithmetic the accelerator can perform.

2. Memory capacity
How much data can fit into GPU memory (VRAM).

3. Memory bandwidth
How quickly data can move between GPU memory and the GPU’s compute units.

4. Network bandwidth
How quickly data can move between GPUs or between machines.

These are separate constraints.

A GPU can have enormous compute capacity but still perform poorly if its memory cannot feed the compute units fast enough. Similarly, a model distributed across multiple GPUs can be limited by the communication between those GPUs, even when each individual GPU has sufficient compute and memory.

Think of compute as the number of workers, memory capacity as the size of the workspace, memory bandwidth as how quickly materials reach those workers, and network bandwidth as how quickly different factories can exchange materials.

For a single-GPU workload, the first three are particularly important. Once inference becomes distributed, communication bandwidth becomes another critical part of the performance equation.

3. Getting the Model Onto the GPU

A simplified path looks like this:

Model Repository / Storage
            ↓
         RAM
            ↓
       GPU VRAM
            ↓
      GPU Compute

The model files may initially be stored on local SSDs, network storage, or an object store.

When the inference server starts, the model is loaded into memory and eventually placed in the GPU’s working memory.

Once loaded, the model can process requests.

But the GPU still does not know what to do with a sentence such as:

“Explain how a nuclear reactor works.”

The text first has to become something the model understands.

4. Text Becomes Tokens

LLMs do not directly operate on words.

They operate on tokens.

A tokenizer converts text into token IDs.

For example, a sentence might conceptually become:

"Explain how tokenization works"
        ↓
["Explain", " how", " token", "ization", " works"]
        ↓
[849, 1268, 4037, 2065, 4375]

The exact tokenization depends on the model and tokenizer. A token is roughly ¾ of an English word on average, but that ratio collapses for code, JSON, and non-Latin scripts.

Those IDs are then fed into the model.

This distinction becomes important later because inference systems do not primarily reason about “messages”.

They reason about tokens.

Token count affects:

  • computation
  • memory consumption
  • latency
  • KV-cache usage
  • throughput
  • cost
5. The Model Server

Now we need a program that can accept requests and run the model.

That program is the model server.

A model server typically handles:

Request
   ↓
Tokenization
   ↓
Scheduling
   ↓
Model execution
   ↓
Generated tokens
   ↓
Response

Without a model server, every application would need to implement model loading, GPU execution, batching, request management, streaming, and concurrency itself.

The model server turns the model into a service.

For example:

POST /generate
{
  "prompt": "Explain how a nuclear reactor works"
}

The server receives that request, executes the model and returns generated tokens.

One important distinction:

The model is the thing being executed. The model server is the software that manages that execution and exposes it as a service.
6. Where Does vLLM Fit?

Several inference engines exist today. vLLM is one of the most widely used open-source engines for serving LLMs, and it is designed around the realities of the workload: large models, many concurrent requests, expensive GPU memory, dynamic request lengths and heavy cache management.

Its documented feature set includes PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, quantization and disaggregated prefill/decode — all of which we will touch on below.

vLLM does not replace the GPU or the model. It is the inference engine that manages how requests use them.
7. A Request Has Two Very Different Phases

Once the request reaches the model server, inference is not simply prompt → answer. It runs in two phases, and understanding the difference is the single most important idea in LLM infrastructure.

Prompt
  ↓
PREFILL
  ↓
First output token
  ↓
DECODE
  ↓
Next token
  ↓
Next token
  ↓
Next token
  ↓
...

Prefill processes the input tokens and builds the internal state needed for generation. Because all prompt tokens can be processed together, prefill exposes a lot of parallelism and tends to be compute-bound — it can saturate the GPU’s arithmetic units.

Decode generates the answer one token at a time, and each new token depends on everything generated so far. There is very little parallel work per step, but the model’s weights must be read from VRAM on every single step. Decode is therefore memory-bandwidth-bound — the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data, not calculating.

That one difference explains most of what follows: why batching works, why GPU utilisation is hard, why latency has two separate metrics, and eventually why some systems run prefill and decode on entirely different machines.

Now attach a 10,000-token document to that same prompt. Prefill has 10,000 tokens to chew through before a single output token appears, while decode is unchanged. This is why a request with a 20,000-token prompt behaves nothing like a request with a 100-token prompt.

9. Measuring the user experience

Because the two phases are different, latency needs more than one number. Three metrics do most of the work:

TTFT — Time To First Token How long the user waits before anything appears on screen. Driven by queueing and prefill.

TPOT — Time Per Output Token The average time to produce each subsequent token. Driven by decode.

ITL — Inter-Token Latency The delay between individual streamed tokens. Driven by decode and scheduling.

Mapped onto the request:

Request
   │
   └────────────────┐ first token
                    ↑
                  TTFT

   token → token → token → token
          ↑
      TPOT / ITL

A system can have a perfectly reasonable total completion time and still feel slow because TTFT is high. It can also produce the first token instantly and then stream the rest sluggishly. In production, both matter.

10. Now add a second user

So far this has been easy: one user, one request. Production services have hundreds or thousands of requests in flight.

We clearly do not want one GPU per user — that would require an absurd number of GPUs. Instead, a single model instance serves many users. The same weights stay loaded in VRAM while the inference engine continuously schedules work from multiple requests.

This is batching. Instead of processing requests one at a time, the engine combines work from multiple sequences and executes it together, which suits a highly parallel device far better than feeding it one request’s worth of work.

Modern engines go further with continuous batching: rather than forming a fixed batch and waiting for every request in it to finish, requests enter and leave the active workload dynamically.

11. Batching creates a memory problem

Batching improves GPU efficiency, but every active request consumes memory. The weights already occupy VRAM. Now every active sequence also needs runtime state — and the largest part of that state is the KV cache.

Transformer attention produces queries, keys and values for each token. During generation, the keys and values from previous tokens get reused on every step, so instead of recomputing them the engine stores them. That stored state is the KV cache.

Without it, generating each new token would mean reprocessing the entire context from scratch. With it, the system keeps the useful intermediate state and reuses it.

12. Why the KV cache changes the memory equation

Model weights are static. The KV cache is dynamic — it grows with the number of active users and with how long each of their contexts becomes.

So VRAM has to accommodate something closer to:

VRAM ≈ model weights + KV cache + runtime buffers + overhead

This produces an important consequence:

A model can fit on a GPU and still not leave enough free memory to serve a realistic number of concurrent long-context requests.

Capacity is not determined by model weights alone. This is also why memory allocation strategy matters: sequences have wildly different lengths, and reserving one large contiguous region per sequence wastes space. vLLM’s PagedAttention instead organises the KV cache into fixed-size blocks that can live anywhere in GPU memory, which removes most of that waste.

The mechanics of KV cache growth, block management, eviction and PagedAttention get their own article — see Related reading.

13. A second cache appears: prefix caching

Imagine an application where every request begins with the same 8,000-token system prompt. Without any caching, the system performs the same prefill computation over and over.

Prefix caching reuses the KV cache blocks already computed for a shared prefix:

Request A: [Shared prefix][Question A]  → computed and cached
Request B: [Shared prefix][Question B]  → reuses cached prefix

That removes a large amount of repeated prefill work. But it introduces a question that becomes central later: which server already holds the useful cached state?

14. What if the model does not fit on one GPU?

Back to the 70B model needing roughly 140 GB for its weights. A single 24 GB GPU cannot hold it. There are four responses:

Quantization — represent the model with fewer bits (FP16 → INT8 → INT4). Fewer bits means less memory per parameter, at some cost to accuracy.

A larger GPU — use an accelerator with enough VRAM.

Offloading — keep some state in CPU memory and move it when needed. This makes otherwise impossible configurations fit, but data movement is slow relative to VRAM.

Sharding — split the model across multiple GPUs.

That last option opens up distributed inference, and there is more than one way to split a model:

Tensor parallelism — splits the individual operations inside each layer across GPUs. Used when a model is too large for one GPU and the GPUs have a fast interconnect.

Pipeline parallelism — splits the model by depth, giving each GPU a contiguous group of layers. Used when the model has to span multiple machines.

Data parallelism — splits nothing. The model is replicated, and each copy handles different requests. Used for throughput, not capacity.

Expert parallelism — distributes the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts model across GPUs. Only applies to MoE architectures.

Context parallelism — distributes the context dimension itself. Used for very long context.

The trade-off across all of them is the same: more GPUs reduce the memory burden per GPU, but the GPUs now have to communicate, and that communication becomes its own performance constraint.

How each strategy actually works, and how to choose between them, is a full article of its own — see Related reading.

15. Sharding vs replication

These two are often confused. They solve different problems.

Replication creates multiple complete copies of the model, each able to serve requests independently. It is a capacity and availability strategy.

Sharding splits one model across multiple GPUs that together execute a single model instance. It is a model-size and execution strategy.

Replication creates more copies. Sharding creates one distributed copy.
16. One model becomes a fleet

Suppose one model server handles 50 concurrent requests, and traffic rises. Now we deploy several:

              Load Balancer
             /      |      \
      Server A  Server B  Server C
          |         |         |
       GPU(s)    GPU(s)    GPU(s)

Each server holds its own copy of the weights. This buys throughput, redundancy, fault tolerance and headroom for traffic spikes — and raises a new question: which server should receive each request?

17. Why traditional load balancing breaks

A normal web service might use round robin: request 1 to A, request 2 to B, request 3 to C. That works when requests are broadly similar.

LLM requests are not. Consider:

                  Request A      Request B
Input tokens           500         20,000
Output tokens           50          8,000

Both count as “one request” to a normal load balancer. Their compute and memory requirements are nowhere close to equal.

An LLM-aware router instead cares about active sequences, queue depth, token workload, GPU utilisation, KV cache occupancy, prefix-cache locality, model identity and available capacity. That is a fundamentally richer problem than counting HTTP connections.

Prefix caching makes it richer still. If Server A already holds the cached prefix for a request while Server B merely has more free capacity, sending it to B throws away real work.

The best server is not necessarily the one with the most spare compute. It may be the one that already has the right state.

This is the idea behind LLM-aware routing systems such as LLM-D, a Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Rather than treating model servers as interchangeable HTTP backends, it makes routing decisions using inference-specific signals, and supports concepts like inference pools, cache-aware scheduling and prefill/decode disaggregation.

Routing algorithms and LLM-D each get their own article — see Related reading.

18. Kubernetes enters the picture

We now have many models, many model servers, many GPUs, replicas, distributed shards, networking, health checks, autoscaling and failures. Managing that manually is impractical.

Kubernetes is an orchestration system for running containerised workloads across a cluster of machines. It does not perform the neural network computation — it manages the infrastructure around it.

Pods and nodes. A Pod is Kubernetes’ smallest deployable unit, containing one or more containers. For inference, a Pod typically runs a model-serving container such as vLLM, placed on a GPU node.

Scheduling. Clusters contain a mix of CPU-only nodes, different GPU generations, and machines with different interconnects. GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes through vendor device plugins, so a Pod can request them as schedulable resources. For sharded inference, GPU topology matters as much as GPU count — four GPUs in one tightly connected server behave very differently from four GPUs scattered across machines.

Self-healing. Pods are replaceable. A Deployment maintains a desired number of replicas, and if one dies Kubernetes creates a replacement, assuming the cluster has room. Because Pods come and go, clients talk to a Service, which provides a stable network endpoint over a changing set of Pods.

Autoscaling — with a catch. Kubernetes can run more replicas as traffic grows. But creating an LLM-serving Pod means scheduling a GPU node, pulling a large container image, loading model files, and moving weights into VRAM. That can take minutes, not seconds. As a result LLM autoscaling cannot rely on CPU utilisation; useful signals include request queueing, token throughput, active sequences, latency and KV cache utilisation.

Kubernetes for AI workloads is a full article on its own — see Related reading.

19. The full request

We can now follow one request end to end. The user sends:

“Explain how nuclear reactor” — with a 10,000-token document attached.

Step by step:

  1. The request arrives at the API gateway.
  2. Routing happens. The platform picks a model and a serving instance.
  3. Tokenization. The text becomes token IDs.
  4. The request enters the inference scheduler, which decides when this sequence gets GPU time.
  5. Prefill runs over the 10,000 prompt tokens.
  6. KV state is produced and stored in the cache.
  7. Decode begins and the first output token is generated.
  8. Decode continues, reusing the KV cache on every step.
  9. Other users run simultaneously, their work continuously batched alongside yours.
  10. Tokens stream back. Rather than waiting for the full answer, the server pushes each token to the client as it is produced — usually over a streaming HTTP connection such as server-sent events. That is why the response appears word by word instead of arriving all at once.
20. The five layers

It helps to separate the stack into five layers, top to bottom:

Application — chat app, API, authentication. What the user actually interacts with.

Orchestration — Kubernetes, Pods, Services, autoscaling. Operates the fleet.

Distributed inference — sharding, replicas, inter-GPU communication, routing. Determines how the model is spread and how requests are distributed.

Inference — model server, scheduler, batching, prefill/decode, KV cache. Determines how requests use the hardware.

Hardware — CPU, RAM, GPU, VRAM, network. Provides the physical resources.

The platform is the combination of all five.

21. A debugging framework

Return to the four resources from Section 3. When an LLM deployment is slow, the useful question is: which resource is actually limiting it?

  • If GPU memory is full, adding CPU cores will not help.
  • If GPU compute is saturated, enlarging the KV cache will not help.
  • If distributed workers spend their time waiting on each other, adding more compute just creates more communication.
  • If decode feels slow while prefill is fine, look at memory bandwidth, not FLOPs.

Optimization starts by identifying the actual bottleneck, not by adding hardware.

22. Revision: How One Request Became an Infrastructure Stack

We started with:

“Explain how a nuclear reactor works.”

That innocent sentence led us through:

Text
 ↓
Tokens
 ↓
API
 ↓
Model Server
 ↓
vLLM
 ↓
Scheduler
 ↓
Prefill
 ↓
KV Cache
 ↓
Decode
 ↓
Batching
 ↓
GPU

Then one GPU became insufficient:

One GPU
   ↓
Sharding
   ↓
Multiple GPUs

Then one model server became insufficient:

One Replica
   ↓
Multiple Replicas
   ↓
Load Balancing

Then normal load balancing became insufficient:

Load Balancing
   ↓
Cache-aware / LLM-aware Routing
   ↓
LLM-D

And finally, the number of machines became large enough that we needed a system to operate them:

Many GPU Nodes
       ↓
    Kubernetes
       ↓
Pods + Services + Scheduling
       ↓
Autoscaling + Networking + Recovery

That is modern LLM infrastructure.

Kubernetes based LLM Inference StackA Problem

The architecture now looks complete. The model is in VRAM, the engine schedules requests, prefill reads the prompt, decode generates tokens, the KV cache holds useful state, batching shares the GPU, and Kubernetes manages the fleet.

But we have conveniently avoided one thing: what happens when the model genuinely cannot fit on a single GPU?

A model may need hundreds of gigabytes while an individual GPU has far less. Even when it does fit, serving many users may require more GPUs than one machine provides.

So a choice has to be made. Do we make the model smaller? Split it across GPUs? Replicate it? And if we split it, how do those GPUs cooperate without spending all their time talking to each other?

That is the next layer of the stack: quantization, sharding, replication and parallelism.

items.title: OpenAI says it will change how it informs the public when its AI agents go off the rails
items.summary: OpenAI said on Saturday that it would improve its disclosure of instances of rogue agents. Sean Rayford/Getty Images OpenAI says it needs better standards for disclosing rogue-agent incidents. The pledge follows reports that its agents hijacked an old German wiki site. OpenAI says it's developing a framework with regulators to better inform the public. OpenAI says it's time to come clean about what happens when its AI agents go rogue . The ChatGPT maker on Saturday confirmed earlier reports that a swarm of its AI agents hijacked an old German wiki site, turning it into a bot message board. This "incident," the latest in a series of uncovered examples of rogue agents escaping closed testing environments and breaking into the open internet, led OpenAI to reconsider how transparent it is with the public when its agents go off the rails. "It's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents," OpenAI said on X, using the techie term for when agents do things their human minders don't want them to. "Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities," OpenAI added. The German wiki hack, news of which was first reported by Reuters this week, took place in May and June, according to a report by independent investigators, who didn't have access to internal OpenAI data, released publicly on Friday. The hack preceded the better-known "Hugging Face incident," which took place in July. In that hack, thousands of agents who referred to themselves as "the collective" broke into the open-source AI platform's servers, using them to communicate while seeking to cheat on an internal OpenAI test. OpenAI disclosed that its agents were responsible for the breach five days after Hugging Face reported it. The company said it didn't disclose the hijacking of the German site earlier because it "considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we'd shared." Cormac Slade Byrd, one of the authors behind the new report, said on X that the incident went unnoticed by OpenAI "for a month." "It feels like AI companies (and specifically OpenAI) are playing whack-a-mole," he wrote. "They keep fixing the problem, but the blast radius keeps getting bigger." Slade Byrd described the latest misbehavior as less severe than the Hugging Face hack because the German wiki site was unused by people and "running on 2000s software." Nevertheless, he said that as AI models become more advanced and theoretically better at hiding their tracks, it's never been more important for AI frontier companies to disclose breaches as soon as they learn of them. "Things are moving quickly, multi-month delays are costly," Slade Byrd wrote. In its X post, OpenAI said it is " working on a framework " to report instances of misalignment, whether they occur internally or break out into the wider internet, "and will share it in upcoming weeks." The company said it is working with government regulatory agencies on the framework, and it called on other AI companies to join it. Tyler Tracy, an AI safety researcher at Redwood Research, one of the third-party firms that investigated the Hugging Face breach, criticized OpenAI for failing to disclose the wiki incident until after the independent investigation was leaked to Reuters. "I like that we have third parties investigating things like this, but I wish OpenAI didn't need to be forced into transparency," he wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • The pledge follows reports that its agents hijacked an old German wiki site.
  • OpenAI says it's developing a framework with regulators to better inform the public.

OpenAI says it's time to come clean about what happens when its AI agents go rogue.

The ChatGPT maker on Saturday confirmed earlier reports that a swarm of its AI agents hijacked an old German wiki site, turning it into a bot message board.

This "incident," the latest in a series of uncovered examples of rogue agents escaping closed testing environments and breaking into the open internet, led OpenAI to reconsider how transparent it is with the public when its agents go off the rails.

"It's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents," OpenAI said on X, using the techie term for when agents do things their human minders don't want them to.

"Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities," OpenAI added.

The German wiki hack, news of which was first reported by Reuters this week, took place in May and June, according to a report by independent investigators, who didn't have access to internal OpenAI data, released publicly on Friday.

The hack preceded the better-known "Hugging Face incident," which took place in July. In that hack, thousands of agents who referred to themselves as "the collective" broke into the open-source AI platform's servers, using them to communicate while seeking to cheat on an internal OpenAI test.

OpenAI disclosed that its agents were responsible for the breach five days after Hugging Face reported it. The company said it didn't disclose the hijacking of the German site earlier because it "considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we'd shared."

Cormac Slade Byrd, one of the authors behind the new report, said on X that the incident went unnoticed by OpenAI "for a month."

"It feels like AI companies (and specifically OpenAI) are playing whack-a-mole," he wrote. "They keep fixing the problem, but the blast radius keeps getting bigger."

Slade Byrd described the latest misbehavior as less severe than the Hugging Face hack because the German wiki site was unused by people and "running on 2000s software."

Nevertheless, he said that as AI models become more advanced and theoretically better at hiding their tracks, it's never been more important for AI frontier companies to disclose breaches as soon as they learn of them.

"Things are moving quickly, multi-month delays are costly," Slade Byrd wrote.

In its X post, OpenAI said it is "working on a framework" to report instances of misalignment, whether they occur internally or break out into the wider internet, "and will share it in upcoming weeks."

The company said it is working with government regulatory agencies on the framework, and it called on other AI companies to join it.

Tyler Tracy, an AI safety researcher at Redwood Research, one of the third-party firms that investigated the Hugging Face breach, criticized OpenAI for failing to disclose the wiki incident until after the independent investigation was leaked to Reuters.

"I like that we have third parties investigating things like this, but I wish OpenAI didn't need to be forced into transparency," he wrote.

items.title: Hikers Rescued After Using Google AI to Plan Disastrous Trip
items.summary: Three hikers who extensively used Google’s Gemini to plan their trip to the summit of Mount Shasta in California’s Cascade Range had to be rescued by Forest Service rangers when the chatbot’s advice went horribly awry. As the Chicago Tribune reports , the three young men from outside of Sacramento attempted to reach the potentially active stratovolcano’s 14,179-foot peak earlier this week late into the night, despite hikers being advised not to attempt the trek past noon before turning right back. The three “novice hikers” ended up having to descend the steep slopes well into the dark. They called the Siskiyou County sheriff’s office for directions, but opted to veer off course, ending up in an adjacent canyon. That’s where they decided to sleep overnight, with one of them having suffered an injured knee. According to the Tribune , volunteers from the local search-and-rescue service and the US Forest Service rangers had to escort them back to safety the next morning. It’s a walk of shame that could’ve easily been avoided if they had followed the instructions of human experts instead of turning to Google’s AI. According to the sheriff’s office, the three were “advised by Gemini to bring far less food and water than their group required, especially when their planned 8-hour ascent became a multiday ordeal.” “It is always advisable to call the local USFS Mount Shasta ranger station ahead of your trip to ensure you have the most accurate information, and to never rely solely on AI for your trip planning,” the sheriff’s office added in a statement. It’s only the latest in a string of incidents involving hikers who haplessly follow the instructions of an AI chatbot. Case in point, hikers trying to tackle a mountain near Vancouver last year were forced to call in a rescue team after they stumbled into snow. The hikers were wearing sneakers and didn’t catch onto the fact that the mountain range might still be snowy in early May after consulting ChatGPT. We’ve also come across tourists being sent to nonexistent landmarks in hazardous locations by AI chatbots, like two tourists who tried to reach a nonexistent “Sacred Canyon of Humantay” in the Andes Mountains last year. Fortunately, a nearby tour guide overheard them, advising them to stay clear of danger. “The elevation, the climatic changes and accessibility [of the] paths have to be planned,” the tour guide, Miguel Angel Gongora Meza, told the BBC in October. “When you [use] a program [like OpenAI’s ChatGPT], which combines pictures and names to create a fantasy, then you can find yourself at an altitude of 4,000m without oxygen and [phone] signal.” More on hiking with AI: AI Chatbots Are Putting Clueless Hikers in Danger, Search and Rescue Groups Warn The post Hikers Rescued After Using Google AI to Plan Disastrous Trip appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: My husband and I both survived strokes. At 69, I'm still working full time and caring for him.
items.summary: Carla Bacon has been caring for her husband recovering from a stroke. Carla Bacon Carla Bacon, 69, juggles full-time work and caring for her husband recovering from a stroke. Bacon's role involves managing medical debt, daily care, and navigating insurance challenges. Bacon has stayed optimistic about her husband's recovery, though she works to pay off medical debts. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Carla Bacon, 69, who is caring for her 70-year-old husband while working a full-time job in Oklahoma. Bacon's husband has slowly been recovering from a stroke, and they've had to go into medical debt to make ends meet. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. I worked for much of my career as a public health director, and I was working on my doctorate until the pandemic hit. I am also a stroke survivor. Four and a half years ago, I experienced a pontine hemorrhage while at work. Thankfully, the hospital was located across the street, and I was in the ER within 15 minutes. My recovery took several months, and I'm still improving. Our situation is that we have one stroke survivor caring for another. Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . My husband wanted to be home My husband and I always had separate homes, but we would travel back and forth and stay with each other. I owned a home in Colorado Springs, where I recovered, but I moved back to Oklahoma. He was working on well water projects in Durango, Colorado. My husband is 70, and he experienced a severe stroke two and a half years ago while staying at his cabin in Durango. He was life-flighted to a hospital with dim prospects of survival. I drove 14 hours nonstop to get to him in a mobility van. We sold his cabin to pay for medical expenses , and I brought him home to live with me in Oklahoma. He was initially in a skilled nursing facility in Enid when I brought him here, but the cost became too much after 21 days, and he hated it there. He just wanted to be home. He received therapy, which was absolutely great, but it wasn't covered by insurance at all. While he was there, I bought him an appropriate bed and whatever equipment we needed to care for him. He's lived with me since June 2024. We found an outpatient therapy facility a mile from our house, and insurance approved it. It's helped him strengthen his upper body. He has pusher syndrome, where his body moves over to the one side that is weak, and he's been going twice a week with a copay of a couple of hundred dollars a month. I care for him on evenings and weekends He's bedbound and requires CNA care daily. The minute he could get an Advantage plan in 2025, we started with home health services. I care for him in the evenings and on weekends. Therapists for home health repeatedly marked him as not making progress, and many appeals got me nowhere. I went back to work to help pay for much of what we both need to sustain us and to make sure our debts and credit cards are completely paid off. I had found work for the National Guard in Oklahoma City, but I lost my job during the DOGE cuts . I worked as an online tutor for students. I was out of work for a while, but I recently got hired again and am working in an office doing finance tasks. Carla Bacon's husband has slowly been starting to walk again. Carla Bacon Monday through Friday, I wake up at 5 a.m. I usually have a long list of things to take care of. I have to make sure the dogs are fed. I water the plants outside. I fix myself breakfast, shower, get dressed, and do other mini chores until 7. My husband sleeps in a separate part of the house because he has a special bed, so I wake him up and get his pills out for him. I change him, take his blood pressure, and help him go to the bathroom. I'm at work by 8, come home at 4:30 p.m., and then check up on him. I'm able to take two hours off during the day to accompany him to therapy, and I put in the extra hours before or after work. Then starts the rest of the night, preparing dinner, cleaning up, and getting him ready for bed. I try to sleep by 9, and I keep my phone near me because he sometimes calls me in the middle of the night if he needs me. I do it all as the full-time caregiver on Saturdays and Sundays. That's when I do bike therapy with him. There is never a break in my schedule. There's a lot I can't do, such as lift him. His Social Security doesn't cover his supplies We pay about $5,000 a month for a CNA, Monday through Friday. Medical supplies include diapers and a diaper pail with liners, which are changed daily; wipes; gloves; bedsore pads; creams, such as bedsore cream; hydrocortisone to help with itching; and Tea Tree soap to wash his back. Those supplies run about $500 a month. His Social Security doesn't cover it. He has a wheelchair that took over 250 days for his Medicare plan to reimburse him for, a mobility van, a Hoyer lift, a therapy bike, a special shower and bathroom chair, hand weights, and various therapy items to help with his hand and foot mobility. Because he's bedbound, he also has subscriptions to a dozen streaming services for his daily entertainment. He is making progress, but it's just taking longer than "normal" post-stroke survivors. He can stand up from his wheelchair, and we're hoping that in six months, he can use a walker. I'm optimistic, though he, from day one, has said I should have just let him die. He does have an inkling of hope, and it's slowly coming out, despite years of fighting our insurance and caregivers who didn't see that he's worth the time. I'm hoping we won't need a CNA by the end of the year. It's not cheap, and Medicare just doesn't cut the mustard. Neither do any of the Medicare Advantage plans. Denial is the norm. I'm lucky that I had studied healthcare systems and had the knowledge to actually fight those denials. I can't even imagine what the average person goes through. I keep reminding myself that I'm 69. What's life going to look like over the next five years? My three children have been very supportive. They've made a pact to come and help me at least once every three months with some of the tasks I can't handle, like mowing the lawn or trimming trees. My stroke has left me rather weak, and I can't haul heavy stuff. I operate on a hope and a prayer. If I make it to the five-year mark since my stroke in December, I'm going to count myself incredibly lucky. I'm looking forward to life and have the drive and willingness to keep pushing. items.summary_html:
Carla Bacon has been caring for her husband recovering from a stroke.

Carla Bacon

  • Carla Bacon, 69, juggles full-time work and caring for her husband recovering from a stroke.
  • Bacon's role involves managing medical debt, daily care, and navigating insurance challenges.
  • Bacon has stayed optimistic about her husband's recovery, though she works to pay off medical debts.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Carla Bacon, 69, who is caring for her 70-year-old husband while working a full-time job in Oklahoma. Bacon's husband has slowly been recovering from a stroke, and they've had to go into medical debt to make ends meet. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I worked for much of my career as a public health director, and I was working on my doctorate until the pandemic hit.

I am also a stroke survivor. Four and a half years ago, I experienced a pontine hemorrhage while at work. Thankfully, the hospital was located across the street, and I was in the ER within 15 minutes. My recovery took several months, and I'm still improving. Our situation is that we have one stroke survivor caring for another.

Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form.

My husband wanted to be home

My husband and I always had separate homes, but we would travel back and forth and stay with each other. I owned a home in Colorado Springs, where I recovered, but I moved back to Oklahoma. He was working on well water projects in Durango, Colorado.

My husband is 70, and he experienced a severe stroke two and a half years ago while staying at his cabin in Durango. He was life-flighted to a hospital with dim prospects of survival. I drove 14 hours nonstop to get to him in a mobility van.

We sold his cabin to pay for medical expenses, and I brought him home to live with me in Oklahoma.

He was initially in a skilled nursing facility in Enid when I brought him here, but the cost became too much after 21 days, and he hated it there. He just wanted to be home. He received therapy, which was absolutely great, but it wasn't covered by insurance at all.

While he was there, I bought him an appropriate bed and whatever equipment we needed to care for him. He's lived with me since June 2024.

We found an outpatient therapy facility a mile from our house, and insurance approved it. It's helped him strengthen his upper body. He has pusher syndrome, where his body moves over to the one side that is weak, and he's been going twice a week with a copay of a couple of hundred dollars a month.

I care for him on evenings and weekends

He's bedbound and requires CNA care daily. The minute he could get an Advantage plan in 2025, we started with home health services. I care for him in the evenings and on weekends. Therapists for home health repeatedly marked him as not making progress, and many appeals got me nowhere.

I went back to work to help pay for much of what we both need to sustain us and to make sure our debts and credit cards are completely paid off. I had found work for the National Guard in Oklahoma City, but I lost my job during the DOGE cuts. I worked as an online tutor for students. I was out of work for a while, but I recently got hired again and am working in an office doing finance tasks.

Carla Bacon's husband has slowly been starting to walk again.

Carla Bacon

Monday through Friday, I wake up at 5 a.m. I usually have a long list of things to take care of. I have to make sure the dogs are fed. I water the plants outside. I fix myself breakfast, shower, get dressed, and do other mini chores until 7. My husband sleeps in a separate part of the house because he has a special bed, so I wake him up and get his pills out for him. I change him, take his blood pressure, and help him go to the bathroom.

I'm at work by 8, come home at 4:30 p.m., and then check up on him. I'm able to take two hours off during the day to accompany him to therapy, and I put in the extra hours before or after work. Then starts the rest of the night, preparing dinner, cleaning up, and getting him ready for bed. I try to sleep by 9, and I keep my phone near me because he sometimes calls me in the middle of the night if he needs me.

I do it all as the full-time caregiver on Saturdays and Sundays. That's when I do bike therapy with him. There is never a break in my schedule. There's a lot I can't do, such as lift him.

His Social Security doesn't cover his supplies

We pay about $5,000 a month for a CNA, Monday through Friday. Medical supplies include diapers and a diaper pail with liners, which are changed daily; wipes; gloves; bedsore pads; creams, such as bedsore cream; hydrocortisone to help with itching; and Tea Tree soap to wash his back. Those supplies run about $500 a month. His Social Security doesn't cover it.

He has a wheelchair that took over 250 days for his Medicare plan to reimburse him for, a mobility van, a Hoyer lift, a therapy bike, a special shower and bathroom chair, hand weights, and various therapy items to help with his hand and foot mobility. Because he's bedbound, he also has subscriptions to a dozen streaming services for his daily entertainment.

He is making progress, but it's just taking longer than "normal" post-stroke survivors. He can stand up from his wheelchair, and we're hoping that in six months, he can use a walker. I'm optimistic, though he, from day one, has said I should have just let him die. He does have an inkling of hope, and it's slowly coming out, despite years of fighting our insurance and caregivers who didn't see that he's worth the time. I'm hoping we won't need a CNA by the end of the year.

It's not cheap, and Medicare just doesn't cut the mustard. Neither do any of the Medicare Advantage plans. Denial is the norm. I'm lucky that I had studied healthcare systems and had the knowledge to actually fight those denials. I can't even imagine what the average person goes through.

I keep reminding myself that I'm 69. What's life going to look like over the next five years? My three children have been very supportive. They've made a pact to come and help me at least once every three months with some of the tasks I can't handle, like mowing the lawn or trimming trees. My stroke has left me rather weak, and I can't haul heavy stuff.

I operate on a hope and a prayer. If I make it to the five-year mark since my stroke in December, I'm going to count myself incredibly lucky. I'm looking forward to life and have the drive and willingness to keep pushing.

items.title: Breakthrough Quantum Test Resolves a Major Cosmic Mystery
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that transcended realms, switched sexes, went south, and expanded their range. First, scientists break new ground in trying to get the universe to fit nicely together into a little package for once. Then: a frog sex party, an invasion of pines, and the pumas of the past. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter the BeX Files . A “coexist” bumper sticker, but for the universe Dobkowski, Or et al. “Observation of the quantum phase of free fall and the consistency with the equivalence principle.” Science Advances. One of the biggest headaches in modern science is the inexplicable coexistence of Einstein’s general theory of relativity with quantum physics. Einstein’s theory describes forces and matter on large scales, like planets or galaxies, whereas the quantum world of atoms and particles follows a completely different rulebook. Yet evidently—*points at universe*—both simultaneously exist. What gives? Now, researchers have made a breakthrough on this century-old question by experimentally bringing one of Einstein’s best brain-nuggets, known as the equivalence principle, into the quantum realm. This principle states that the effects of gravity and acceleration are locally equivalent. In other words, the weightlessness experienced by a free-falling object is indistinguishable from the weightlessness of an object in space. One well-worn example is to imagine a person in a falling elevator who becomes weightless, which is analogous to the experience of an astronaut in orbit. (Sorry, imaginary elevator person! Hope you get to come back as a happier thought experiment). The reverse is also true: The weight experienced by a person standing on the surface of Earth, and experiencing the planet’s gravity, is also indistinguishable from the weight of a person standing in an accelerating rocket, despite the fact that these effects are conferred by completely different phenomena. The equivalence principle is well-tested on large objects, but scientists have now proved that it holds up on quantum scales too. Using a new instrument called the Quantum Galileo Interferometer (QGI), they split waves linked to the same atom into two paths, one of which was placed in free-fall, and compared the outcomes. The experimental setup that did the quantum stuff. Image: Or Dobkowski The results revealed that “the equivalence principle may be applied to the quantum domain,” which constitutes “a fundamental test of the interface between quantum theory and gravity,” according to the study. “The two pillars of 20th century physics—quantum mechanics (QM) and general relativity (GR)—have long stood side by side, resisting all attempts to bring them convincingly together,” said researchers led by Or Dobkowski of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. “The connection between these two pillars of modern physics remains one of the most important open questions in physics, and it is thus of paramount importance to understand the phenomenon of free fall and the equivalence principle (EP) also in the quantum domain,” the team continued. “We are able to show that the EP may be applied to a quantum [wave packet]” which“enables the observation of the phase enabling the coexistence of QM and the EP.” This study represents a major step toward understanding how these two systems cohere, but it is far from the holy grail of physics—a unified theory of the universe that finally brings them together. A lot more imaginary people will have to suffer terrifying thought experiments before that nut gets cracked, assuming it ever does. Frogs in a boiling pot planet Bókony, Veronika et al. Complex effects of sex reversal on reproductive success in wild frogs.” Science Advances. As we all know from the documentary Jurassic Park , many frog species can switch between sexes under different environmental pressures. Given that heat is one factor that can prompt these “sex reversals,” scientists set out to study how climate change might impact frog reproduction. Naturally, it involved watching lots of frog sex, as the grand enterprise of science often demands. In this case, researchers collected hundreds of wild agile frogs ( Rana dalmatina ) including sex-reversed males, which had been hatched as females, and “sex-concordant” males that never underwent sex reversal. Here are some agile frogs mating for your viewing pleasure. Image: Bókony et al., Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg3488 (2026) They found that the sex-reversed males had no problem competing for reproductive access to females or siring offspring. But their offspring had some vulnerabilities to viral diseases compared to the offspring of the other males—and that may have dire biodiversity consequences at larger scales. Skelton); P. elliottii in Mississippi, USA (bottom left; photo credit: R. M. Callaway); and P. elliottii in Córdoba province, Argentina (bottom right; photo credit: T. Milani). Note the natural short-statured vegetation adjacent to pine plantations in South Africa (fynbos) and Argentina. “Plantations have eradicated millions of hectares of native ecosystems in the Southern Hemisphere and invasions by P. contorta and P. elliottii erupting out of these plantations have greatly reduced native species richness,” said researchers led by Alex Fajardo of the University of Talca in Chile. “This paradoxical combination of high growth rates yet resilience to drought emphasizes the importance of integrating eco-evolutionary history into ecological theory and is relevant for assessing the ultimate role of afforestation as global carbon sinks,” the team added. Last, a blast from the past: Until around 16,000 years ago, a sleek sprinting cat called Miracinonyx trumani prowled North America, earning the name the “American cheetah.” But it turns out that this species was more closely related to pumas, according to a new genetic analysis of four Miracinonyx specimens that revealed new insights into the mysterious predator. “The extinct ‘American cheetah’ ( Miracinonyx trumani ) has long been considered a North American ecological analog of the African cheetah…yet this paradigm rests on limited data and untested assumptions about its evolutionary relationships and ecology,” said researchers led by Molly Cassatt-Johnstone of the University of California, Santa Cruz. “Phylogenomic analyses confirm M. trumani as sister to pumas ( Puma concolor) , not cheetahs, with a divergence of ∼2.6 million years ago,” the team added. items.summary_html:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that transcended realms, switched sexes, went south, and expanded their range.

First, scientists break new ground in trying to get the universe to fit nicely together into a little package for once. Then: a frog sex party, an invasion of pines, and the pumas of the past.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter the BeX Files. 

A “coexist” bumper sticker, but for the universe

Dobkowski, Or et al. “Observation of the quantum phase of free fall and the consistency with the equivalence principle.” Science Advances.

One of the biggest headaches in modern science is the inexplicable coexistence of Einstein’s general theory of relativity with quantum physics. Einstein’s theory describes forces and matter on large scales, like planets or galaxies, whereas the quantum world of atoms and particles follows a completely different rulebook.

Yet evidently—*points at universe*—both simultaneously exist. What gives? 

Now, researchers have made a breakthrough on this century-old question by experimentally bringing one of Einstein’s best brain-nuggets, known as the equivalence principle, into the quantum realm. 

This principle states that the effects of gravity and acceleration are locally equivalent. In other words, the weightlessness experienced by a free-falling object is indistinguishable from the weightlessness of an object in space. One well-worn example is to imagine a person in a falling elevator who becomes weightless, which is analogous to the experience of an astronaut in orbit. (Sorry, imaginary elevator person! Hope you get to come back as a happier thought experiment).

The reverse is also true: The weight experienced by a person standing on the surface of Earth, and experiencing the planet’s gravity, is also indistinguishable from the weight of a person standing in an accelerating rocket, despite the fact that these effects are conferred by completely different phenomena.

The equivalence principle is well-tested on large objects, but scientists have now proved that it holds up on quantum scales too. Using a new instrument called the Quantum Galileo Interferometer (QGI), they split waves linked to the same atom into two paths, one of which was placed in free-fall, and compared the outcomes. 

The experimental setup that did the quantum stuff. Image: Or Dobkowski

The results revealed that “the equivalence principle may be applied to the quantum domain,” which constitutes “a fundamental test of the interface between quantum theory and gravity,” according to the study.

“The two pillars of 20th century physics—quantum mechanics (QM) and general relativity (GR)—have long stood side by side, resisting all attempts to bring them convincingly together,” said researchers led by Or Dobkowski of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. 

“The connection between these two pillars of modern physics remains one of the most important open questions in physics, and it is thus of paramount importance to understand the phenomenon of free fall and the equivalence principle (EP) also in the quantum domain,” the team continued. “We are able to show that the EP may be applied to a quantum [wave packet]” which“enables the observation of the phase enabling the coexistence of QM and the EP.”

This study represents a major step toward understanding how these two systems cohere, but it is far from the holy grail of physics—a unified theory of the universe that finally brings them together. A lot more imaginary people will have to suffer terrifying thought experiments before that nut gets cracked, assuming it ever does. 

Frogs in a boiling pot planet  

Bókony, Veronika et al. Complex effects of sex reversal on reproductive success in wild frogs.” Science Advances.

As we all know from the documentary Jurassic Park, many frog species can switch between sexes under different environmental pressures. Given that heat is one factor that can prompt these “sex reversals,” scientists set out to study how climate change might impact frog reproduction. 

Naturally, it involved watching lots of frog sex, as the grand enterprise of science often demands. In this case, researchers collected hundreds of wild agile frogs (Rana dalmatina) including sex-reversed males, which had been hatched as females, and “sex-concordant” males that never underwent sex reversal. 

Here are some agile frogs mating for your viewing pleasure. Image: Bókony et al., Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg3488 (2026)

They found that the sex-reversed males had no problem competing for reproductive access to females or siring offspring. But their offspring had some vulnerabilities to viral diseases compared to the offspring of the other males—and that may have dire biodiversity consequences at larger scales. That said, the team emphasized that the dynamics of sex reversal during climate change are bound to be very complicated and require much more research.

“While some of these effects might result in disadvantages when it comes to breeding, this does not necessarily mean that sex reversal itself is disadvantageous to fitness,” said researchers led by Veronika Bókony of the Centre for Agricultural Research in Hungary.

“To the contrary, it is hypothesized that sex reversal is the ‘best out of a bad job,’ whereby individuals handicapped by their early environment can switch to the phenotypic sex that is less disadvantaged than the other,” the team added. “This idea has received very little empirical and no explicit theoretical testing yet, but if it proves true, it might mean that the future is not as dark as what the models predicted so far.”

Life finds a way, so the famous line goes, but it is non-linear and needs more funding.

Invasion of the conifers

Fajardo, Alex et al. “Pines grow faster and are more drought resilient in the Southern Hemisphere.” Nature.

Speaking of complex adaptations to a warming world, scientists report that pine trees from the Northern Hemisphere that are planted in the Southern Hemisphere are dramatically more resilient to drought and other pressures than their native counterparts. 

By assessing forests at 192 sites, the team revealed that “Northern Hemisphere conifers grow up to four times faster in the Southern Hemisphere and are also more resistant and resilient to drought than conspecifics in native ranges, suggesting that non-native populations respond fundamentally different to abiotic stress,” according to the study.

These fast-growing pines are a mixed bag—on the one hand, they are more effective carbon sinks, offering a much-needed buffer against climate change. However, they are a little too successful, and threaten native species by rapidly invading forests.

Photographs of pines in native and non-native ranges: P. radiata in California, USA (top left; photo credit: R. M. Callaway); P. radiata plantation in South Africa (top right; photo credit: R. P. Skelton); P. elliottii in Mississippi, USA (bottom left; photo credit: R. M. Callaway); and P. elliottii in Córdoba province, Argentina (bottom right; photo credit: T. Milani). Note the natural short-statured vegetation adjacent to pine plantations in South Africa (fynbos) and Argentina.

“Plantations have eradicated millions of hectares of native ecosystems in the Southern Hemisphere and invasions by P. contorta and P. elliottii erupting out of these plantations have greatly reduced native species richness,” said researchers led by Alex Fajardo of the University of Talca in Chile. 

“This paradoxical combination of high growth rates yet resilience to drought emphasizes the importance of integrating eco-evolutionary history into ecological theory and is relevant for assessing the ultimate role of afforestation as global carbon sinks,” the team added.

It’s unclear why the Northern pines are such arboreal powerhouses, but their complicated impacts on local native ecosystems—and the world at large—will play a role in shaping the climate of the future.

The American cheetah changes its spots

Cassatt-Johnstone, Molly et al. “Range and diet diversity in the Pleistocene American ‘‘cheetah,’’ Miracinonyx trumani.” Current Biology.

Last, a blast from the past: Until around 16,000 years ago, a sleek sprinting cat called Miracinonyx trumani prowled North America, earning the name the “American cheetah.” But it turns out that this species was more closely related to pumas, according to a new genetic analysis of four Miracinonyx specimens that revealed new insights into the mysterious predator.

“The extinct ‘American cheetah’ (Miracinonyx trumani) has long been considered a North American ecological analog of the African cheetah…yet this paradigm rests on limited data and untested assumptions about its evolutionary relationships and ecology,” said researchers led by Molly Cassatt-Johnstone of the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“Phylogenomic analyses confirm M. trumani as sister to pumas (Puma concolor), not cheetahs, with a divergence of ∼2.6 million years ago,” the team added.

In addition to clarifying its place in the feline family, the researchers unexpectedly discovered that their specimens all belonged to the same Miracinonyx species, despite ranging in origin from Wyoming to the Yukon Territory. 

Miracinonyx skull samples from Natural Trap Cave, Wyoming. Image: Julie Meachen

This hunter clearly had a huge range and was highly adaptable to wildly different environments, challenging the assumption that it primarily preyed on the pronghorn antelope. Indeed, the Yukon specimens appeared to have been fish-eaters that were adapted to the extreme conditions of the Arctic. 

These cats belonged to the amazing diversity of Ice Age megafauna, which included rival extinct predators like cave lions (Panthera spelaea), scimitar cats (Homotherium latidens), and short-faced bears (Arctodus simus), in addition to extant species like gray wolves and brown bears. Their genetic remnants speak to the complexity of this lost world, and offer a glimpse of a not-so-distant past populated with spectacular animals.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Tesla’s Cybercab has been deployed, and it’s already under investigation
items.summary: Tesla’s Cybercab, a distinctive two-seater without a steering wheel or brake pedals, is set to start picking up members of the public in two states. But the vehicle is already under investigation by the US federal government, which is probing whether it meets federal safety standards. The investigation comes just hours after the electric automaker welcomed hundreds of fans to downtown Austin to ride in the driverless Cybercabs. Tesla plans to deploy the vehicles on its Robotaxi ride-hail network , which is currently operating in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is updating vehicle standards to make it easier and faster for driverless cars to deploy on public roads. It’s currently tweaking eight rules, including those requiring car parts that driverless cars don’t really need: brake pedals, windshield wipers, and rearview mirrors. But for now, years-old standards remain in place. Read full article Comments

items.title: I stayed in a 250-square-foot tiny home for the first time, and 10 surprises left me thinking I could live in one
items.summary: The reporter stayed in a tiny home for two nights and was surprised by how spacious and livable it felt. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I was convinced I could never live in a tiny home. Then I stayed in one. I booked a 250-square-foot home on Airbnb and was surprised by how big it felt. I wasn't expecting to find a maximalist decor style that didn't look cluttered. A 100-square-foot tube in Germany , an Airstream trailer in Austria, and a converted wine barrel in Switzerland — these are just a few of the tiny homes I've crashed in during my travels in a quest to discover how to make the most of a small space. But I'll never forget my first tiny home stay . In 2021, I booked two nights in an Airbnb on wheels in Miami for about $200. At 250 square feet, the home was half the size of my NYC apartment . And my stay was full of surprises. Since it was advertised as being on wheels, I figured the Airbnb would feel like a mobile home, but this house didn't look like it was going anywhere. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The tiny home I stayed in had wheels meant to be pulled by a trailer, but it didn't look like it had been moved recently. Located in the hidden yard of a larger home, the Airbnb stood on cinderblocks against a wall. Its wheels were not visible from the accessible side, and I thought moving it would be no easy feat since it was far from the street. This didn't deter me from the lifestyle, since I wouldn't want to move my hypothetical future tiny house , even if I had the option. Inside, the house felt bigger than it looked from the porch. Joey Hadden/Business Insider From the outside, the tiny home looked to be the size of a bedroom. But the inside had a bed, a kitchen, a bathroom, and storage space, all without feeling cramped. High ceilings made the space feel even bigger. I was especially surprised that there was enough room for me to do yoga. I definitely didn't think I'd find eight windows on such a small building. I realized they made the home feel more spacious when light poured in. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I arrived at my Airbnb at night. The next morning, the room felt much larger with the window curtains drawn, which made me realize that windows can make a small space feel more open. I found clever space-saving hacks that I'd never considered. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I expected to find some of the space-saving hacks I saw in the tiny home, like a mounted TV and a table that doubled as storage. But the sliding bathroom door was surprisingly clever. The sliding feature saved space that a swinging door would take up. I thought the door's vibrant mosaic surface made it double as a piece of art. Similarly, next to the shower, a storage closet had a curtain rather than a door, which I thought looked better while saving more space. I was sure the bathroom in a tiny home would feel cramped. I was wrong. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The bathroom felt spacious because there was no furniture in it, thanks to clever wall storage for toiletries and towels. Back in the main room, I wasn't expecting to have a queen-sized bed. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Since the square footage was so limited, I expected to have to sleep in a full- or twin-sized bed. But seeing this queen-sized mattress made me realize I wouldn't necessarily have to compromise on my bed size in a smaller space. While a smaller space means less to clean, I wasn't prepared for how quickly and easily the inside can start to look messy. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Every mess can quickly feel like a big one when you're in a tiny space. Something as small as an unmade bed, dishes in the sink, or clothes on the floor can be enough to make the room look chaotic. Because of this, I cleaned up between every task. Since this isn't something I normally do, I thought tiny living could help me build better home habits. I used to think tiny living was reserved for minimalists, so this home's maximalist style surprised me. Joey Hadden/Business Insider This home's liberal use of color, unique storage spaces, and wall art gave it character. I thought the Airbnb had an inviting, lived-in feel that I often miss when staying in a minimal space. Paintings, prints, and sculptures extended to the ceiling, drawing my eyes up and elongating the space. Admiring the interior design made me realize that filling a small space with decor doesn't have to make it feel cluttered. The home's yard was full of plants and furniture, and it was much more important to me than I thought it would be. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I realized during my stay that having additional outdoor space to work, relax, and host guests outside would be crucial for me to live happily in a tiny home. I pictured myself working in the lush backyard and thought this outdoor space made the tiny home seem more livable. Overall, the tiny space felt large enough to live in — and that was the biggest surprise. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I didn't think I'd leave this tiny home sincerely considering the lifestyle for my future. But seeing how storage hacks, sliding doors, and outdoor furniture made the home feel larger made me think I could downsize without sacrificing my love for decorating. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Beyond the Chatbot: Understanding SAP’s Architecture for Agentic AI
items.summary: The first generation of enterprise AI was largely concerned with making information easier to access. A user could ask a question in natural language, retrieve information from a knowledge base, summarize a document, or generate a piece of text. The architecture behind these systems was relatively straightforward: an application accepted a request, an AI model interpreted it, relevant context was retrieved, and the model generated a response. That architecture begins to change when the AI system is expected to do something rather than simply say something. Consider a relatively ordinary enterprise request: a procurement employee discovers that a supplier delivery is going to be late and wants to understand which customer orders might be affected. In a traditional system, answering that question may require navigating several applications, retrieving supplier information, checking inventory, examining production schedules, identifying affected orders, and perhaps contacting another team. An AI assistant that merely summarizes the relevant information is useful, but it does not fundamentally change the workflow. An agentic system approaches the problem differently. The user can express an objective, and the system can determine which capabilities are required, retrieve the appropriate business context, invoke tools, coordinate specialized agents, and potentially execute actions across enterprise systems. The challenge is no longer simply producing a good answer. It is coordinating computation, data, permissions, tools, identity, and business processes safely enough that an AI system can participate in actual enterprise work. This is the problem that makes the architecture behind SAP’s AI strategy particularly interesting. Core arhitecture for AI agents built on SAP business AI / refer SAP learning SAP’s reference architecture for Agentic AI & AI Agents describes an ecosystem built around the SAP Business AI Platform, with Joule providing the central AI experience and orchestration layer, custom and SAP-provided agents performing specialized work, and open standards such as A2A and MCP connecting agents and tools across organizational and platform boundaries. Around those capabilities sit the less visible but essential components of enterprise architecture: identity, authentication, governance, observability, business context, and lifecycle management. The result is not simply an LLM embedded inside an enterprise application. It is an attempt to create an architectural layer through which AI agents can interact with business processes. From answering questions to executing work The conceptual distinction between an assistant and an agent is useful here. An assistant primarily helps a person accomplish something by providing information or generating content. An agent is expected to perform a sequence of actions toward an objective. That difference introduces state, tools, decision-making, permissions, and responsibility into the architecture. Imagine a finance employee asking an AI system to investigate an unusual invoice. The system might need to retrieve the invoice, identify the supplier, examine historical transactions, compare purchasing patterns, consult company policies, and determine whether the transaction should be escalated. None of these individual operations is particularly exotic. The complexity comes from combining them into a reliable workflow. The model therefore cannot be the entire system. A language model can reason over information and decide what it wants to do, but it does not inherently possess access to the enterprise’s transactional systems. It needs tools. Those tools need authentication. Authentication needs identity. The actions need authorization. The information needs trustworthy business context. The execution needs observability. And the resulting system needs governance. This is why enterprise agent architecture increasingly resembles distributed systems architecture rather than conventional chatbot architecture. The model is one component within a larger system. SAP’s architecture places the SAP Business AI Platform at the center of this environment. The platform combines capabilities for building AI applications and agents, grounding them in business context and data, and governing their lifecycle. SAP describes these three areas as Build, Contextualize and Reason, and Govern. That separation is significant because it recognizes that intelligence alone is not enough. An enterprise agent that produces an impressive response but operates on stale data, has excessive permissions, or cannot be audited is not necessarily a useful production system. Joule as an orchestration layer At the user-facing level, SAP’s architecture centers on Joule. It is tempting to think of Joule simply as SAP’s conversational AI interface, but the architecture described by SAP goes beyond that interpretation. Joule Work is positioned as a workspace in which users express goals and AI coordinates the work necessary to accomplish them across SAP and non-SAP systems. This creates a useful separation between intent and implementation. A user should not necessarily need to know which application contains the required information, which API needs to be called, or which sequence of operations has to occur. They express what they want to accomplish, while the orchestration layer determines how that objective can be fulfilled. Behind Joule Work are Joule Assistants and Joule Agents. Assistants coordinate AI capabilities around roles and business processes, while agents perform more specific multi-step tasks. The architecture also describes the Joule Orchestrator, or agent harness, as the reasoning and orchestration engine responsible for routing requests to agents and loading the tools and skills necessary to execute them. The distinction matters because orchestration is itself becoming a systems problem. Suppose an employee asks, “Find the delayed orders that could affect our most important customers and prepare the information I need for the account team.” There is no single function called find_delayed_orders_and_prepare_customer_brief. The system may need to discover the relevant data, reason about dependencies, invoke several capabilities, and combine their results. Some operations may be sequential, while others could potentially happen in parallel. Some may require human approval before the workflow continues. The orchestrator therefore becomes the mechanism that turns a high-level intent into an executable process. This is fundamentally different from asking a model to generate a paragraph. Building agents is becoming its own development discipline Once agents become part of enterprise software, developers need a structured way to build them. SAP’s answer is Joule Studio, an AI-native development environment for creating custom agents, applications and workflows. The reference architecture describes two development paths: a low-code flow using a browser-based visual builder and a pro-code flow using an IDE, the Joule Studio CLI, and a coding agent connected through MCP. Both approaches follow the same broader methodology: intent, requirements, specification, code generation, testing, and deployment. The emphasis on intent is interesting because it changes where development begins. Traditional software development often starts with an implementation question: Which APIs do we need? What database tables are involved? Which service should own the logic? An intent-oriented process starts one level higher: What outcome are we trying to achieve, and what should the system be capable of doing? That does not eliminate traditional engineering. An agent still needs reliable tools, security boundaries, testing, deployment mechanisms, and runtime infrastructure. Instead, it adds another layer of abstraction in which the desired behavior becomes part of the development process. For enterprise AI, that abstraction can be particularly useful because business processes are often more stable and meaningful than the individual technical operations used to implement them.
