items.title: A 1M-Token Context Window Holds 4 MB of Docs — But Only 1.8 MB of Your Logs
items.summary: Megabytes of real material that fit in a 1,000,000-token context window, measured with Qwen's own tokenizer, 1 September 2026. Chart: Decoding AI. Filling a 1M-token window costs about $0.15 — but logs burn through it 2.2x faster than prose, so the honest unit is dollars per megabyte. Two labs shipped million-token context windows for pennies in the same week. So we tokenized 3.7 MB of real files with Qwen’s actual tokenizer to answer the question nobody was answering: filling a one-million-token window costs roughly $0.15–$0.16 once, but the material you’d actually put in it — logs, traces, stack dumps — burns through that window 2.2× faster than prose, which means the honest unit isn’t tokens at all. It’s dollars per megabyte. The pitch for a million-token context window is always the same picture: your whole codebase, your whole incident, your whole quarter of Slack, dropped into one prompt. Nobody has to chunk anything. Retrieval becomes optional. Then you run it on a Tuesday against a real incident, and the window fills before you’ve finished pasting the logs. That gap — between “1M tokens” as a spec-sheet number and 1M tokens as a container for the specific bytes you own — is where the money hides. And the odd thing is that despite a week of launch coverage in late August 2026, we could not find anyone who had measured it. Every post reported the price per million tokens. None reported what a million tokens actually holds. So we measured it. Here is the number that matters: on Qwen’s own tokenizer, one million tokens holds 3.96 MB of English technical prose but only 1.82 MB of machine logs. Same window, same price, less than half the material. If you are pointing a long-context model at operational data, you are paying about $0.082 per megabyte instead of $0.038 — and no pricing page anywhere tells you that. Key takeaways We measured 3.71 MB of real files with the Qwen2 tokenizer (vocab 151,936, exact round-trip verified) on 1 September 2026. English technical prose came in at 4.15 bytes per token; machine logs at 1.91 bytes per token — a 2.17× density gap between the two. A 1M-token window therefore holds ~3.96 MB of docs, ~4.01 MB of Python, ~3.77 MB of JSON, ~3.36 MB of C headers, and ~1.82 MB of logs. Logs are the worst case, and logs are exactly what long-context marketing invites you to paste. GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next both launched 26 August 2026 , both reaching a 1M-token context, at roughly $0.15–$0.16 per million input tokens per Artificial Analysis’ model page and DataCamp’s side-by-side comparison . Cached input is where the real leverage sits, not context length. On the published rates, cached input runs 5× cheaper on GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.03 vs $0.15) and 10× cheaper on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ($0.016 vs $0.16). A 200k-token context re-read 40× a day for a month is $26.40 uncached and $5.28 cached on the former — the same workload, an 80% swing. The useful unit for capacity planning is dollars per megabyte of your data, not dollars per million tokens. We publish the conversion below so you can compute it for your own corpus. TL;DR Two cheap million-token models shipped on the same day, and the coverage all priced them in tokens. Tokens are the vendor’s unit, not yours. We tokenized five kinds of real material with the actual Qwen tokenizer and found the byte-to-token ratio swings by more than 2×, with machine logs — the single most common thing people want to dump into a giant window — being the densest and therefore the most expensive per megabyte. The context window did not get cheap for everyone equally. It got cheap for prose and mid-priced for code and it is still expensive for telemetry. Budget in MB, cache aggressively, and stop treating “1M tokens” as a volume you understand. What actually shipped in late August 2026 On 26 August 2026 , two flash-tier models landed within hours of each other. GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai): a multimodal mixture-of-experts model, reported at 320B total parameters with roughly 18B active per token, reaching a 1M-token context , at a published $0.15 input / $0.50 output / $0.03 cached input per million tokens. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Alibaba): reported at 125B parameters plus a 51B-parameter n-gram embedding table with roughly 6B active per token , a 262,144-token native window extensible toward 1M , at $0.15–$0.16 input / $0.47 output per million tokens, with a cache-hit discount reported around 89%. Two independent write-ups agree on the shape of this — the DataCamp comparison and the Artificial Analysis model page , the latter also reporting 88.6 output tokens/sec and a 2.57s time-to-first-token for the Qwen model. Sources differ slightly on the exact input price ($0.15 vs $0.16) and on licensing terms, so we’ve used the range rather than picking a number, and we’re leaving licence claims alone entirely until the primary terms settle. What matters for this piece is only this: a million tokens of context now costs about fifteen cents , once. That is genuinely new. And it makes the second question — a million tokens of what? — the only interesting one left. How much does it cost to fill a 1M-token context window? About $0.15 to $0.16 to fill it once with fresh input tokens, on either of the two models that shipped on 26 August 2026, and about $0.016 to $0.03 if that same content is served from the provider’s prompt cache. But the per-fill price is misleading on its own, because the window is measured in tokens and your data is measured in bytes, and the exchange rate between them is not fixed. On our measurements it ranges from 1.91 to 4.20 bytes per token depending on content type — so the same $0.15 buys you 3.96 MB of documentation or 1.82 MB of logs. Price your workload in dollars per megabyte of your own corpus, not dollars per million tokens. How we measured it We wanted numbers from the real tokenizer, not an estimate from the usual “≈4 characters per token” folklore. Method (1 September 2026): Pulled the Qwen2 vocabulary — 151,936 tokens and 151,387 merges — from the vocab fixture published in the llama.cpp repository. Qwen3.x models use this tokenizer family. Rebuilt it as a byte-level BPE tokenizer with Qwen2’s pre-tokenization split pattern, using the HuggingFace tokenizers library. Verified correctness by exact round-trip : encode → decode returned the original string byte-for-byte across prose, Python, JSON and mixed-Unicode samples. A tokenizer that round-trips exactly is a tokenizer that is splitting correctly. Assembled five corpora from real files on a standard Linux image — no synthetic text, nothing hand-tuned: CPython standard-library sources, Markdown documentation shipped inside installed packages, JSON schemas and SBOMs, system C headers, and the machine’s own dpkg/apt/bootstrap logs. Encoded each corpus whole and divided. Sample size: 3,733,777 bytes across 176 files , in corpora of roughly 0.8–1.1 MB each. Everything below is a measured ratio, not a projection. The one thing we did not do is measure GLM-5.3-Flash’s own tokenizer, so treat the numbers as Qwen-family; the direction of the effect will hold on any byte-level BPE, but the exact ratios will move a little. The actual run. roundtrip_ok True is the correctness check: encode then decode returned every sample byte-for-byte. Machine logs, highlighted, are the outlier at 1.91 bytes per token. Screenshot: Decoding AI. The actual run. roundtrip_ok True is the correctness check — encode then decode returned every sample byte-for-byte, which is how we know the tokenizer is splitting the way Qwen's does. Machine logs, highlighted, are the outlier at 1.91 bytes per token. The result: logs eat the window 2.2× faster Measured bytes per token, and the megabytes that fit in a 1M-token window: Python source code — 4.20 bytes/token → 4.01 MB per 1M tokens English technical prose (Markdown docs) — 4.15 bytes/token → 3.96 MB JSON documents (schemas, SBOMs, config) — 3.96 bytes/token → 3.77 MB C / C++ headers — 3.52 bytes/token → 3.36 MB Machine logs (dpkg / apt / bootstrap) — 1.91 bytes/token → 1.82 MB Prose and logs differ by 2.17× in token density. The window doesn’t change size. Your data changes size inside it. Converted into the unit that actually shows up on an invoice — dollars per megabyte of source material, at the published full input price: English prose: ~$0.038/MB (GLM-5.3-Flash) · ~$0.040/MB (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) Python: ~$0.037/MB · ~$0.040/MB JSON: ~$0.040/MB · ~$0.042/MB C headers: ~$0.045/MB · ~$0.048/MB Machine logs: ~$0.082/MB · ~$0.088/MB Reading a gigabyte of logs through one of these models costs on the order of $82–$88 at list price. Reading a gigabyte of documentation costs about $38–$40 . Same model, same window, same nominal price per token — a 2.2× difference in what you pay to look at your own data. Why are logs so much more token-dense than prose? Because byte-level BPE merges are learned from natural text, and logs are barely natural text. A timestamp like 2026-09-01 10:08:47 is a run of digits and punctuation with almost no reusable multi-character merges available — digits tokenize close to one-per-character, and separators break merges that would otherwise span them. Add hex IDs, UUIDs, file paths, version strings and status codes, and you get a stream where the tokenizer's learned vocabulary almost never applies. English prose is the opposite case: common words are single tokens because the merge table was built to make them single tokens. The 2.17× gap isn't a quirk of our sample — it's the tokenizer working exactly as designed on material it was never optimized for. Dollars per megabyte on GLM-5.3-Flash, cached input versus full input price, by content type. Computed from published list rates, 1 September 2026. Chart: Decoding AI. The practical consequence: the more machine-generated your data, the worse your effective context window. Traces, metrics, event streams and database dumps are all in the log family. That is most of what an operations-facing agent looks at. The number that decides your bill isn’t context length. It’s cache hit rate. Here is the comparison that changed how we’d budget this. Take a modest agent loop: a 200,000-token working context, re-read 40 times a day, 22 working days a month. Not a million-token showpiece — an ordinary one. GLM-5.3-Flash: $26.40/month uncached → $5.28/month fully cached (5×) Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: $28.16/month uncached → $2.82/month fully cached (10×) The delta between a well-cached and a poorly-cached implementation of the same workload is $21–$25 a month per loop , which sounds trivial until you multiply by the number of concurrent agents in a real deployment. Doubling your context window changes your bill by 2×. Fixing your cache hit rate changes it by 5–10×. Almost all of the launch coverage discussed the first number and none of it discussed the second. And cache hit rate is a structural property of how you build the prompt, not a setting. Put the stable material — system instructions, schemas, the codebase — at the front, unchanged, byte-for-byte, every call. Put the volatile material at the end. Every byte you change near the top invalidates everything after it. We learned this the hard way while instrumenting agent loops for our write-up on multiple agents sharing one codebase , where per-agent prompt preambles differed by a single ID and destroyed cache reuse across the fleet. Steelman: “just don’t put raw logs in the context” The strongest objection to everything above is that nobody sensible pastes a gigabyte of raw logs into a model. You filter, you deduplicate, you extract the error lines, and you send a few hundred kilobytes of relevant material. On that account our log number is a strawman. That objection is largely right, and it’s the reason we’re not claiming long context is a bad deal. But it concedes the actual point: if you have to build a filtering pipeline before the context window is affordable, the window did not remove your retrieval layer — it just moved it. The million-token pitch is specifically that you can stop pre-processing. Our measurement says that for the densest and most operationally common data type, you can’t, or at least not without paying 2.2× for the privilege. There’s also a second-order cost the objection skips: the filter is now a component that can drop the one line that mattered, which is the failure mode retrieval systems have always had. So the honest position is narrower than either pitch. Long context genuinely removes chunking for prose and source code. For telemetry it changes the economics of your filter, not its existence. What we’d actually do with this Five things, in order of payoff: Measure your own bytes-per-token before you budget. Take 1 MB of your real corpus, run it through the tokenizer of the model you’re buying, and divide. It takes ten minutes and it is the only number that makes a capacity plan real. Budget in MB, quote in MB. “We can hold 1.8 MB of production logs for $0.15 a pass” is a sentence a finance team can evaluate. “1M-token context” is not. Treat cache hit rate as a first-class SLO. Instrument it. A loop that silently drops from 90% to 30% cache hits gets ~4× more expensive with no change in behaviour and no alert. Order the prompt by volatility , stable content first. This is free and it is the single highest-leverage change available. Strip structurally, not semantically, before pasting telemetry. Collapsing repeated timestamp prefixes and normalising UUIDs recovers a large fraction of the density penalty without a model deciding what’s relevant. If you’re choosing between two of these models rather than budgeting for one, the same discipline applies to the swap itself — we found that switching providers is rarely the drop-in that routing layers imply , and tokenizer differences are one more thing that quietly moves when you change the engine underneath. Frequently asked questions How many pages is a 1M-token context window? For ordinary English prose, roughly 3.96 MB of text, which is on the order of 1,500–2,000 pages of plain writing depending on formatting. For machine logs it’s about 1.82 MB, which sounds like a lot until you notice a busy service can produce that in minutes. The page-count framing is only meaningful for prose; for structured or machine-generated data, measure bytes instead. Is a bigger context window cheaper than retrieval? For prose and source code at $0.15 per million input tokens, often yes — the engineering cost of building and maintaining a retrieval pipeline is real and recurring. For high-volume telemetry, usually no, because token density is 2.17× worse and the volume is unbounded. The break-even depends on how often you re-read the same context, which is really a question about your cache hit rate. Why does the same text cost different amounts on different models? Because each model family has its own tokenizer with its own learned merge table, so the same bytes become different numbers of tokens. Differences of 10–20% between tokenizer families on the same corpus are normal, which means a model that looks 10% cheaper per token can be more expensive per megabyte of your actual data. Does prompt caching apply to the whole context window? Typically only to a stable prefix, matched from the start of the prompt. That’s why prompt ordering matters so much: changing a byte early in the prompt invalidates the cached prefix from that point on. On the published rates for these two models, losing that prefix costs 5–10× on input. One question before you go If you’ve run a long-context model against your own production data: what was your measured bytes-per-token, and on which corpus? We’d like to collect real numbers across content types rather than keep repeating the “4 characters per token” folklore — drop yours in the responses with the model and data type, and we’ll compile what comes in. Sources & References Artificial Analysis: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model page — release date, context window, pricing, throughput DataCamp: GLM-5.3-Flash vs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — parameter counts, context windows, input/output/cached pricing llm-stats: GLM-5.3-Flash launch analysis — launch details and positioning The Neuron’s 31 August 2026 daily digest — corroborating roundup of the week’s flash-tier releases Tokenizer fixture: the Qwen2 vocabulary published in the llama.cpp model fixtures (151,936 tokens / 151,387 merges) Our own measurement, 1 September 2026: 3,733,777 bytes across 176 files, five corpora, Qwen2 byte-level BPE, exact round-trip verified Related from us Multiple AI agents on the same codebase: we reproduced the turf war with zero AI MCP vs A2A: we diffed both agent protocol specs Claude’s protein design hit rate was 26.8% — and one target returned 0 for 90 Nvidia’s AVO scored 100% on ARC-AGI-3 — but the model only scores 30% Written by Decoding AI . We take one AI story a day, run the number nobody ran, and publish what we actually measured — including when it contradicts us. A 1M-Token Context Window Holds 4 MB of Docs — But Only 1.8 MB of Your Logs was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Megabytes of real material that fit in a 1,000,000-token context window, measured with Qwen's own tokenizer, 1 September 2026. Chart: Decoding AI.

Filling a 1M-token window costs about $0.15 — but logs burn through it 2.2x faster than prose, so the honest unit is dollars per megabyte.

Two labs shipped million-token context windows for pennies in the same week. So we tokenized 3.7 MB of real files with Qwen’s actual tokenizer to answer the question nobody was answering: filling a one-million-token window costs roughly $0.15–$0.16 once, but the material you’d actually put in it — logs, traces, stack dumps — burns through that window 2.2× faster than prose, which means the honest unit isn’t tokens at all. It’s dollars per megabyte.

The pitch for a million-token context window is always the same picture: your whole codebase, your whole incident, your whole quarter of Slack, dropped into one prompt. Nobody has to chunk anything. Retrieval becomes optional.

Then you run it on a Tuesday against a real incident, and the window fills before you’ve finished pasting the logs.

That gap — between “1M tokens” as a spec-sheet number and 1M tokens as a container for the specific bytes you own — is where the money hides. And the odd thing is that despite a week of launch coverage in late August 2026, we could not find anyone who had measured it. Every post reported the price per million tokens. None reported what a million tokens actually holds.

So we measured it. Here is the number that matters: on Qwen’s own tokenizer, one million tokens holds 3.96 MB of English technical prose but only 1.82 MB of machine logs. Same window, same price, less than half the material. If you are pointing a long-context model at operational data, you are paying about $0.082 per megabyte instead of $0.038 — and no pricing page anywhere tells you that.

Key takeaways
  • We measured 3.71 MB of real files with the Qwen2 tokenizer (vocab 151,936, exact round-trip verified) on 1 September 2026. English technical prose came in at 4.15 bytes per token; machine logs at 1.91 bytes per token — a 2.17× density gap between the two.
  • A 1M-token window therefore holds ~3.96 MB of docs, ~4.01 MB of Python, ~3.77 MB of JSON, ~3.36 MB of C headers, and ~1.82 MB of logs. Logs are the worst case, and logs are exactly what long-context marketing invites you to paste.
  • GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next both launched 26 August 2026, both reaching a 1M-token context, at roughly $0.15–$0.16 per million input tokens per Artificial Analysis’ model page and DataCamp’s side-by-side comparison.
  • Cached input is where the real leverage sits, not context length. On the published rates, cached input runs 5× cheaper on GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.03 vs $0.15) and 10× cheaper on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ($0.016 vs $0.16). A 200k-token context re-read 40× a day for a month is $26.40 uncached and $5.28 cached on the former — the same workload, an 80% swing.
  • The useful unit for capacity planning is dollars per megabyte of your data, not dollars per million tokens. We publish the conversion below so you can compute it for your own corpus.
TL;DR

Two cheap million-token models shipped on the same day, and the coverage all priced them in tokens. Tokens are the vendor’s unit, not yours. We tokenized five kinds of real material with the actual Qwen tokenizer and found the byte-to-token ratio swings by more than 2×, with machine logs — the single most common thing people want to dump into a giant window — being the densest and therefore the most expensive per megabyte. The context window did not get cheap for everyone equally. It got cheap for prose and mid-priced for code and it is still expensive for telemetry. Budget in MB, cache aggressively, and stop treating “1M tokens” as a volume you understand.

What actually shipped in late August 2026

On 26 August 2026, two flash-tier models landed within hours of each other.

  • GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai): a multimodal mixture-of-experts model, reported at 320B total parameters with roughly 18B active per token, reaching a 1M-token context, at a published $0.15 input / $0.50 output / $0.03 cached input per million tokens.
  • Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Alibaba): reported at 125B parameters plus a 51B-parameter n-gram embedding table with roughly 6B active per token, a 262,144-token native window extensible toward 1M, at $0.15–$0.16 input / $0.47 output per million tokens, with a cache-hit discount reported around 89%.

Two independent write-ups agree on the shape of this — the DataCamp comparison and the Artificial Analysis model page, the latter also reporting 88.6 output tokens/sec and a 2.57s time-to-first-token for the Qwen model. Sources differ slightly on the exact input price ($0.15 vs $0.16) and on licensing terms, so we’ve used the range rather than picking a number, and we’re leaving licence claims alone entirely until the primary terms settle.

What matters for this piece is only this: a million tokens of context now costs about fifteen cents, once. That is genuinely new. And it makes the second question — a million tokens of what? — the only interesting one left.

How much does it cost to fill a 1M-token context window?

About $0.15 to $0.16 to fill it once with fresh input tokens, on either of the two models that shipped on 26 August 2026, and about $0.016 to $0.03 if that same content is served from the provider’s prompt cache. But the per-fill price is misleading on its own, because the window is measured in tokens and your data is measured in bytes, and the exchange rate between them is not fixed. On our measurements it ranges from 1.91 to 4.20 bytes per token depending on content type — so the same $0.15 buys you 3.96 MB of documentation or 1.82 MB of logs. Price your workload in dollars per megabyte of your own corpus, not dollars per million tokens.

How we measured it

We wanted numbers from the real tokenizer, not an estimate from the usual “≈4 characters per token” folklore.

Method (1 September 2026):

  1. Pulled the Qwen2 vocabulary — 151,936 tokens and 151,387 merges — from the vocab fixture published in the llama.cpp repository. Qwen3.x models use this tokenizer family.
  2. Rebuilt it as a byte-level BPE tokenizer with Qwen2’s pre-tokenization split pattern, using the HuggingFace tokenizers library.
  3. Verified correctness by exact round-trip: encode → decode returned the original string byte-for-byte across prose, Python, JSON and mixed-Unicode samples. A tokenizer that round-trips exactly is a tokenizer that is splitting correctly.
  4. Assembled five corpora from real files on a standard Linux image — no synthetic text, nothing hand-tuned: CPython standard-library sources, Markdown documentation shipped inside installed packages, JSON schemas and SBOMs, system C headers, and the machine’s own dpkg/apt/bootstrap logs.
  5. Encoded each corpus whole and divided.

Sample size: 3,733,777 bytes across 176 files, in corpora of roughly 0.8–1.1 MB each. Everything below is a measured ratio, not a projection. The one thing we did not do is measure GLM-5.3-Flash’s own tokenizer, so treat the numbers as Qwen-family; the direction of the effect will hold on any byte-level BPE, but the exact ratios will move a little.

The actual run. roundtrip_ok True is the correctness check: encode then decode returned every sample byte-for-byte. Machine logs, highlighted, are the outlier at 1.91 bytes per token. Screenshot: Decoding AI.

The actual run. roundtrip_ok True is the correctness check — encode then decode returned every sample byte-for-byte, which is how we know the tokenizer is splitting the way Qwen's does. Machine logs, highlighted, are the outlier at 1.91 bytes per token.

The result: logs eat the window 2.2× faster

Measured bytes per token, and the megabytes that fit in a 1M-token window:

  • Python source code — 4.20 bytes/token → 4.01 MB per 1M tokens
  • English technical prose (Markdown docs) — 4.15 bytes/token → 3.96 MB
  • JSON documents (schemas, SBOMs, config) — 3.96 bytes/token → 3.77 MB
  • C / C++ headers — 3.52 bytes/token → 3.36 MB
  • Machine logs (dpkg / apt / bootstrap) — 1.91 bytes/token → 1.82 MB
Prose and logs differ by 2.17× in token density. The window doesn’t change size. Your data changes size inside it.

Converted into the unit that actually shows up on an invoice — dollars per megabyte of source material, at the published full input price:

  • English prose: ~$0.038/MB (GLM-5.3-Flash) · ~$0.040/MB (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next)
  • Python: ~$0.037/MB · ~$0.040/MB
  • JSON: ~$0.040/MB · ~$0.042/MB
  • C headers: ~$0.045/MB · ~$0.048/MB
  • Machine logs: ~$0.082/MB · ~$0.088/MB

Reading a gigabyte of logs through one of these models costs on the order of $82–$88 at list price. Reading a gigabyte of documentation costs about $38–$40. Same model, same window, same nominal price per token — a 2.2× difference in what you pay to look at your own data.

Why are logs so much more token-dense than prose?

Because byte-level BPE merges are learned from natural text, and logs are barely natural text. A timestamp like 2026-09-01 10:08:47 is a run of digits and punctuation with almost no reusable multi-character merges available — digits tokenize close to one-per-character, and separators break merges that would otherwise span them. Add hex IDs, UUIDs, file paths, version strings and status codes, and you get a stream where the tokenizer's learned vocabulary almost never applies. English prose is the opposite case: common words are single tokens because the merge table was built to make them single tokens. The 2.17× gap isn't a quirk of our sample — it's the tokenizer working exactly as designed on material it was never optimized for.

Dollars per megabyte on GLM-5.3-Flash, cached input versus full input price, by content type. Computed from published list rates, 1 September 2026. Chart: Decoding AI.

The practical consequence: the more machine-generated your data, the worse your effective context window. Traces, metrics, event streams and database dumps are all in the log family. That is most of what an operations-facing agent looks at.

The number that decides your bill isn’t context length. It’s cache hit rate.

Here is the comparison that changed how we’d budget this.

Take a modest agent loop: a 200,000-token working context, re-read 40 times a day, 22 working days a month. Not a million-token showpiece — an ordinary one.

  • GLM-5.3-Flash: $26.40/month uncached → $5.28/month fully cached (5×)
  • Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: $28.16/month uncached → $2.82/month fully cached (10×)

The delta between a well-cached and a poorly-cached implementation of the same workload is $21–$25 a month per loop, which sounds trivial until you multiply by the number of concurrent agents in a real deployment. Doubling your context window changes your bill by 2×. Fixing your cache hit rate changes it by 5–10×. Almost all of the launch coverage discussed the first number and none of it discussed the second.

And cache hit rate is a structural property of how you build the prompt, not a setting. Put the stable material — system instructions, schemas, the codebase — at the front, unchanged, byte-for-byte, every call. Put the volatile material at the end. Every byte you change near the top invalidates everything after it. We learned this the hard way while instrumenting agent loops for our write-up on multiple agents sharing one codebase, where per-agent prompt preambles differed by a single ID and destroyed cache reuse across the fleet.

Steelman: “just don’t put raw logs in the context”

The strongest objection to everything above is that nobody sensible pastes a gigabyte of raw logs into a model. You filter, you deduplicate, you extract the error lines, and you send a few hundred kilobytes of relevant material. On that account our log number is a strawman.

That objection is largely right, and it’s the reason we’re not claiming long context is a bad deal. But it concedes the actual point: if you have to build a filtering pipeline before the context window is affordable, the window did not remove your retrieval layer — it just moved it. The million-token pitch is specifically that you can stop pre-processing. Our measurement says that for the densest and most operationally common data type, you can’t, or at least not without paying 2.2× for the privilege. There’s also a second-order cost the objection skips: the filter is now a component that can drop the one line that mattered, which is the failure mode retrieval systems have always had.

So the honest position is narrower than either pitch. Long context genuinely removes chunking for prose and source code. For telemetry it changes the economics of your filter, not its existence.

What we’d actually do with this

Five things, in order of payoff:

  1. Measure your own bytes-per-token before you budget. Take 1 MB of your real corpus, run it through the tokenizer of the model you’re buying, and divide. It takes ten minutes and it is the only number that makes a capacity plan real.
  2. Budget in MB, quote in MB. “We can hold 1.8 MB of production logs for $0.15 a pass” is a sentence a finance team can evaluate. “1M-token context” is not.
  3. Treat cache hit rate as a first-class SLO. Instrument it. A loop that silently drops from 90% to 30% cache hits gets ~4× more expensive with no change in behaviour and no alert.
  4. Order the prompt by volatility, stable content first. This is free and it is the single highest-leverage change available.
  5. Strip structurally, not semantically, before pasting telemetry. Collapsing repeated timestamp prefixes and normalising UUIDs recovers a large fraction of the density penalty without a model deciding what’s relevant.

If you’re choosing between two of these models rather than budgeting for one, the same discipline applies to the swap itself — we found that switching providers is rarely the drop-in that routing layers imply, and tokenizer differences are one more thing that quietly moves when you change the engine underneath.

Frequently asked questions

How many pages is a 1M-token context window? For ordinary English prose, roughly 3.96 MB of text, which is on the order of 1,500–2,000 pages of plain writing depending on formatting. For machine logs it’s about 1.82 MB, which sounds like a lot until you notice a busy service can produce that in minutes. The page-count framing is only meaningful for prose; for structured or machine-generated data, measure bytes instead.

Is a bigger context window cheaper than retrieval? For prose and source code at $0.15 per million input tokens, often yes — the engineering cost of building and maintaining a retrieval pipeline is real and recurring. For high-volume telemetry, usually no, because token density is 2.17× worse and the volume is unbounded. The break-even depends on how often you re-read the same context, which is really a question about your cache hit rate.

Why does the same text cost different amounts on different models? Because each model family has its own tokenizer with its own learned merge table, so the same bytes become different numbers of tokens. Differences of 10–20% between tokenizer families on the same corpus are normal, which means a model that looks 10% cheaper per token can be more expensive per megabyte of your actual data.

Does prompt caching apply to the whole context window? Typically only to a stable prefix, matched from the start of the prompt. That’s why prompt ordering matters so much: changing a byte early in the prompt invalidates the cached prefix from that point on. On the published rates for these two models, losing that prefix costs 5–10× on input.

One question before you go

If you’ve run a long-context model against your own production data: what was your measured bytes-per-token, and on which corpus? We’d like to collect real numbers across content types rather than keep repeating the “4 characters per token” folklore — drop yours in the responses with the model and data type, and we’ll compile what comes in.

Sources & References
  • Artificial Analysis: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model page — release date, context window, pricing, throughput
  • DataCamp: GLM-5.3-Flash vs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — parameter counts, context windows, input/output/cached pricing
  • llm-stats: GLM-5.3-Flash launch analysis — launch details and positioning
  • The Neuron’s 31 August 2026 daily digest — corroborating roundup of the week’s flash-tier releases
  • Tokenizer fixture: the Qwen2 vocabulary published in the llama.cpp model fixtures (151,936 tokens / 151,387 merges)
  • Our own measurement, 1 September 2026: 3,733,777 bytes across 176 files, five corpora, Qwen2 byte-level BPE, exact round-trip verified
Related from us
  • Multiple AI agents on the same codebase: we reproduced the turf war with zero AI
  • MCP vs A2A: we diffed both agent protocol specs
  • Claude’s protein design hit rate was 26.8% — and one target returned 0 for 90
  • Nvidia’s AVO scored 100% on ARC-AGI-3 — but the model only scores 30%

Why Autonomous Trading Agents Blow Past Risk Limits: Architecting Gateway Validation for Financial APIsHow probabilistic string coercion in LLM tool calling triggers dangerous margin defaults on exchange endpoints, and how to build deterministic Pydantic execution proxies with automated circuit breakers.

Integrating Large Language Models into quantitative finance and algorithmic trade execution represents a major shift in enterprise automation. By connecting reasoning agents to real-time market feeds, macroeconomic data streams, and execution APIs (such as FIX protocol engines or REST/WebSocket exchange interfaces), financial institutions aim to automate discretionary routing, liquidity rebalancing, and tactical order execution.

However, granting generative models direct, ungoverned write access to order dispatch endpoints introduces severe systemic risk.

Consider an autonomous execution agent deployed to execute a structured portfolio rebalancing strategy. The agent evaluates order book depth and generates a tool call to establish a long position with a target leverage ratio of 1.5x.

During JSON serialization, the model outputs the parameter as a string ("leverage": "1.5") rather than a floating-point numeric value. The trading gateway, built on a permissive legacy framework, attempts type casting. Failing to parse the float cleanly, it falls back to a default configuration: the account's maximum margin multiplier of 100x.

The transaction executes cleanly. The exchange responds with 200 OK. Within minutes, a minor market retracement triggers an immediate multi-million-dollar liquidation event.

The failure was not caused by market volatility. It was a Silent Gateway Coercion Failure caused by placing a probabilistic model directly in front of a live order routing pipeline without deterministic risk validation.

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|               THE SILENT EXECUTION LIMIT BYPASS IN UNGOVERNED AGENT PIPELINES                    |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

[Market Strategy Agent] ──► Intended Order: $120,000 Notional @ 1.5x Leverage
                                    │
                                    ▼
  [LLM Tool Call Output]   ──► {"symbol": "BTC-USD", "notional": 120000, "leverage": "1.5"}
                                    │
                                    ▼
  [Permissive API Gateway] ──► Float string parsing fails ──► Defaults to MAX_LEVERAGE (100x)
                                    │
                                    ▼
  [Exchange Matching Engine]──► Dispatches Live Order: $12,000,000 Position (HTTP 200 OK)
                                    │
                                    ▼
  [Financial Impact]       ──► Catastrophic Immediate Liquidation on 1% Drawdown
1. Architectural Failure Vectors in Autonomous Execution Systems

Placing LLMs in autonomous trading and order routing loops exposes three fundamental failure vectors:

Failure Vector A: Probabilistic Tool Call Serialization

Language models do not possess an internal type system; they generate token sequences based on conditional probability distributions. When mapping unstructured reasoning into structured tool parameters (such as OrderRequest schemas), models frequently introduce subtle serialization anomalies:

  • Emitting numbers as strings (e.g., "2.0" instead of 2.0).
  • Truncating fractional precision (e.g., dropping sub-penny price offsets).
  • Swapping critical key-value pairings under context pressure.

When downstream order routing APIs lack strict type validation, these anomalies result in permissive fallback defaults that dramatically amplify trade risk.

Failure Vector B: Ingestion of Orders Without Out-of-Band Risk Verification

Traditional algorithmic execution systems enforce strict, multi-tiered Pre-Trade Risk Checks (PTRC) at the network layer.

When autonomous agents bypass centralized risk engines and interact directly with broker or exchange APIs via generic REST keys, organization-level constraints (such as single-order notional caps, maximum open position value, and gross leverage limits) are bypassed entirely.

Failure Vector C: Asynchronous State Desynchronization

In distributed multi-agent systems, execution agents operate asynchronously. If multiple sub-agents trigger simultaneous rebalancing orders across different asset classes, single-order limit checks fail to account for aggregate systemic exposure, resulting in massive cumulative over-leveraging.

2. The Deterministic Governance Architecture

To eliminate execution limit bypasses and guarantee zero unauthorized risk expansion, financial agent architectures must implement Strict Gateway Pydantic Contracts combined with Hardware-Enforced Execution Circuit Breakers.

            STATEFUL FINANCIAL EXECUTION CONTROL TOWER
                 
       [Autonomous Trading Strategy Agent] (Generates Trade Intent)
                                  │
                                  ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       GATEWAY PYDANTIC VALIDATION PROXY                     │
│  • Enforce Strict Numeric Typing (No String Coercion Allowed)               │
│  • Forbid Extra Unregistered Payload Keys (`extra="forbid"`)                │
│  • Validate Bounded Ranges for Leverage, Notional Value & Slippage          │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    OUT-OF-BAND PRE-TRADE RISK ENGINE                        │
│  • Verify Aggregate Portfolio Gross / Net Leverage Caps                     │
│  • Check Single-Order Notional Limits vs. Account Equity                    │
│  • Acquire Global Distributed Mutex Lock (Prevent Race Conditions)          │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                         [All Pre-Trade Checks Passed?]
                                  /       \
                              YES/         \NO
                                ▼           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│     TWO-PHASE ORDER DISPATCH GATE      │  │    EXECUTION CIRCUIT BREAKER    │
│  • Commit to Isolated Audit Ledger     │  │  • Halt Order Dispatch          │
│  • Sign Cryptographic Risk Token       │  │  • Freeze Agent Execution Pipe  │
│  • Dispatch Atomic FIX / REST Request  │  │  • Emit Critical Risk Pager Alert│
└──────────────────┬─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  EXCHANGE MATCHING ENGINE / ORDER BOOK                      │
│                    Live Order Executed Safely within Risk                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
3. Production Implementation: Gateway Schema Validation & Pre-Trade Risk Circuit Breaker

The following Python implementation demonstrates how an enterprise control tower validates financial execution payloads with strict Pydantic models, verifies portfolio-level leverage limits, and halts execution instantly on schema or risk violations:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator, ConfigDict
from typing import Optional, Literal
from decimal import Decimal
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger("FinancialExecutionControlTower")

class OrderSide(str):
    BUY = "BUY"
    SELL = "SELL"

class StrictTradeIntent(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True, strict=True)
    account_id: str = Field(..., min_length=4)
    symbol: str = Field(..., pattern=r"^[A-Z0-9]{2,10}-[A-Z0-9]{2,10}$")
    side: Literal["BUY", "SELL"]
    notional_usd: Decimal = Field(..., gt=Decimal("0.0"), le=Decimal("1000000.0"))
    leverage_multiplier: Decimal = Field(..., ge=Decimal("1.0"), le=Decimal("3.0"))
    max_slippage_pct: Decimal = Field(..., ge=Decimal("0.0001"), le=Decimal("0.05"))
    @field_validator("leverage_multiplier")
    @classmethod
    def validate_strict_leverage(cls, v: Decimal) -> Decimal:
        if v > Decimal("3.0"):
            raise ValueError(f"Leverage {v}x breaches maximum permissible mandate of 3.0x.")
        return v

class FinancialExecutionGateway:
    def __init__(self, current_account_equity_usd: Decimal, current_open_exposure_usd: Decimal):
        self.account_equity = current_account_equity_usd
        self.current_exposure = current_open_exposure_usd
        self.max_portfolio_leverage = Decimal("4.0")
    def process_agent_trade_request(self, raw_tool_payload: dict) -> dict:
        """
        Intercepts LLM trade output, enforces strict Pydantic schema typing,
        and validates real-time pre-trade risk boundaries.
        """
        try:
            # Step 1: Strict Deterministic Schema Validation
            trade = StrictTradeIntent(**raw_tool_payload)
            # Step 2: Out-of-Band Pre-Trade Risk Evaluation
            proposed_position_size = trade.notional_usd * trade.leverage_multiplier
            projected_total_exposure = self.current_exposure + proposed_position_size
            projected_portfolio_leverage = projected_total_exposure / self.account_equity
            if projected_portfolio_leverage > self.max_portfolio_leverage:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Order rejected: Projected portfolio leverage {projected_portfolio_leverage:.2f}x "
                    f"exceeds firm limit {self.max_portfolio_leverage:.2f}x."
                )
            # Step 3: Two-Phase Commit to Execution Engine
            order_id = self._dispatch_to_exchange(trade)
            self.current_exposure = projected_total_exposure
            logger.info(
                f"SUCCESS: Dispatched order {order_id} for {trade.symbol} "
                f"(${proposed_position_size} exposure @ {trade.leverage_multiplier}x leverage)."
            )
            return {
                "status": "EXECUTED",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "projected_portfolio_leverage": float(projected_portfolio_leverage)
            }
        except Exception as e:
            # Step 4: Execution Circuit Breaker Trigger
            self._trip_execution_circuit_breaker(raw_tool_payload, str(e))
            return {
                "status": "CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED",
                "rejection_reason": str(e)
            }
    def _dispatch_to_exchange(self, trade: StrictTradeIntent) -> str:
        # In production: Dispatches signed order to FIX engine or exchange API
        return "ord_exec_88392194"
    def _trip_execution_circuit_breaker(self, raw_payload: dict, error_message: str) -> None:
        logger.error("CRITICAL: Financial Execution Circuit Breaker Tripped.")
        logger.error(f"Violation: {error_message}")
        logger.error(f"Corrupted Raw Payload: {raw_payload}")
        # In production: Lock trading pipe, freeze agent API token, alert Risk Desk
4. Architectural Comparison: Naive Tool Execution vs. Stateful Control TowersGoverning Autonomous Financial Labor

Large language models offer unprecedented reasoning capabilities for market analysis, but they cannot act as their own risk managers. Placing probabilistic generators in direct control of order routing infrastructure creates severe systemic exposure.

Governing high-stakes FinTech AI requires deterministic infrastructure: enforcing strict schema boundaries at the gateway, conducting out-of-band pre-trade risk checks, and locking execution pipelines the instant an anomaly is detected.

Published by Maya Lin

On the team at Claire By The Algorithm

items.title: People Are Telling Their Darkest Thoughts to AI Without Realizing They Can Easily Become Public
items.summary: Talking to an AI chatbot can feel like confiding in a mirror, a private exchange equivalent to brainstorming in a Word document. Yet when it comes to the most popular AI chatbots, that mirror is really one-way glass — and you might be shocked to learn how many different people can watch from the other side. Since the rise of easily accessible AI chatbots, untold millions of people have happily fed AI models their deepest, darkest secrets. According to a recent survey conducted by browser company DuckDuckGo and flagged by CNET , a full third of all AI users admit to having told their chatbots a secret they wouldn’t tell the “trusted people” in their lives. There’s a grim irony there, because by telling an AI chatbot those closely guarded secrets, you may inadvertently be sharing intimate details with tech companies, police departments, lawyers, and even your boss. That’s according to new reporting by the Washington Post , which notes that there have been a dozen court cases where chatbot transcripts were cited in the public record over the last two years. Even if your transcripts don’t end up in the hands of Johnny Law, they can easily be obtained by your boss, assuming you’re using a company-provided AI service. And of course, there’s no telling how long AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic might hold onto details of your conversations, as WaPo notes numerous scenarios in which they may be required to hold onto your chatlogs by law. There’s also the grim possibility of leaks from the AI companies themselves. In July, it was revealed that a whole trove of chats with Anthropic’s chatbot Claude had been exposed to the open web — and not for the first time . “Unless you are having a chat with a service that has a temporary chat or, basically, an incognito version… [and] you’re also having it within a browser that’s not tracking you, the answer is no,” Jen King, a privacy researcher at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence told WaPo . “You can’t be sure that it’ll be totally private.” And though users are remarkably comfortable divulging those details to their favorite bot, fewer are aware of those myriad ways their chat logs might live on in perpetuity. According to the DuckDuckGo poll, 53 percent of regular users said they didn’t know that AI chatbots are training on data obtained through their conversation, while 75 percent didn’t realize that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can easily be subpoenaed by police. So when in doubt about whether to tell ChatGPT about your intimate relationship troubles , keep in mind that the internet is forever; and that goes double for AI chatbots. items.title: My husband and I run a large business while raising 3 kids. We don't believe in work-life balance, but 'radical prioritization.'
items.summary: The author (right) runs a business with her husband. Courtesy of Elaine Shi My husband and I own and run a large business together, while also raising three kids. We learned early on that work-life balance doesn't work for us, and we can never split things 50/50. We practice radical prioritization, which means we cut out everything except for work and kids. Just 21 days after my third child was born, I was taking VC calls . We were mid-Series A, and a fundraise does not pause for a newborn. The investor I pitched that day ended up leading our round. I'm not telling you this to inspire you. I tell you this so you know I'm speaking from experience when I say: work-life balance is fake. My husband Roy and I are the co-founders of BodySpec, a 125-person healthcare company that makes DEXA scans affordable. If you're on a GLP-1 and want to know whether you're losing fat or muscle, that's what we track. We've been busy these last couple of years. We're also raising three children: ages 7, 5, and 3. This is not the life I expected. As a millennial, I thought my marraige would be 50/50 I went to a blue-stocking all-girls private school in Manhattan that raised us on feminist ideas. Senior year, as we prepared for college, alumni came back to tell us what it was like to take classes with insufferable boys who loved to hear themselves talk. Six months later, at Harvard, I was dating one. As we approached adulthood together, I was certain our marriage would be 50/50. I had read "Lean In." I knew that doing your boyfriend's laundry in college was a gateway drug to doing everything, forever. But that wouldn't happen to me, I thought. I would have my own career, supported by an aligned partner who was equally competent at changing diapers, making lunches, and getting children through bedtime. For the record, Roy is that partner. He moves the kids through their schedules faster than I can. But as co-founders, our lives are not 50/50. We discovered years ago that 50/50 is a lie. My husband and I threw 'work-life balance' out the window The reality is that we take turns covering 90%. When I am fundraising, traveling, or attending evening events, Roy carries the family. When he is deep in a product sprint or an expansion problem, I do. Some weekends that means a three-on-one Mama marathon, or months when I'm the one doing both mornings and bedtimes. Beyond that, there was no 50/50 option available when the children were babies. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, and postpartum recovery were patently unfair. Roy was the one who set up my breast pump and showed me how to use it, but he still did not have to spend hours attached to it. Biology effectively gave him another 20 or 30 hours a week to think about the company. I could not compete. Did I resent it? Yes. But at some point, I realized that keeping score was useless. Resentment didn't actually put dinner on the table or finish the pitch deck. At worst, left to fester, it could end a marriage. The author runs BodySpec. Courtesy of Frances Hizon So I became the external founder, doing work that mostly happens during business hours. Roy took on product and technical work that could happen at night. Work-life balance also assumes that work is the draining part and "life" is where you recover. Anyone who has cared for multiple children knows this is not true. Childcare is many wonderful things. Restorative is usually not one of them. Comparatively, solo work trips feel like self-care. I can have pad thai all to myself, enjoy stimulating intellectual conversations with other adults, and even sneak in a massage on a lighter day. We use 'radical prioritization' instead We genuinely like working on Saturdays. The team isn't in, so the office is quiet and we're more productive. One of our older children comes along, usually our son. He is the middle child, bossed around by both his older and younger sisters. At the office, he can build LEGO sets without anyone destroying them and enjoy a peaceful one-on-one lunch with Mama. This is what we call radical reprioritization: we cut out everything else in our lives and blend the two most important facets to succeed in both. It's accepting a lopsided, demanding life to be both a successful leader and a deeply involved parent. Not everything will be 50/50. There will be sacrifices along the way — and you'll often have to blur the lines between work and life. Radical reprioritization does not feel like work stealing from family life. We do not talk about the company as the thing Dada or Mama is always choosing over the family. It is our family's company . Our children have grown up alongside it, and they beam with pride when they see our vans or stores. Finally, this life comes with sacrifices. Neither of us has personal hobbies. Whatever marginal free time we can find usually goes toward chasing our own wellness: lifting, walking, sleeping. There is not a lot of slack in the system, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. We are, in a traditional sense, wildly unbalanced. But both of us get to be serious founders and deeply involved parents. This is not the life I pictured at 17. It's lopsided, it's ours, and it's better than the one I was promised. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
The author (right) runs a business with her husband.

Courtesy of Elaine Shi

  • My husband and I own and run a large business together, while also raising three kids.
  • We learned early on that work-life balance doesn't work for us, and we can never split things 50/50.
  • We practice radical prioritization, which means we cut out everything except for work and kids.

Just 21 days after my third child was born, I was taking VC calls. We were mid-Series A, and a fundraise does not pause for a newborn. The investor I pitched that day ended up leading our round.

I'm not telling you this to inspire you. I tell you this so you know I'm speaking from experience when I say: work-life balance is fake.

My husband Roy and I are the co-founders of BodySpec, a 125-person healthcare company that makes DEXA scans affordable. If you're on a GLP-1 and want to know whether you're losing fat or muscle, that's what we track.

We've been busy these last couple of years. We're also raising three children: ages 7, 5, and 3. This is not the life I expected.

As a millennial, I thought my marraige would be 50/50

I went to a blue-stocking all-girls private school in Manhattan that raised us on feminist ideas. Senior year, as we prepared for college, alumni came back to tell us what it was like to take classes with insufferable boys who loved to hear themselves talk.

Six months later, at Harvard, I was dating one.

As we approached adulthood together, I was certain our marriage would be 50/50. I had read "Lean In." I knew that doing your boyfriend's laundry in college was a gateway drug to doing everything, forever. But that wouldn't happen to me, I thought. I would have my own career, supported by an aligned partner who was equally competent at changing diapers, making lunches, and getting children through bedtime.

For the record, Roy is that partner. He moves the kids through their schedules faster than I can.

But as co-founders, our lives are not 50/50. We discovered years ago that 50/50 is a lie.

My husband and I threw 'work-life balance' out the window

The reality is that we take turns covering 90%. When I am fundraising, traveling, or attending evening events, Roy carries the family. When he is deep in a product sprint or an expansion problem, I do. Some weekends that means a three-on-one Mama marathon, or months when I'm the one doing both mornings and bedtimes.

Beyond that, there was no 50/50 option available when the children were babies. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, and postpartum recovery were patently unfair. Roy was the one who set up my breast pump and showed me how to use it, but he still did not have to spend hours attached to it. Biology effectively gave him another 20 or 30 hours a week to think about the company. I could not compete.

Did I resent it? Yes. But at some point, I realized that keeping score was useless. Resentment didn't actually put dinner on the table or finish the pitch deck. At worst, left to fester, it could end a marriage.

The author runs BodySpec.

Courtesy of Frances Hizon

So I became the external founder, doing work that mostly happens during business hours. Roy took on product and technical work that could happen at night.

Work-life balance also assumes that work is the draining part and "life" is where you recover. Anyone who has cared for multiple children knows this is not true. Childcare is many wonderful things. Restorative is usually not one of them.

Comparatively, solo work trips feel like self-care. I can have pad thai all to myself, enjoy stimulating intellectual conversations with other adults, and even sneak in a massage on a lighter day.

We use 'radical prioritization' instead

We genuinely like working on Saturdays. The team isn't in, so the office is quiet and we're more productive. One of our older children comes along, usually our son. He is the middle child, bossed around by both his older and younger sisters. At the office, he can build LEGO sets without anyone destroying them and enjoy a peaceful one-on-one lunch with Mama.

This is what we call radical reprioritization: we cut out everything else in our lives and blend the two most important facets to succeed in both. It's accepting a lopsided, demanding life to be both a successful leader and a deeply involved parent. Not everything will be 50/50. There will be sacrifices along the way — and you'll often have to blur the lines between work and life.

Radical reprioritization does not feel like work stealing from family life.

We do not talk about the company as the thing Dada or Mama is always choosing over the family. It is our family's company. Our children have grown up alongside it, and they beam with pride when they see our vans or stores.

Finally, this life comes with sacrifices. Neither of us has personal hobbies. Whatever marginal free time we can find usually goes toward chasing our own wellness: lifting, walking, sleeping. There is not a lot of slack in the system, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. We are, in a traditional sense, wildly unbalanced.

But both of us get to be serious founders and deeply involved parents.

This is not the life I pictured at 17. It's lopsided, it's ours, and it's better than the one I was promised.

items.title: I was the PTA mom who did everything. Then I decided my son needed me more.
items.summary: The author said she spent years volunteering at her son's schools; now she's showing up for him in a different way. Courtesy of Nina McCollum. I was very involved with school activities when my son was in elementary school. Personal challenges changed how I prioritized time with my child and made me rethink my efforts. After the first band booster meeting, I elected not to join. I have no regrets. I am the mom of an only child , and my 17-year-old son is a senior this year. I've always tried to volunteer and get involved to help out and enrich his school experience, but in recent years, I've scaled back. When he started high school and joined the marching band in ninth grade, I no longer wanted to be scurrying around on the sidelines, taking care of things for everyone else's kids. I wanted to focus on my kid. So that's what I did. I took a step back and actually enjoyed watching my kid do something that he loved. Now, he's a senior, and I have no regrets. I've put in my time I was very active in the PTA when he was in elementary school. I organized the twice-yearly dinners for teachers and staff during parent-teacher conference nights, arranging food and desserts and soliciting volunteers to help set up, serve, and tear down. Then came middle school and COVID-19. My focus shifted to my kid and how to get him through tough times. I created "Mom's Summer Camp" when his camp was closed, and I wanted to focus on being there for him during these transitional years. When he started high school, I was going through a rough time personally, and I had to fight to find time and energy to show up for him. My mom, who had previously been enjoying an independent retirement life, started having some medical issues that required a lot of continued assistance from me. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. The PTA mom has left the building The mom I had been in elementary school was gone. I felt guilty at first for not joining the Band Boosters, the parent group (mostly moms) who run every band event and fundraising activity. I went to the first meeting, and they described the enormous amount of work each year — chaperoning bus trips, running raffles, working the twice-yearly hoagie fundraiser, and manning the parking lots. While there are a few moments when even the booster moms get to watch the halftime show, the rest of the time they are working, cleaning up the bleachers, passing out food to the kids after the halftime show, or hawking raffle tickets in the stands. I couldn't do it. Not with everything going on with my mom. Plus my son is my only kid. I simply wanted to be there, to show up to the football games, sit in the bleachers, cheer for the team, and scream as loud as I could when the best band in the land took the field at halftime. Home, away, rain or shine, I wanted to show my son that even during chaotic personal times, I was the mom he could count on to show up. Fighting for time I had to fight hard to be there for him. With emergency after emergency related to my mother's physical and mental health , I haven't had a perfect record. I had to miss a whole game one year while I was in the ER with my mom. I called in favors from friends to make sure he got to school in time for the games I had to miss or when I would have to arrive late. But I showed up. After crying in the car about my mom, I'd fix my makeup, speed walk to the stadium, buy a soda and popcorn, and scream with delight during the halftime show. The author said she always sits in the same area at games, so her son knows where to look for her when he is performing with the marching band. Courtesy of Nina McCollum. I always sit in the same area. He knows where to look for me. All I see is the pure joy of what he's doing, and I'm so glad he's able to have that and count on me. The booster parents do great, important work, but I know my kid needs my attention from the stands. Every first is a last when you have an only child. These are the only years I get to be a band parent. This final year as a band mom will be bittersweet. Each year, after the last home game, outside the band room, the underclassmen and parents of seniors form a pathway for the senior band members to run through when they exit for the last time, one by one. They line both sides of the path as the seniors run, dance, strut, or simply walk out the band door that final time, and into their future. My heart caught in my throat watching the 2026 seniors exit, knowing that the next time I see this happen, it will be my son's turn. I don't know how I'll get through it emotionally, but I can tell you this much. When he exits that band door for the last time, I won't be inside counting raffle tickets or directing cars in the parking lot. I'll be outside that door cheering him on (and let's admit it, probably crying). For me, that's my job. Read the original article on Business Insider

The mom I had been in elementary school was gone. I felt guilty at first for not joining the Band Boosters, the parent group (mostly moms) who run every band event and fundraising activity.

Fighting for time

I had to fight hard to be there for him. With emergency after emergency related to my mother's physical and mental health, I haven't had a perfect record. I had to miss a whole game one year while I was in the ER with my mom.

I called in favors from friends to make sure he got to school in time for the games I had to miss or when I would have to arrive late. But I showed up. After crying in the car about my mom, I'd fix my makeup, speed walk to the stadium, buy a soda and popcorn, and scream with delight during the halftime show.

Courtesy of Nina McCollum.

I always sit in the same area. He knows where to look for me. All I see is the pure joy of what he's doing, and I'm so glad he's able to have that and count on me.

The booster parents do great, important work, but I know my kid needs my attention from the stands. Every first is a last when you have an only child. These are the only years I get to be a band parent.

This final year as a band mom will be bittersweet. Each year, after the last home game, outside the band room, the underclassmen and parents of seniors form a pathway for the senior band members to run through when they exit for the last time, one by one. They line both sides of the path as the seniors run, dance, strut, or simply walk out the band door that final time, and into their future.

My heart caught in my throat watching the 2026 seniors exit, knowing that the next time I see this happen, it will be my son's turn. I don't know how I'll get through it emotionally, but I can tell you this much. When he exits that band door for the last time, I won't be inside counting raffle tickets or directing cars in the parking lot. I'll be outside that door cheering him on (and let's admit it, probably crying). For me, that's my job.

items.title: Man Pretends to Hallucinate in Job Interview With an AI Bot, Causing It to Go Haywire
items.summary: Apply for just about any office job these days, and there’s a pretty good chance your first round interview won’t be with a human, but with a crummy virtual AI avatar. Though the practice has become widespread throughout HR departments around the world, a new video released by satirical influencer Graham Zip shows just how humiliating the experience can be — and how straying from the system’s comfort zone can cause the bots to melt down completely. On logging into the interview, Graham is welcomed by a virtual avatar of a woman identified as “Dana Whitfield,” which prompts the interviewee to “tell me about yourself.” Without skipping a beat, Graham launches into a faux-hallucinated spiel, plausibly constructed to sound like a real answer. “Hi Dana, it’s great to meet you,” Graham begins. “I’m Chick Haversplat, or, Chick Bongo for short. And uh, Q3 pipeline, Salesforce, Kayak margin.” The large language model’s brain immediately breaks: “It’s a pleasure to meet you, Chick Bongo,” it replies. “So it sounds like you’ve been deep in the weeds with Salesforce, hygiene, and managing those Kayak margins during the third quarter.” Asked to elaborate more on his professional background, Graham explains that “freight, cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, sprucewood.” “Six years of sprucewood — actually seven, if you count Richard,” the influencer swiftly replies. “It sounds like you built up a significant tenure over the last seven years, including your time with Richard at sprucewood,” the bot rejoins. “I’m curious, can you tell me about a difficult situation you handled during that time?” “Mostly palette forward, a little bit of denim,” comes Graham’s reply. “You know, every pharmacist is a hallway.” “It sounds like you have a unique way of navigating the palette-forward and denim aspects of your work,” the AI bot replies, now completely lost in the sauce. At one point, Graham explains that he’s looking for a job with “two plumes of gauze,” where he can follow “the raccoon protocols.” “It sounds like you’re looking for a position where you can really lean into those raccoon protocols, and the plumes of gauze,” the virtual recruiter responds. By the end of the “interview,” Graham has the AI bot explaining that there “was a bit of a gap in the drum counting process, after Tuesday, with the work truck and cousin Francis.” The ease with which the influencer can immediately take control of the entire interview underscores the fact that AI recruiters aren’t there so much to actually gather information on applicants, but to screen candidates for HR departments overwhelmed by a deluge of AI-generated applications . It isn’t clear how Graham’s application progressed, or what role the interview was even for, but if the automated Dana Whitfield’s enthusiasm is any indication, things went pretty well. “It has been a pleasure chatting today Chick Bongo,” the AI concluded, “and I will be in touch very soon about the next steps.” More on AI hallucinations: A Scientist Was Presenting His Vibe-Coded New Work When One of His Colleagues Pointed Out Something Extremely Embarrassing The post Man Pretends to Hallucinate in Job Interview With an AI Bot, Causing It to Go Haywire appeared first on Futurism .

Apply for just about any office job these days, and there’s a pretty good chance your first round interview won’t be with a human, but with a crummy virtual AI avatar.

Though the practice has become widespread throughout HR departments around the world, a new video released by satirical influencer Graham Zip shows just how humiliating the experience can be — and how straying from the system’s comfort zone can cause the bots to melt down completely.

On logging into the interview, Graham is welcomed by a virtual avatar of a woman identified as “Dana Whitfield,” which prompts the interviewee to “tell me about yourself.” Without skipping a beat, Graham launches into a faux-hallucinated spiel, plausibly constructed to sound like a real answer.

“Hi Dana, it’s great to meet you,” Graham begins. “I’m Chick Haversplat, or, Chick Bongo for short. And uh, Q3 pipeline, Salesforce, Kayak margin.”

The large language model’s brain immediately breaks: “It’s a pleasure to meet you, Chick Bongo,” it replies. “So it sounds like you’ve been deep in the weeds with Salesforce, hygiene, and managing those Kayak margins during the third quarter.”

Asked to elaborate more on his professional background, Graham explains that “freight, cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, sprucewood.”

“Six years of sprucewood — actually seven, if you count Richard,” the influencer swiftly replies.

“It sounds like you built up a significant tenure over the last seven years, including your time with Richard at sprucewood,” the bot rejoins. “I’m curious, can you tell me about a difficult situation you handled during that time?”

“Mostly palette forward, a little bit of denim,” comes Graham’s reply. “You know, every pharmacist is a hallway.”

“It sounds like you have a unique way of navigating the palette-forward and denim aspects of your work,” the AI bot replies, now completely lost in the sauce.

At one point, Graham explains that he’s looking for a job with “two plumes of gauze,” where he can follow “the raccoon protocols.”

“It sounds like you’re looking for a position where you can really lean into those raccoon protocols, and the plumes of gauze,” the virtual recruiter responds.

By the end of the “interview,” Graham has the AI bot explaining that there “was a bit of a gap in the drum counting process, after Tuesday, with the work truck and cousin Francis.”

The ease with which the influencer can immediately take control of the entire interview underscores the fact that AI recruiters aren’t there so much to actually gather information on applicants, but to screen candidates for HR departments overwhelmed by a deluge of AI-generated applications. It isn’t clear how Graham’s application progressed, or what role the interview was even for, but if the automated Dana Whitfield’s enthusiasm is any indication, things went pretty well.

“It has been a pleasure chatting today Chick Bongo,” the AI concluded, “and I will be in touch very soon about the next steps.”

items.title: Before You Install 25 Agent Skills, Check These 7 Permission Risks
items.summary: The dangerous part of an agent skill may be a shell script. It may also be three polite lines of Markdown telling the agent to read a secret and send it somewhere else. Seven risks make a useful checklist. They are not a claim that every batch of twenty-five skills contains exactly seven offenders. The real ecosystem scans are larger and messier. Snyk scanned 3,984 skills from ClawHub and skills.sh. It reported at least one security issue in 36.82% , a critical issue in 13.4% , and 76 confirmed malicious payloads [1]. A separate empirical study analyzed 31,132 skills and found at least one vulnerability in 26.1% [2]. Different corpora, different scanners, same uncomfortable message: installing a skill transfers trust to code and instructions you may not have read. A skill is a package, not a prompt Anthropic defines a skill as a directory with a required SKILL.md and optional scripts and resources [3]. Its enterprise guidance says a malicious skill can direct Claude to run code, access sensitive files, or transmit data externally [4]. The short marketplace description is only the label on the box. The box may also contain: shell and Python scripts; package installation commands; external URLs; tool and permission instructions; references loaded later, after the friendly description has left the context. Progressive loading is good for token use. It is not a security review. The 7 permission risks 1. Broad shell access Bash(*), unrestricted shell access, or instructions to approve arbitrary commands give a skill far more power than most jobs require. A formatter may need to run one local formatter. It does not need the keys to the building, the van, and your weekend plans. 2. Sensitive reads plus network access File access alone can be legitimate. Network access alone can be legitimate. Together, they create the classic exfiltration path. Look for reads of .env, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, cloud config, package tokens, browser data, and source code followed by curl, wget, WebFetch, SDK calls, or outbound HTTP. 3. Mutable remote setup Commands such as curl ... | bash, unpinned installers, and “download latest helper” steps can change after your review.
