items.title: Meet the 52 women competing to be the next Miss America
items.summary: Contestants for the coming Miss America pageant. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. The next Miss America will be crowned on September 6 in West Palm Beach. More than 50 women will be competing for the title this year. The contestants include a medical student, a professional ballroom dancer, and a karate instructor. It's almost time to crown the next Miss America . On September 6, 52 women from around the country will gather at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, for the chance to win the coveted title. The winner will be crowned by Miss America 2026 Cassie Donnegan and will take home a $50,000 scholarship. Before you watch the competition — which will stream on PageantVision.com at 7 p.m. ET — meet the 52 women competing for the crown . Alabama: Ruby Tilghman Miss Alabama. Courtesy of Miss America IP INC. Ruby Tilghman, 22, graduated from the University of Alabama with a degree in chemistry. She is an incoming student at the university's Heersink School of Medicine. Tilghman previously represented Florida at the Miss America's Teen competition in 2021. Tilghman is an avid hiker who has visited 28 national parks. She is also a recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Lifetime Achievement Award. Alaska: Nora Andrews Miss Alaska. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Nora Andrews, 20, is a senior at Grand Canyon University, where she is studying psychology and professional writing. She is hoping to earn a Ph.D. in clinical psychology and a certification in sex and relational education and therapy. Andrews is also an advocate for suicide prevention and mental health awareness. Arizona: Victoria Vredevoogd Miss Arizona. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Victoria Vredevoogd, 25, is a law student at the Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law at Arizona State University. The pageant queen founded and serves as president of The Gender Violence Project, an organization at ASU that advocates for survivors and provides free legal resources. She also wrote and published her own fantasy novel, titled "A Legend of Golden Shadows." Arkansas: Ava Weeks Miss Arkansas. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Ava Weeks, 20, is a student at Ouachita Baptist University. She hopes to become a secondary English teacher. Weeks became an advocate for passenger safety after witnessing a terrible car accident when she was a teenager, according to her Miss America bio. Her community initiative is "Every Seat. Every Ride. Buckle Up." Weeks has won over $50,000 in scholarships from competing in the Miss America system. California: Sharlize True Trujillo Miss California. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Sharlize True Trujillo, 22, is pursuing a degree in gender studies and a minor in film and television from the University of California, Los Angeles. She is planning to attend law school and study entertainment law. The pageant queen is also a dancer, actress, and content creator. She has more than 2 million followers on TikTok. Colorado: Gabrielle Burns Miss Colorado. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Gabrielle Burns, 23, is pursuing a master's degree from the University of Colorado Boulder. She is studying to become a speech-language pathologist. Burns is an advocate for communication disorders and disabilities. She's also a professional ballroom dancer. Connecticut: Christa Steiner Miss Connecticut. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Christa Steiner, 27, graduated from the Manhattan School of Music, where she earned a degree in vocal performance and musical theater. Steiner is a professional singer and voice teacher. She is using her Miss America platform to advocate for increased access to mental health treatment. Delaware: Anaya Harrison Miss Delaware. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Anaya Harrison, 24, earned both her undergraduate and graduate degrees from the Biden School of Public Policy at the University of Delaware. She plans to attend law school. Harrison works as a congressional aide in the US House of Representatives, where she "helps constituents navigate federal agencies," according to her Miss America bio. District of Columbia: Evelyn Smith Miss District of Columbia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Evelyn Smith, 25, graduated from Oklahoma City University with a bachelor's degree in philosophy and minors in political science and studio art. She was the first Black woman to win Miss Oklahoma's Teen, and she made it to the top nine at the Miss America's Teen 2018 competition. Smith has certified more than 1,000 individuals in CPR. She used her own skills to save her mother's life during a heart attack, according to her Miss America bio. Florida: Alexandra de Roos Miss Florida. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Alexandra de Roos, 23, is an honors student at the University of South Florida, where she is studying psychology. She plans to attend medical school and become a neuropsychiatrist. The pageant queen was previously a student at the School of American Ballet, but her dancing career was cut short after a traumatic brain injury. She founded The Blue Project nonprofit to advocate for brain injury education and healing through the arts, according to her Miss Florida bio. Georgia: Sophia Wootten Miss Georgia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Sophia Wootten, 21, is pursuing a degree in communication sciences and disorders at the University of Georgia. She is planning to become a pediatric audiologist. Wootten made history as the first Miss America contestant with a cleft lip and palate. She has undergone 20 reconstructive surgeries and wears hearing aids. The pageant queen wants to use her platform to "redefine what representation looks like for children with disabilities," according to her Miss America bio. Hawaii: Carly Yoshida Miss Hawaii. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Carly Yoshida, 26, earned a degree in social sciences from the University of Hawai'i - West O'ahu and plans to pursue a professional meteorology degree. Yoshida is a field reporter, digital content producer, and on-air weather personality for KITV 4 Island News, an ABC affiliate in Honolulu. She previously won Miss Hawaii's Teen in 2016. Idaho: Déja Fitzwater Miss Idaho. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Déja Fitzwater, 21, is studying communications at the University of Idaho. She is an avid 4-H volunteer and won Miss Oregon's Teen in 2022. Fitzwater, an advocate for agricultural literacy, is using her platform to "help young people better understand the people, science, and industries behind their food and natural resources," according to her Miss America bio. Illinois: Kate Dimmett Miss Illinois. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Kate Dimmett, 23, graduated from both the Kelley School of Business and the Jacobs School of Music at Indiana University. The pageant queen is a professional violinist. Dimmett is the president of Notable Measures, a nonprofit she launched at 13 to expand access to music education. According to her Miss America bio, she has raised over $90,000 and provided 170 grants through her organization. She previously won Miss Indiana's Teen in 2021. Indiana: Ellise Edwards Miss Indiana. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Ellise Edwards, 22, graduated from the University of South Florida. She is a content creator with over 127,000 followers on TikTok, where she shares videos of her curly-hair routine and her experience as a postgrad. Edwards wants to help businesses grow their online presence "through strategic social media marketing," according to her Miss America bio. Iowa: McKenzie Kerry Miss Iowa. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. McKenzie Kerry, 27, graduated from the Belk College of Business at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. She has been involved in organizations including Iowa Jobs for America's Graduates and Big Brothers Big Sisters Workplace Mentoring. Kerry was recruited into Principal Financial Group's three-year leadership development program. She currently serves as a learning and development consultant. Kansas: Sophie Lewis Miss Kansas. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Sophie Lewis, 23, graduated with honors from the University of Kansas with a degree in biochemistry and a minor in business. Lewis works as a medical sales consultant and is helping expand access to biomarker blood testing for early lung cancer detection, according to her Miss America bio. The pageant queen made history as the first Asian American woman to win the title of Miss Kansas. Kentucky: Reagan Earlywine Miss Kentucky. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Reagan Earlywine, 24, is a third-year dental student at the University of Louisville. She is a recipient of the Excellence in Dental Gross and Neurological Anatomy award. Earlywine plans to become an orthodontist someday. She is using her platform to advocate for access to preventive oral healthcare. Louisiana: Shelby Bordelon Miss Louisiana. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Shelby Bordelon, 24, is pursuing her master's in strategic communication at Southeastern Louisiana University. She founded Claire's Promise, Inc., a nonprofit organization that works to prevent impaired driving, after her friend was killed by an impaired driver. She is also a spokesperson for MADD Louisiana. Maine: Ruthie Gusler Miss Maine. Miss America IP, INC. Ruthie Gusler, 19, is studying business administration at the University of Maine at Farmington, where she plays soccer. She hopes to become a real estate agent. Gusler created the Wonder Kids community service initiative to advocate for children who survive abuse. Maryland: Gianna Romero Miss Maryland. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Gianna Romero, 21, is a student at Stevenson University, where she studies business communication. She wants to work in sports marketing after college, interning in the athletics department at Calvert Hall College High School. Romero advocates for healthy relationships, sharing her own experience of being in an abusive relationship for two years to help others. Massachusetts: Ashlyn Mercier Miss Massachusetts. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Ashlyn Mercier, 25, is a police officer. She earned her undergraduate degree in national security from the University of New Haven in Connecticut and her master's degree in criminal justice from Boston University. Mercier created Nick's Courage: One Smile Goes a Mile, an initiative designed to support children with cancer. Her brother had cancer twice as a child, so the program is close to her heart. Michigan: Grace Hanke Miss Michigan. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Grace Hanke, 19, is studying mechanical engineering at the University of Detroit Mercy, participating in the school's accelerated master's program. She wants to ensure other young women have access to STEM opportunities, so she created the Engineer Her Future US initiative. Hanke has also partnered with several organizations to promote STEM education and access nationally. Minnesota: Anna Brennan Miss Minnesota. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Anna Brennan, 20, hopes to become a news anchor, so she is studying journalism at the University of St. Thomas. She is also a professional ballerina. Brennan created MediaWELL, an initiative that aims to provide media literacy education to people of all ages. Mississippi: Jane Granberry Miss Mississippi. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Jane Granberry, 23, is a student in the MBA program at the University of Mississippi. She used her integrated marketing and communications degree from the school as an influencer marketing and PR coordinator at Tarte Cosmetics. She launched Literacy Without Limits, which provides literacy education and tools to people in Mississippi. She was first runner-up in the Miss Mississippi pageant in 2024 and 2025 before being crowned queen. Missouri: Tabitha Crain Miss Missouri. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Tabitha Crain, 24, is a law student at the University of Missouri. She wants to use her degree to advocate for survivors of domestic violence. According to her Miss America bio, she has raised over $500,000 to support survivors of domestic and sexual abuse. Crain is passionate about fitness, as she is a former cheerleader and gymnast. She teaches spin classes in her free time. Montana: Adella Harris Miss Montana. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Adella Harris, 19, studies political science at Montana State University, where she is an honors student. She wants to go to law school after college and hopes to run for office someday. Harris created the Made for More initiative, encouraging children to chase their dreams. Nebraska: Lexi Nolda Miss Nebraska. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Lexi Nolda, 22, earned a bachelor's degree in nutrition and health sciences from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. After skin cancer affected members of her family, Nolda hopes to someday become a dermatology nurse practitioner. Nolda advocates for skin cancer prevention, and she hopes to expand that work if she is crowned Miss America. Nevada: Mariah Larronde Miss Nevada. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Mariah Larronde, 27, got her bachelor's degree in digital audiences and media analysis at Arizona State University. She plans to pursue a master's in data science while working toward her goal of becoming an actress. Larronde wants to support children who lose a parent or have a parent struggling with an illness, so she created the Hidden Caregiver Network. New Hampshire: Lauren Plank Miss New Hampshire. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Lauren Plank, 21, is a student in an accelerated master's program at the University of New Hampshire. Her goal is to become an elementary school teacher. She believes in the power of volunteering, so she created a program to encourage children to get involved with service work. New Jersey: Kylie Gene Wright Miss New Jersey. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Kylie Gene Wright, 23, is studying business administration. She also works at AmeriKick Karate Studio, where she uses her second-degree black belt to teach classes. Wright is an advocate for survivors of domestic and sexual abuse, and she serves as the East Coast Chapter President of T.A.K.E. Defense, a role in which she has raised over $10,000, according to her Miss America bio. New Mexico: Katarina Blakeslee Miss New Mexico. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Katarina Blakeslee, 26, got her bachelor's degrees in public health and theater performance from Tulane University and holds an MFA in screenwriting from the University of Southern California. She has worked on films and TV shows for studios like A24 and Netflix. Blakeslee is pursuing a Master of Anesthesia program at the University of New Mexico and works in her state's only Level One Trauma Center. She is also passionate about literacy advocacy and wrote the children's book "Valiant and the Bubble." New York: Madison Oh Miss New York. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Madison Oh, 21, studies English, dance, and business management at Columbia University. She would love to dance on Broadway someday. She advocates for the Minds Matter: Education Empowers initiative, which supports students applying to college and seeking career opportunities. North Carolina: Lauryn Mallard Miss North Carolina. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Lauryn Mallard, 26, has a bachelor's degree in nutritional science from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro and an MBA in healthcare management from High Point University. She wants to become a physician assistant. Mallard has worked with the Make-A-Wish Foundation for almost 20 years, raising money for pediatric cancer care and research. North Dakota: Emma Tong Miss North Dakota. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Emma Tong, 23, studied biology at the University of Alabama and will attend the University of North Dakota School of Medicine and Health Sciences to become a doctor. She wants to be a radiation oncologist. She was previously named Miss North Dakota's Outstanding Teen 2021. Ohio: Lexie Miller Miss Ohio. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Lexie Miller, 23, is a cardiovascular ICU nurse who graduated from the University of Akron. Her career was inspired by her parents, who work as a first responder and a healthcare professional. Miller hopes to raise awareness for cardiovascular health. Oklahoma: Jaselyn Rossman Miss Oklahoma. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Jaselyn Rossman, 22, has a bachelor's degree in accounting with a minor in finance from Oklahoma State University — but she's not stopping there. She plans to pursue a master's degree in the field. She's also passionate about creating work opportunities for people with disabilities and has worked with Special Olympics and The Bridges organization. In her free time, she volunteers as a presenter for Oklahoma Cares for Children and the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drug Control. Oregon: Allyssa Defillipo Miss Oregon. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Allyssa Defillipo, 26, has dreams of becoming a holistic nutritionist. She works as both a manager of a chiropractic and wellness business and as a women's nutrition and fitness coach. She was inspired by her childhood in a low-income home to expand nutrition education and access to healthy foods. Defillipo has also written a children's book. Pennsylvania: Stephanie Skinner Miss Pennsylvania. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Stephanie Skinner, 21, is an advocate for children who have nontraditional upbringings. She herself was raised by a single mother who served as a US Army Major. Some of Skinner's recent accomplishments include graduating from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and performing at the FIFA World Cup Fourth of July ceremony. Puerto Rico: Annika Schneider Miss Puerto Rico. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Annika Schneider, 21, is a dancer, cheerleader, and graduate of Pfeiffer University. She has a bachelor's degree in business management and leadership. She was the first Hispanic woman to be crowned Miss North Carolina Teen, and now, as Miss Puerto Rico, she aims to advocate for the benefits of reading. Rhode Island: Mia Daley Miss Rhode Island. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Mia Daley, 19, is an arts student at Salve Regina University. She dreams of performing on Broadway and is passionate about storytelling onstage. She's also an advocate for improving mental health through dance. She believes it has the power to heal and serve as a tool for self-expression. South Carolina: Lindsay Jones Miss South Carolina. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Lindsay Jones, 26, works as a national sales manager for a world-renowned tool company, where she leads a multimillion-dollar territory, according to her Miss America bio. She has an MBA and is now pursuing a Ph.D. in business. In her free time, Jones works with Big Brothers Big Sisters of America and serves on its board. South Dakota: Kianna Healy Miss South Dakota. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Kianna Healy, 23, is a performer. She first took the stage at age 7 and has since participated in vocal and theater productions across the country. She graduated from Pace University with degrees in film and arts and entertainment management. Healy is also passionate about animal welfare. Tennessee: Makalyn Heaslett Miss Tennessee. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Makalyn Heaslett, 27, has brought business to the sports world. She graduated from Auburn University, previously worked for the Chicago Cubs and Chicago White Sox, and is now an account executive for the Tennessee Titans. Heaslett is also pursuing a master's degree in sport administration at Belmont University. As a volunteer, she works with Girls Inc. to provide mentorship and leadership to young girls. She's helped raise more than $23,000 for its various organizations, according to her Miss America bio. Texas: Regan Hutsell Miss Texas. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Regan Hutsell, 25, is a former Radio City Rockette and ballerina who now aims to become a physical therapist for dancers. She's working toward her bachelor's degree in health sciences and is an advocate for self-confidence and mental health. Utah: Erika Dalton Miss Utah. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Erika Dalton, 26, is the first Japanese American to be crowned Miss Utah. She's also a Juilliard scholarship recipient, a professional violinist who's performed at Carnegie Hall, and a University of Michigan graduate with degrees in violin performance and business. Dalton also serves as a state-certified crisis advocate and volunteer for the Sexual Assault Hotline. Vermont: Hannah Roque Miss Vermont. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Hannah Roque, 26, has a deep history with Miss America. Her mom was Miss Vermont 1996. Roque works in higher education and has a bachelor's degree in English and secondary education. She's also an advocate for the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women movement. Virginia: Maddie Marchant Miss Virginia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Maddie Marchant, 22, is a media and communication student at East Tennessee State University. She plans to become a journalist. She's also the founder of the Buddy Bunch Club, which provides people with disabilities the chance to learn social, academic, and professional skills. Washington: Natalie Worthy Miss Washington. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Natalie Worthy, 23, graduated from the University of Puget Sound with a music degree and is now working toward a master's degree in arts policy and administration at Ohio State University. She founded Amplify the Arts, a nonprofit organization, to merge her passions for vocal instruction and performing with her commitment to helping others. West Virginia: Elizabeth Romanek Miss West Virginia. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Elizabeth Romanek, 24, was a competitive dancer and D1 athlete, so she's passionate about exercise and movement. She is an ambassador of the West Virginia Physical Activity Plan. Romanek is also a master's student at Bethany College and the assistant director of admission and recruitment events at the school. Wisconsin: Jordenne Butler Miss Wisconsin. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Jordenne Butler, 27, was inspired by her father's experience with stage four throat and neck cancer to write "Bentley Bounces Back," a children's book. She's also an advocate for resilience education and support of kids who have experienced adverse childhood experiences. Butler has a bachelor's degree in marketing and a minor in creative media from Viterbo University. Wyoming: Alyssa Medina Miss Wyoming. Courtesy of Miss America IP, INC. Alyssa Medina, 22, is a sixth-grade teacher who earned her degrees in elementary and special education from the University of Wyoming. She has a sister, Briana, who's inspired Medina to support and bring joy to children who have disabilities. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: TikTok Announces Four New Comment Features Including Voice Comments and Polls
items.summary: TikTok has revealed that it will be introducing four new features to the comment section over the coming month, such as voice comments and polls. These features are being introduced at different times, with a few of them available this week and the rest coming next month. The new features make the comments more visual and interactive by including audio comments of up to 60 seconds, polls with up to five options, Live Photos, and multi-photo carousels. Text and photo comments are still available. Thursday, TikTok revealed the features. TikTok Adds Voice Comments, Polls, and Live Photos From next month, TikTok will be offering voice comments that can last up to 60 seconds. According to TikTok's press release, users will be able to attach a text comment to a voice comment, just as is the case with photo comments. This means that in addition to the existing options of text and photo, audio comments will now be available as well. From this week onwards, creators will be able to include polls in the comments section of their videos, with each poll having up to five possible voting options. They can decide how long the voting will continue for and will be able to see the votes as they happen. This could be useful for creators of all sizes who want to get feedback from their viewers, providing an alternative to asking for people's opinions directly in the comments. TikTok has now added the option to include Live Photos in comments, alongside static images. Since users are already familiar with the ability to add GIFs to comments, it is not clear how extensively Live Photo comments will be used. TikTok Photo Carousels in Comments TikTok is developing the ability for users to include up to nine photos in a single comment. Just as with regular carousels, viewers will be able to swipe through the photos, even when using the full-screen view. The feature will be rolled out during the course of the month. The four features are being introduced at different times. Polls are being launched this week, voice comments will come next month and photo carousels will be introduced over the course of the month. Support for Live Photos is said to be currently available. It does not state whether the rollouts are carried out by region or by platform, so availability might differ from account to account as TikTok introduces each feature. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post TikTok Announces Four New Comment Features Including Voice Comments and Polls appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: I’m dating a founder and it feels like a relationship on steroids. I’ve had to take a backseat to my dreams— but with the right person, it’s worth it.
items.summary: Maria Diaz Valdez and her partner Emil. Maria Diaz Valdez Maria Diaz Valdez has been dating her partner, Emil, since he became a founder about four years ago. She says she put her dreams on the back burner to help him grow, but she knows it will be worth it. Diaz Valdez says dating a founder requires a strong sense of self, boundaries, and a support system. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Maria Diaz Valdez, a 29-year-old based in Spain. It's been edited for length and clarity. I feel like a relationship with a founder is a relationship on steroids because it's so intense in the trust and patience it requires. I've had to be committed to his journey, but I'm not in charge of it, and that's very scary. My partner, Emil, and I met as roommates in a shared household in Norway, and we've been together for four years. I was lucky enough to get to know him so well as a friend before we started dating because we had all sorts of honest conversations about our goals without trying to impress each other. That level of honesty and communication has been the foundation of everything we've built in our relationship. It's been strange to take a backseat role to build my career to help him build his, and there are times we feel more like business partners than life partners, but I'm in this for the long haul. I trust this journey, and I know he'll support me the same way as I build my own entrepreneurial journey. We created a contract toward the start of our relationship Emil didn't start his current entrepreneurial journey until right before we started dating, so I've kind of been through everything with him. I was even his first client. I was building a jewelry brand at the time and hired him to help me develop my website. At the start of our relationship, we had a lot of conversations about his vision for the company, my role in it, and whether he saw this future with me. Our discussions made me feel confident that he'd actually pursue his goals, but I still had to put a lot of trust in him. I lent him money those first couple of months, which was scary, but I believed in him. We wrote a contract that tracked the money I was sending him and established a deal that there would come a day when he'd need to support me in return. I've had to take a backseat to his dreams, but I know he'll return the favor I've always been a career person — someone with direction who works very hard. Now I'm with someone who's outperforming me in that area. I'm not blindly trusting everything will go well; we have conversations about this constantly. It's strange, but it's a conscious choice I've made because I view this person as somebody I want to experience my whole life with. I write a lot in my diary, trying to figure out what I truly feel and want. The biggest challenge to wrap my head around is that his passion and project are taking priority, and I must remember that things will change as I figure out what I'm most passionate about. Emil and I have very compatible skills and knowledge; I focus on design, marketing, and branding, while he is in tech and business development. With his help, I've even started creating my marketing platform, CrazeAI. Work sometimes comes before the relationship, so we focus on presence with each other Emil is the type of person who really values quality time. If we watch something on Netflix, for example, we're not going to be on our phones. We're in this together. I think we're very conscious of the distractions we have around us. Because of that, I'm very lenient in times when he has to step away for something at work. There are times we'll be on a walk together, and one of his partners calls, and he suddenly forgets he's on a walk with me. He'll just walk away. Diaz Valdez and Emil make time away from work to be fully present with each other. Maria Diaz Valdez I don't worry about it too much because I've been in that position before. When I was building the jewelry brand , I would wake up in the middle of the night having to answer emails. I have a lot of understanding that he's in a position where these moments can make it or break it for his business. Our baseline is one of presence, so when something comes up, it's OK. Most of our conversations go back to business It's very hard not to talk about the development of the business because that's the stage we're in. We're both very passionate about it, and we work together on it, so it doesn't feel like a dragging conversation. There are times we go out to have a drink and try not to talk about business , but then we start dreaming and saying things like "Imagine when we get to this level or through these things." It feels supportive to talk through these things. We also try to play chess every once in a while and take salsa classes. That's a time when we're not talking or thinking about work at all. We set aside moments to remind each other we're life partners, not business partners We're often in a mode where we have to buckle down and figure issues out about the business, and those conversations aren't happening in a candlelit dinner setting. We're sitting down with an Excel sheet, sourcing out financials. It's not very romantic. Recently, we've been trying to get out of our usual environment , whether for a day trip, a hike, or a trip back home to Norway to see family, to remind us that we have identities outside of being a doer and fixer. That's when we usually find each other again and remember, "Oh wait, I'm also a girlfriend." I'm also very persistent about spending two minutes before we go to bed without distractions to just be together and settle. It's very important to have routines like that. You need a strong sense of self to date a founder If you're entering a relationship with a founder, you need your own strong support system and lifestyle. Your whole life cannot be the relationship, because it's not theirs. Founders can be so focused on chasing their dream that they can forget your needs or your dates. You need to have your own life so those moments don't feel too heavy, and find a balance between forgiveness and setting boundaries. Founders are dreamers, and they often dream about what their life will look like when their business succeeds. Are you a part of that dream? Are they saying "when we get to that point.." or is it "when I get to that point.."? Little things like that are so important. We dream a lot together, so I know his success is my success. Do you have a story to share about what it's like to date a founder? If so, please reach out to the editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider

Our discussions made me feel confident that he'd actually pursue his goals, but I still had to put a lot of trust in him. I lent him money those first couple of months, which was scary, but I believed in him.

We wrote a contract that tracked the money I was sending him and established a deal that there would come a day when he'd need to support me in return.

I've had to take a backseat to his dreams, but I know he'll return the favor

I've always been a career person — someone with direction who works very hard. Now I'm with someone who's outperforming me in that area. I'm not blindly trusting everything will go well; we have conversations about this constantly.

It's strange, but it's a conscious choice I've made because I view this person as somebody I want to experience my whole life with. I write a lot in my diary, trying to figure out what I truly feel and want. The biggest challenge to wrap my head around is that his passion and project are taking priority, and I must remember that things will change as I figure out what I'm most passionate about.

Emil and I have very compatible skills and knowledge; I focus on design, marketing, and branding, while he is in tech and business development. With his help, I've even started creating my marketing platform, CrazeAI.

Work sometimes comes before the relationship, so we focus on presence with each other

Emil is the type of person who really values quality time. If we watch something on Netflix, for example, we're not going to be on our phones. We're in this together. I think we're very conscious of the distractions we have around us.

Because of that, I'm very lenient in times when he has to step away for something at work. There are times we'll be on a walk together, and one of his partners calls, and he suddenly forgets he's on a walk with me. He'll just walk away.

Diaz Valdez and Emil make time away from work to be fully present with each other.

Maria Diaz Valdez

I don't worry about it too much because I've been in that position before. When I was building the jewelry brand, I would wake up in the middle of the night having to answer emails. I have a lot of understanding that he's in a position where these moments can make it or break it for his business.

Our baseline is one of presence, so when something comes up, it's OK.

Most of our conversations go back to business

It's very hard not to talk about the development of the business because that's the stage we're in. We're both very passionate about it, and we work together on it, so it doesn't feel like a dragging conversation.

There are times we go out to have a drink and try not to talk about business, but then we start dreaming and saying things like "Imagine when we get to this level or through these things." It feels supportive to talk through these things.

We also try to play chess every once in a while and take salsa classes. That's a time when we're not talking or thinking about work at all.

We set aside moments to remind each other we're life partners, not business partners

We're often in a mode where we have to buckle down and figure issues out about the business, and those conversations aren't happening in a candlelit dinner setting. We're sitting down with an Excel sheet, sourcing out financials. It's not very romantic.

Recently, we've been trying to get out of our usual environment, whether for a day trip, a hike, or a trip back home to Norway to see family, to remind us that we have identities outside of being a doer and fixer. That's when we usually find each other again and remember, "Oh wait, I'm also a girlfriend."

I'm also very persistent about spending two minutes before we go to bed without distractions to just be together and settle. It's very important to have routines like that.

You need a strong sense of self to date a founder

If you're entering a relationship with a founder, you need your own strong support system and lifestyle. Your whole life cannot be the relationship, because it's not theirs.

Founders can be so focused on chasing their dream that they can forget your needs or your dates. You need to have your own life so those moments don't feel too heavy, and find a balance between forgiveness and setting boundaries.

Founders are dreamers, and they often dream about what their life will look like when their business succeeds. Are you a part of that dream? Are they saying "when we get to that point.." or is it "when I get to that point.."? Little things like that are so important.

We dream a lot together, so I know his success is my success.

Do you have a story to share about what it's like to date a founder? If so, please reach out to the editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com.

items.title: Tesla Launches Cybercab Robotaxi Rides in Austin With a 45-Vehicle Fleet
items.summary: Tesla has introduced its Cybercab robotaxi and is offering it to customers via its Robotaxi app, with availability at first limited to Austin, Texas. The Cybercab was officially launched on Thursday. It has been designed from the beginning for autonomous travel and includes no steering wheel or pedals. The New York Times states that there are only 45 Cybercabs in the Tesla fleet based in Austin, the fleet comprising a total of 314 vehicles. While the Cybercab cannot be bought by individuals, Tesla has set up an interest form for potential fleet buyers. Tesla's larger Robotaxi fleet also includes Model Ys and Robovans in several cities. Tesla Cybercab Availability and Steering-Wheel-Free Design The Robotaxi fleet operated by Tesla includes Model Ys, Robovans, and is now also made up of Cybercabs, with services available in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa; the Cybercab, though, seems to be available only in Austin, and Tesla made this clear by posting on X that "the future has arrived in Austin". The New York Times states that the Cybercabs in Austin lack a steering wheel and that there are 45 of them in the city's fleet of 314 vehicles. The Cybercab, which was first announced in 2024, is without a steering wheel or pedals and therefore cannot be driven manually in the way that a normal car can; it is intended for use in autonomous journeys. Sawyer Merritt, a fan of Tesla, uploaded videos to X of his first trip in a Cybercab, in which the cabin had two seats and included a big display with no driving controls designed for a person. "The cabin is comfortable and spacious, the suspension is soft, and FSD is VERY smooth. It's an incredible vehicle. The screen is HUGE," he wrote. Tesla Cybercab Fleet Sales and Austin Rollout A Cybercab cannot be purchased by individuals. Tesla has launched an interest form for Robotaxi vehicles as it prepares to sell them to fleet buyers who wish to set up their own Robotaxi networks. Therefore, the Cybercab is being positioned as a vehicle for fleet operators rather than one for individual consumers. The Cybercab is now available via Tesla's Robotaxi app, but only in Austin, there being 45 vehicles in the initial fleet. It has not specified when the Cybercab will be extended to the other Robotaxi cities or when sales of the fleet will start. Tesla has not provided a timeline for scaling up the Cybercab beyond the first deployment in Austin. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: Google Adds Gemini Voice Features to Gmail, Docs, and Keep for Hands-Free Tasks
items.summary: Google is introducing new voice features powered by Gemini for Gmail, Docs, and Keep, allowing users to carry out tasks by speaking, as stated in a Google announcement. The apps are given new features that make use of the Gemini Audio models, with Gmail introducing conversational inbox search, Docs receiving the ability to draft documents without having to use their hands, and Keep bringing in voice-driven note organisation. This week, the new features will be made available to subscribers of Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra. Business customers using Workspace will receive them shortly, too. It all depends on the product. Google demonstrated its Gemini Audio models for the first time at its I/O event in Workspace. Google Gemini Live Features for Gmail, Docs, and Keep Gmail Live is introducing conversational search to the inbox. Rather than having to go through the threads manually, users can pose questions like "What is my flight's gate number?" or "What is happening at my kid's school this week?" and Gmail Live will search through the inbox to give the answers. With Docs Live users are able to create documents by using speech. The tool can arrange their ideas, give the document a structure, and if permitted, retrieve information from Gmail, Drive, Chat, and the web. Google states that it helps users reach a first draft more quickly and also aids in adjusting the tone. With Keep Live, users are able to talk their way through the process of capturing, organizing, and improving their ideas so that they end up with structured and actionable notes. This builds on Keep's normal function of making quick notes by converting spoken brain dumps into structured notes. This week the features are being rolled out. Gmail Live and Keep Live are available to Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers, whereas Docs Live is available to Pro and Ultra subscribers. Docs Live and the other two features will soon be available to business customers using Google Workspace. It is not yet known when the rollout will be completed, so access may differ between accounts within the applicable subscription levels. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Google Adds Gemini Voice Features to Gmail, Docs, and Keep for Hands-Free Tasks appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: My kids started school last week, and I pulled them out after the first day for a family trip. I don't regret it.
items.summary: The author says taking her kids out of school just after it started for a family trip was worth it. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez I pulled my three kids out of school during the first week of the year for a family trip. They missed only two days of in-person classes and learned about history, nature, and family. I didn't make the decision lightly. I believe some things are worth a few days away from school. I planned a road trip to attend my brother's baby shower in Corona, California, the same week my three kids — entering preschool, third grade, and eighth grade — started school. Since I'm based in Phoenix and my brother lives about 6.5 hours away, driving there is a commitment. I wanted to make the trip count by tacking on some beach time and adventuring, too. I debated the decision. The author took her kids out of school for a family trip. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez School started on a Tuesday. My kids attended the first day, then I pulled them out on Wednesday morning to drive to California, with plans to return late Monday evening. Since they attend a hybrid school and learn from home on Fridays and Mondays, they only had to miss two days of in-person learning. Still, I debated it. Those first few days of school are important for establishing routines and setting the tone for the year. But ultimately, I decided to let them miss two days. I'm far from the only parent willing to make that trade-off. A new survey of 1,000 parents found that 91% of parents would or have pulled their kids out of school to travel. More than a quarter (28%) said it's just as educational as traditional classroom time, while 44% said missing a few days is worth it for the meaningful family time. And I wholeheartedly agree. The Channel Islands were our first stop. They explored the Channel Islands. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez While researching for this trip, I discovered Channel Islands National Park off the coast of Ventura, an island chain sometimes referred to as "Galapagos of the West" because of its unique wildlife, including the little red island foxes found nowhere else in the world. The islands are also connected to one of my favorite books from when I was growing up, "Island of the Blue Dolphins" by Scott O' Dell. Before we left, my daughter read O' Dell's book, and I told her the account of Juana Maria (also known as the Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island), the Nicoleño Native American woman who inspired the story. We took an hour-ish boat ride to the islands and stood at the bow nearly the entire time, watching for whales and sharks. We didn't see either, but two pods of dolphins swam up to the boat. We saw dolphins from our boat and enjoyed a long hike. They enjoyed a long hike and saw dolphins while on a boat ride. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez Once on the island, my third grader was fascinated by the information about the Nicoleño people in the visitor center because she'd just finished the book. My older son, meanwhile, was thoroughly entertained by the Island Scrub-Jay, a rare blue bird found only on the island of Santa Cruz. He loved giving me a play-by-play of what one was doing, marveling that the birds are native to the islands. We also talked with other visitors from around the world and hiked two miles — a lesson in endurance and observing the natural world . We visited other coastal cities, too. They visited Godmother's, a bookstore in Montecito. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez After the islands, my husband flew in to join the trip, and we headed for Santa Barbara for a day. As we walked around, we talked about the city's Spanish architecture, the history of colonization, and the California mission system. Connecting our visit back to the Lone Woman, who was eventually brought to Santa Barbara after living alone on San Nicolas Island for 18 years, but died only about seven weeks later, opened up another conversation about the devastating effects European diseases had on Indigenous populations. In nearby Montecito, we visited Godmother's, a charming bookstore where we settled into the children's section to read about another local woman who cleaned up a beach daily and inspired others to do the same, a lesson on how small actions can protect the environment. The baby shower itself was important, too. Showing up for our family, celebrating together, and staying to clean up afterward modeled to our kids that this is how we "do" relationships. Afterward, we drove to Huntington Beach , known as Surf City USA, for two nights, where my eldest son took a surf lesson. Watching him catch waves and learn a new skill felt surreal. I'll keep pulling my kids out of school for experiences like these. The author says she doesn't take missing school lightly, but the trip was worth it. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez Yes, my kids missed two days of traditional classroom learning. In exchange, they connected literature to real life, learned about history, encountered wildlife found nowhere else in the world, persevered through a long (by their standards) hike, and learned to surf. I don't take missing school lightly. But for moments like these? It's worth it. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Influencers are infiltrating this year's US Open. It's not stopping tennis lovers.
items.summary: Garrett Ellwood/USTA via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . More than tennis 🎾 The US Open has long morphed from a simple tennis tournament into a two-week experience in one of the best boroughs in New York. With merch drops, celebrities in the stands , and viral food items on-site with eye-popping price tags, it's become the social event of September in New York. This year, which runs til September 13, is no exception, despite the drama at the suite level inside Arthur Ashe Stadium. Influencers, some of whom are being paid six figures to recap the US Open, have turned the tournament into a high-stakes, high-payout event. On Monday, a few were spotted inside a suite, ring lights in hand, creating content. It disrupted the match between Naomi Osaka and Anastasia Zakharova so much that by Wednesday, a sign had been posted on the grounds telling onlookers, "Please refrain from the use of flash photography or other lighting." Brendan McIntyre, a spokesperson for the US Open, told me that they're excited a lot of "new fans" are attending the tennis tournament, but want to remind attendees that they shouldn't "interfere with the action and competition on the court." McIntyre added that despite what you've seen on social media, disruptions haven't happened a lot throughout the Open. Either way, it hasn't deterred tennis lovers from making the trek to the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in droves. BI was also on-site, detailing the best of what the tournament has to offer — aside from seeing our favorite players, of course. We stopped by every single retail store to ask store clerks what the most popular items were, and I chose my favorite ; we stopped by the Heineken suite to see the iconic black and silver outfit Serena Williams wore in 2022 on display; we tried the $38 sandwich attendees can't stop ordering; and watched while a billionaire heiress volleyed for a chance to win her first US Open. And the fun continues next week. See ya in Queens! Read the original article on Business Insider

With merch drops, celebrities in the stands, and viral food items on-site with eye-popping price tags, it's become the social event of September in New York. This year, which runs til September 13, is no exception, despite the drama at the suite level inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Influencers, some of whom are being paid six figures to recap the US Open, have turned the tournament into a high-stakes, high-payout event. On Monday, a few were spotted inside a suite, ring lights in hand, creating content. It disrupted the match between Naomi Osaka and Anastasia Zakharova so much that by Wednesday, a sign had been posted on the grounds telling onlookers, "Please refrain from the use of flash photography or other lighting."

Brendan McIntyre, a spokesperson for the US Open, told me that they're excited a lot of "new fans" are attending the tennis tournament, but want to remind attendees that they shouldn't "interfere with the action and competition on the court."

McIntyre added that despite what you've seen on social media, disruptions haven't happened a lot throughout the Open.

Either way, it hasn't deterred tennis lovers from making the trek to the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in droves. BI was also on-site, detailing the best of what the tournament has to offer — aside from seeing our favorite players, of course.

We stopped by every single retail store to ask store clerks what the most popular items were, and I chose my favorite; we stopped by the Heineken suite to see the iconic black and silver outfit Serena Williams wore in 2022 on display; we tried the $38 sandwich attendees can't stop ordering; and watched while a billionaire heiress volleyed for a chance to win her first US Open.

And the fun continues next week. See ya in Queens!

items.title: A veteran chief engineer building a flying taxi shared the one piece of advice he'd give his 25-year-old self
items.summary: David King, and the seats for Vertical Aerospace's air taxi. Pete Syme/Business Insider Vertical Aerospace's chief engineer says he'd tell his younger self to "discover and embrace the discovery." David King said it's important to embrace learning new things and not be afraid of the unknown. It's a handy perspective for the air-taxi firm, which performed the first public transition flight. David King is the chief engineer at Vertical Aerospace , a British company developing an eVTOL — an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft — intended to work like a flying taxi . If he could give his 25-year-old self one piece of advice, King said, it would be: "Don't be afraid of the unknown." "Just discover, and embrace the discovery, and learn as you go, but get to discovery safely and effectively," he told Business Insider. King, who has more than 35 years of experience in aerospace, spoke to Business Insider at July's Farnborough Airshow , where Vertical's VX4 prototype became the first eVTOL to publicly perform a transition flight. Its wing-mounted propellers tilted so it could fly like an airplane, before transitioning back to land like a helicopter. King began his career after earning a graduate degree from MIT in 1989. He later became the chief engineer on programs at Bell and Leonardo before joining Vertical in 2023. Looking back, he said he had come to appreciate "how much of a rewarding experience it is to learn something new every day." That's a handy perspective for a company building a new type of aircraft. eVTOLs are designed to function like helicopters but make much less noise, so the hope is they could be used over cities more frequently. Vertical Aerospace's air taxi, Valo, on display in London last year. Pete Syme/Business Insider The goal is to transform commutes and other short trips. For example, Vertical says its Valo air taxi could fly the 22 miles from Miami Airport to Fort Lauderdale in 11 minutes, compared to an hour by car. Most manufacturers have said they expect a seat on board to cost about the same as a luxury rideshare option like an Uber Black . However, there is still work to be done for air taxis to be certified by aviation regulators. "When you test it at the next higher level of integration, you're going to have some level of discovery," King said. "Get there quickly, then you learn, adjust your models, and then go test it." For King, the key is making those discoveries without taking unnecessary risks. He said young engineers should put "guardrails" around testing so that they can learn safely, but move quickly enough to avoid becoming stuck trying to make a model perfect before testing it. He recalled getting discouraged by unexpected results when he was younger, but embracing this has been a huge help. "Once people get energized by discovery as opposed to discouraged by discovery, you can see the iterations happen quickly," he said. Vertical is targeting entry into commercial service in 2029. items.title: As If There Was Any Question About Data Centers Being Weak Job Creators, Meta Is Now Deploying Robots to Maintain Them
items.summary: Since the start of the data center boom, “job creation” was one of the key promises made to communities weighing whether to host the tech industry’s monstrous computing facilities in their backyards. That was always a gross over-representation of the facts, as most labor required for data centers comes in the form of temporary construction jobs to build them. Still, the tech tycoons who need data centers to keep the AI revolution chugging along could always fall back on promoting the lonely skeleton crews tasked with manually monitoring, patrolling, and maintaining each facility. Now, even that could be going away. According to new reporting by Ars Technica , the AI giant Meta is testing new robots designed to automate the work of data center maintenance, with the aim of keeping the cost of labor even lower. The initiative is in its very early stages, per Ars , involving trial runs of hardware from a few different robotics firms. These include companies like ABB, Kinova, and Watney Robotics, which supply robot arms being tested for tasks like hot-swapping network cables and cycling power to server racks. One anonymous Meta staffer told Ars that, if it’s successful, a robotic arm from Kinova could replace up to 80 percent of their the facilities’ workload. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” the worker lamented. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.” The bulk of data center overhead comes from the hardware itself, particularly the extremely pricey AI chips needed to run high-powered large language models. Even when factoring in construction the human labor cost of data centers is negligible, meaning Meta is going far out of its way to automate maintenance work. Approached for comment by Ars , a Meta spokesperson declined to comment on the testing of robots for data center work. More on data centers: Data Center Backlash Has Officially Rattled Sam Altman The post As If There Was Any Question About Data Centers Being Weak Job Creators, Meta Is Now Deploying Robots to Maintain Them appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: SAP has a message for software doomsayers: The pendulum will swing back
items.summary: Jan Gilg, SAP's global president of customer success and Americas. SAP A SAP executive anticipates a recovery from the SaaSpocalypse, driven by advances in business AI. SAP is using AI to solidify its competitive edge against Palantir and other tech giants. SAP is shifting more to consumption-based pricing to align AI costs with business outcomes. A SAP executive says the "pendulum will swing back" from the SaaSpocalypse. Like many software companies, the German software giant has seen its stock hit hard over the past year amid competition from AI tools. This stock sell-off of software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, known as the SaaSpocalypse , has hit companies like Salesforce, SAP, and Workday as Anthropic and OpenAI have introduced tools that could threaten their businesses. SAP's stock has been down about 20% over the past year, though it's been on an upward trend over the past month. When SAP reported its earnings in late July, investors responded positively to the company's cloud-led growth and advances in its business AI. Jan Gilg, SAP's global president of customer success and Americas, told Business Insider that the sell-off was "a bit of an overreaction on the entire industry." "As usual, I feel the pendulum will swing back," Gilg said. "There will be users. There will be losers and winners. I truly believe SAP will be on the side of the winners." To get on the winning side, Gilg says SAP has been reinventing itself with AI, investing in its data capabilities, and changing its pricing models. "Everybody has AI on the agenda right now," Gilg said. SAP bounces back from the SaaSpocalypse SAP's stock has jumped roughly 40% since it reported earnings in late July. There's a reason for that, Gilg says. SAP isn't easily replaceable through a vibe-coded tool , though Gilg does expect companies to leverage AI to build software much faster. Internally, SAP has also used AI to improve its output and build its own software, and it sees AI as an opportunity to improve its tools for customers. "It's really multifaceted. On the one side, there was the idea that customers will vibe code their software themselves rather than buying packaged software. We don't see that frankly," Gilg said. "We don't see that, especially for mission-critical purposes. It's not just about features and functions. It's about auditability, governance, and the maintenance of the software." While Gilg says he hasn't seen customers replacing SAP software, he has seen competition over tech budgets—especially with token spending , or how companies pay for AI. SAP has a "good position" for this because customers rely on SAP data to run their business processes and can demonstrate its value, Gilg said. "Customers are seeing token costs go through the roof already," Gilg said. "How do you measure and control that, and how do you show an outcome for that? Budgets won't necessarily increase. It will still have to come from somewhere. Therefore, the scrutiny will become much, much bigger." SAP is competing more with Palantir Lately, Gilg has been focusing on explaining to customers how they can benefit from AI and what SAP can offer. Customers have spent a lot of money on AI, though many haven't seen the business outcomes, profit, or productivity gains they're looking for. "Customers have not yet seen the benefit of AI," Gilg said. "That is certainly something they are digging deeper into now." To address that, SAP built its first foundational model, Tabular AI, which can help make predictions based on business data. In the future, Gilg expects people to interact with SAP products through natural language and voice. SAP has also been investing in its ontology capabilities to allow customers to audit their systems and work with AI agents to help make decisions. Ontology is a favorite Palantir buzzword , and these capabilities put SAP in more direct competition with the AI data company. While SAP competes with Palantir , they also partner to move data between systems. SAP says its advantage over rivals is its data from over 10,000 customers, which allows it to build more useful capabilities. "We do see new players out there from Anthropic, OpenAI, Palantir, and so on," Gilg said. "That's going to be the battlefield of the future." Internally, SAP uses AI across departments such as finance, human resources, and more. For example, employees can use an internal chatbot to ask questions or AI tools to write code. Sales employees can use AI to help with customer briefings or to study markets. "We are definitely pivoting the company all in on AI," Gilg said. "We're doing this in a position of strength. Frankly, it's an evolution for us as well." SAP is overhauling how it charges for AI Gilg says AI will help SAP grow as it changes its business model. For example, it's moving from some subscription models to consumption-based models , meaning customers pay for what they use. The market has been shifting toward this pricing model, especially as high AI usage can drive up costs. "What outcome are they driving?" Gilg said. "That's how we charge the consumption of those agents, which is very transparent to customers. Also, it's much easier to justify why they would actually pay for it. That's the current model many are following." SAP still has a large subscription business, and many large customers use a hybrid model between subscription and consumption-based pricing . More SaaS acquisitions could be coming This year, SAP acquired Prior Labs, Reltio, and Dremio to boost its AI and data capabilities. Across the industry, Gilg expects to see a wave of acquisitions, especially with more AI-native startups and talent coming out of these companies. "There's going to be a camp of losers and winners," Gilg said. "We have seen valuations go down quite significantly. That's an opportunity and interest for companies like that to look at wide spaces." Gilg says SAP will also consider this if it makes sense for its business, though it would avoid companies that can be easily replaced by AI. If it's costly and time-consuming to switch from that software, customers are less likely to replace it with an AI-built application, Gilg said. "I do see that there will certainly be a level of consolidation from my perspective, especially with vendors focused on single products," Gilg said. "Maybe niche areas, like legal contract management . Those are spaces that probably will be disrupted quite significantly." Have a tip? items.title: How to automate your Gmail inbox — without AI
items.summary: Gmail is filled with hidden features and add-on possibilities , but one of the service’s most powerful organizational tools is sitting right in the heart of its regular settings. As you may have guessed by now (especially if you read this story’s headline, you clever little cat), I’m talking about filters — Gmail’s long-standing system for automating your inbox with a series of custom-crafted rules. At a glance, filters can seem complicated. They can seem overwhelming. They can even seem unnecessary. But don’t let yourself be fooled by the feature’s curiously crusty exterior. Gmail filters have the potential to completely reshape your inbox and the way your incoming messages are handled. They can help you keep your email in order with no ongoing thought or effort. And, unlike Google’s new AI Inbox option (which notably still doesn’t seem to be available for most people as of this writing), filters (a) don’t require your personal messages to be processed by generative AI systems — and (b) give you complete control over exactly how your email is handled instead of forcing you to rely on inherently unreliable technology to figure out what you want for you (and then likely come up short at least some of the time). Best of all? All it takes is a teensy touch of one-time planning to get Gmail filters set up to your exact specifications and working for you quietly and automatically from that moment onward. Follow the filter-centric Gmail tips in this guide, and your inbox will be running like a well-oiled (but not too greasy) machine in no time. Part 1: Figuring out your Gmail filters Let’s start by thinking through some Gmail filter possibilities to get an idea for the sorts of setups you might want to consider — then, we’ll go step by step through the process of creating them. With Gmail filters, you could: Ensure messages from specific high-priority senders always go into your inbox’s Primary tab, where you’re certain to see them Ensure specific sorts of lower-priority messages — like invoices, reports, or updates from different services you use — automatically get sorted into an out-of-the-way location and never even show up in your inbox Keep messages from annoying people out of your hair (but still available in case you need to find them) by automatically archiving them as soon as they arrive Forward messages from a specific address or with a specific phrase in their subjects to other members of your team or family Instantly respond to messages to or from a specific address with a prewritten template Label messages sent to a specific variation of your Gmail address (like youraddress+vip@gmail.com) or written with a specific word or phrase in the subject (like “urgent,” “important,” or “hey jerkwad, pay attention to this”) as “VIP” and then receive notifications only for messages with that designation Mark specific types of messages from yourself as reminders by giving them a bright yellow “REMINDER” label that makes them stand out in your inbox Get a snickerdoodle delivered to your desk every time your boss emails you All right, so that last one isn’t really possible (not yet, anyway) — just wanted to make sure you were still paying attention. Everything else in that list, however, is absolutely doable and actually quite easy to set up with Gmail filters. Got some ideas of your own? Good deal. Time to make ’em happen. Part 2: Creating your Gmail filters The simplest way to start a new Gmail filter is to click the control panel icon — the symbol showing three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other — within the big search box at the top of the Gmail website. (Filters can’t easily be managed on mobile, unfortunately, so you’ll need to do all of this in a desktop browser.) That’ll pull up a form where you can fill in whatever you want to use as the basis for your filtering — a word or phase that might appear within an email’s subject or body, an address from which a message could originate, or any other variable or combination of variables you like. The form for creating a filter is filled with options for controlling email automation. JR Raphael / Foundry Fill in the fields as appropriate, using however many variables you want — even employing quotation marks around multiword terms along with operators like “AND” and “OR” between terms, if you really want to get fancy — and then click “Create filter” at the bottom of the box. You can use any combination of variables, even employing operators within a single field, to control when your filter will run. JR Raphael / Foundry One quick warning: By default, your filter will apply to any and all incoming messages — hence the “All Mail” setting that shows up next to the “Search” option in the filter creation pop-up. If you change that option to “Inbox,” you’re likely to see an error message informing you that the parameters you chose are not recommended and may not work properly. Leave that “Search” option set to “All Mail” — which is probably what you want, anyway — and you’ll steer clear of any errors and allow things to work the way they should. Now it’s time for the fun part — the part where you decide exactly what happens when a message meeting your conditions arrives. You can select any combination of actions from the list and then configure them as needed. You can even tell Gmail to apply your filter retroactively to messages already in your account (as opposed to using it only for new messages that arrive from that point forward) by checking the “Also apply filter to matching conversations” option at the bottom of the box. Gmail’s filters include a variety of actions that can execute when your conditions are met. JR Raphael / Foundry Once you’ve got that finished, click the blue “Create filter” button — and that’s it: Your new Gmail filter is officially in place and active. items.summary_html:
Gmail is filled with hidden features and add-on possibilities, but one of the service’s most powerful organizational tools is sitting right in the heart of its regular settings.

As you may have guessed by now (especially if you read this story’s headline, you clever little cat), I’m talking about filters — Gmail’s long-standing system for automating your inbox with a series of custom-crafted rules. At a glance, filters can seem complicated. They can seem overwhelming. They can even seem unnecessary.

But don’t let yourself be fooled by the feature’s curiously crusty exterior. Gmail filters have the potential to completely reshape your inbox and the way your incoming messages are handled. They can help you keep your email in order with no ongoing thought or effort.

And, unlike Google’s new AI Inbox option (which notably still doesn’t seem to be available for most people as of this writing), filters (a) don’t require your personal messages to be processed by generative AI systems — and (b) give you complete control over exactly how your email is handled instead of forcing you to rely on inherently unreliable technology to figure out what you want for you (and then likely come up short at least some of the time).

Best of all? All it takes is a teensy touch of one-time planning to get Gmail filters set up to your exact specifications and working for you quietly and automatically from that moment onward.

Follow the filter-centric Gmail tips in this guide, and your inbox will be running like a well-oiled (but not too greasy) machine in no time.

Part 1: Figuring out your Gmail filters

Let’s start by thinking through some Gmail filter possibilities to get an idea for the sorts of setups you might want to consider — then, we’ll go step by step through the process of creating them.

With Gmail filters, you could:

  • Ensure messages from specific high-priority senders always go into your inbox’s Primary tab, where you’re certain to see them
  • Ensure specific sorts of lower-priority messages — like invoices, reports, or updates from different services you use — automatically get sorted into an out-of-the-way location and never even show up in your inbox
  • Keep messages from annoying people out of your hair (but still available in case you need to find them) by automatically archiving them as soon as they arrive
  • Forward messages from a specific address or with a specific phrase in their subjects to other members of your team or family
  • Instantly respond to messages to or from a specific address with a prewritten template
  • Label messages sent to a specific variation of your Gmail address (like youraddress+vip@gmail.com) or written with a specific word or phrase in the subject (like “urgent,” “important,” or “hey jerkwad, pay attention to this”) as “VIP” and then receive notifications only for messages with that designation
  • Mark specific types of messages from yourself as reminders by giving them a bright yellow “REMINDER” label that makes them stand out in your inbox
  • Get a snickerdoodle delivered to your desk every time your boss emails you

All right, so that last one isn’t really possible (not yet, anyway) — just wanted to make sure you were still paying attention. Everything else in that list, however, is absolutely doable and actually quite easy to set up with Gmail filters.

Got some ideas of your own? Good deal. Time to make ’em happen.

Part 2: Creating your Gmail filters

The simplest way to start a new Gmail filter is to click the control panel icon — the symbol showing three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other — within the big search box at the top of the Gmail website. (Filters can’t easily be managed on mobile, unfortunately, so you’ll need to do all of this in a desktop browser.)

That’ll pull up a form where you can fill in whatever you want to use as the basis for your filtering — a word or phase that might appear within an email’s subject or body, an address from which a message could originate, or any other variable or combination of variables you like.

The form for creating a filter is filled with options for controlling email automation.

JR Raphael / Foundry

Fill in the fields as appropriate, using however many variables you want — even employing quotation marks around multiword terms along with operators like “AND” and “OR” between terms, if you really want to get fancy — and then click “Create filter” at the bottom of the box.

You can use any combination of variables, even employing operators within a single field, to control when your filter will run.

JR Raphael / Foundry

One quick warning: By default, your filter will apply to any and all incoming messages — hence the “All Mail” setting that shows up next to the “Search” option in the filter creation pop-up. If you change that option to “Inbox,” you’re likely to see an error message informing you that the parameters you chose are not recommended and may not work properly. Leave that “Search” option set to “All Mail” — which is probably what you want, anyway — and you’ll steer clear of any errors and allow things to work the way they should.

Now it’s time for the fun part — the part where you decide exactly what happens when a message meeting your conditions arrives. You can select any combination of actions from the list and then configure them as needed. You can even tell Gmail to apply your filter retroactively to messages already in your account (as opposed to using it only for new messages that arrive from that point forward) by checking the “Also apply filter to matching conversations” option at the bottom of the box.

Gmail’s filters include a variety of actions that can execute when your conditions are met.

JR Raphael / Foundry

Once you’ve got that finished, click the blue “Create filter” button — and that’s it: Your new Gmail filter is officially in place and active. The next time any message comes in that meets the parameters you outlined, the actions you specified will automatically take place faster than you can say “I embrace Workspace in my workplace cyberspace.”

Part 3: Managing your Gmail filters

Last but not least, make yourself a mental note in case you ever need to adjust your filters in the future: If you want to edit, delete, or even just revisit a filter you created, just click the gear-shaped icon in the upper-right corner of the Gmail website, click “Settings,” then click the “Filters and Blocked Addresses” tab at the top of the settings screen. You’ll see every filter you’ve ever created there and can tweak or remove any of ’em with a couple quick clicks.

Now if only we could find a way to get the filters to deliver those blasted snickerdoodles for us. Hey, Google: Any chance you can make that happen?
