items.title: Walmart's copycat strategy: Restaurant delivery is its latest use of heft to break into established markets
items.summary: Walmart's main business is still its stores, but the company is always trying new things too. Bloomberg/Getty Images Walmart's move into restaurant delivery is another expansion from selling general merchandise. Since Sam Walton, the retail giant has placed big bets on new lines of business inspired by others. Here's a look back at some of the strategies that worked well for Walmart — and a few that didn't. Walmart got its start in 1962 selling general merchandise as a discount store in Rogers, Arkansas. Founder Sam Walton was constantly on the lookout for new retail concepts to try, and he wasn't shy about borrowing ideas from other successful entrepreneurs. "He just tried things, and he would learn, and if it didn't work, it wasn't a failure," CEO John Furner said during a conversation with reporters at Walmart's headquarters in June. "We just learned from it." Last week, Walmart moved to grow its delivery service in a partnership with Dunkin', putting the company on a collision course with delivery services like DoorDash and Uber Eats. The retailer will eventually offer delivery from most of the 10,000 Dunkin' locations across the US, moving onto turf long dominated by DoorDash and Uber Eats. Walmart described itself as "a rapidly emerging contender in the restaurant delivery business." That delivery experiment is a continuation of a pattern that Furner says is part of Walmart's DNA. "We constantly want to learn. We see where the world's going. Some things apply, some things don't," he said. "We'll learn from it and figure out the best way that we can accelerate the business." Here are eight bets Walmart has placed over the years in its bid to grow beyond traditional discount retailing. Home improvement Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images One of Walmart's first attempts at branching out came in 1975 with the launch of the Sav-Co Home Improvement Center chain. The brand didn't take off, and Walmart shifted its focus to adding new features to its stores. While local hardware stores were common in this era, large-store formats were relatively uncommon. Home Depot didn't open its first stores until 1979. Pharmacy John Gress/Corbis via Getty Images One of Walmart's early in-store experiments was in the pharmacy business, which began in 1978 and has since grown into one of the company's key business lines. Walmart dispensed an estimated $36.8 billion in prescriptions last year, making it the fifth largest pharmacy in the US, according to the Drug Channels Institute, which tracks the pharmaceutical industry. More recently, Walmart has stepped up prescription delivery speeds, with some orders filled in 30 minutes or less . Auto service Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Walmart opened its first auto care center in Oklahoma in 1979 and the service has expanded to nearly 2,600 locations across the US. Walmart's auto centers have also served as a testing ground for the company's expanding third-party marketplace, with customers able to order products like tires online that are shipped to a local store for scheduled installation. Warehouse club Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images The 80's were a busy decade for Walmart and Sam Walton in terms of experimentation. "'82, '83 I think he opened four different formats in that two year period," Furner said in June. "Sam's Club came out of it and was really successful, and the others we decided not to go forward with." Walton's approach to the wholesale club was modeled on Saul Price's concepts FedMart and Price Club, the latter of which also inspired and eventually merged with Costco. Sam's Club now has more than 600 US locations with $90 billion in sales last year. Grocery Scott Olson/Getty Images The Walmart supercenter is a quintessentially American phenomenon, but Walton famously modeled the concept off the European hypermarket format, which combined general merchandise retail with groceries under a single roof. "It took probably five or six years until there was a store in Washington, Missouri, that worked," Furner said of Walton's attempts to adapt the hypermarket concept to the US. It still took Walmart opening about a dozen more supercenters for the idea to really gain traction, he added. There are now more than 3,500 supercenters and more than 650 neighborhood market grocery stores in the US. Walmart is the largest grocery chain in the country, pulling in roughly one in five dollars spent in the category, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator. Specialty retail Stephen Zenner/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images About a decade ago, Walmart embarked on a flurry of merger activity, snapping up specialty retailers Bonobos, Moosejaw, and Modcloth in a bid to expand the company's reach with specialty brands and e-commerce customers. All three chains remained independent of Walmart's core operations and were subsequently sold off to other owners as the company refocused on its own offerings. Advertising Katie Jones/Variety via Getty Images In 2019, Walmart brought its advertising business in-house with what would become Walmart Connect, which sells ad space for the company's physical and digital properties. Combined with a growing third-party e-commerce marketplace and the acquisition of TV-maker Vizio, Walmart's ads business has delivered significant revenue growth in recent years. Restaurant delivery Walmart Walmart's latest bet puts the company on a course to compete more directly with food delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats. After letting grocery-delivery customers add meals from in-store Subway shops , Walmart said in September it would bring thousands of off-site Dunkin' locations to the service. Walmart has already established itself as a powerhouse in fast delivery for merchandise, groceries, and medicine — now it's set to fulfill more of what other chains sell too. items.title: He waited nearly 20 years to start a company. Now he's the cofounder of a double unicorn.
items.summary: Snehal Antani became a cofounder in his late 30s. His AI hacking startup, Horizon3, now has a market value above $2 billion. Courtesy of Horizon3 Horizon3 CEO Snehal Antani spent two decades building the skills he believed he'd need to be a founder. Antani said that experience helped the startup survive a funding crunch and the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank. There was one skill, though, he hadn't learned and got a crash course in: fundraising. Earlier this month, the AI hacking startup Horizon3 achieved a rare milestone: a $250 million funding round pushed its market valuation above $2 billion, making it a so-called double unicorn. CEO Snehal Antani said he spent nearly two decades acquiring the skills he needed to build the business, which simulates cyberattacks on companies' systems to identify vulnerabilities before real hackers can exploit them. The knowledge he gained turned out to be crucial, first when the tech funding market tightened and, later, when the bank where Horizon3 held all its money collapsed. "I wanted to make sure I built the right experiences," Antani, now 46, told Business Insider. After graduating from college, he said he learned about launching products at IBM, organizational management at GE Capital, scaling a hypergrowth company at software maker Splunk, and leadership at the US Joint Special Operations Command, or JSOC. It was also at JSOC where Antani met Air Force veteran Anthony Pillitiere, his Horizon3 cofounder. A different path Antani's path runs counter to the familiar Silicon Valley image of the college-dropout founder, embodied by figures like Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates , who started Facebook and Microsoft, respectively, as teenagers. Yet research suggests successful founders are often older than startup-culture stereotypes imply. An MIT Sloan study published in 2020 analyzed 2.7 million US entrepreneurs and found that the average age of founders behind the fastest-growing 0.1% of new ventures was 45. For Antani, the value of a later start was quickly put to the test. Three years after he founded Horizon3 in 2019, the tech funding environment abruptly changed, and the company suddenly had to make the cash it had raised last much longer than planned. Antani said he recalled a lesson from the CEO of one of his former employers about how to weather an economic downturn: Rather than cut your way through it, sell your way through it. He said Horizon3 did both. The company found about $3 million in costs to cut or redirect, including changes to benefits, hiring plans, and other operating expenses. Then it reinvested that money in sales and marketing, which Antani said helped grow revenue nearly fivefold year over year. Flirting with disaster In 2023, Horizon3 came closer to disaster. As Silicon Valley Bank was collapsing , Antani said he got a text from an investor asking how much of the startup's money was held there. His answer: "100%." By the time federal regulators took it over, Horizon3 had opened an account at another bank. But its funds in Silicon Valley Bank were frozen, and missing payroll could have triggered about $750,000 a day in California penalties — enough, Antani said, to put the company out of business within a week. To prevent that from happening, Antani said he drew $1 million from a personal line of credit. He and his executive team then agreed to tell employees what was happening and what they were doing about it. After regulators restored access to Horizon3's Silicon Valley Bank funds, the company repaid Antani. He said the episode put to use the leadership lessons he learned at JSOC, particularly the importance of dealing with crises. "It's all about being steady, calm, controlled," he said. "You can't be panicked." One learning curve For all the experience Antani brought to Horizon3, there was one part of the founder's job he had never done before: fundraising. To overcome that gap, he said he treated his early investor meetings as a crash course, repeatedly refining his pitch deck, financial model, and market case in response to the questions he was asked. "The first time, you kind of suck," said Antani. "You have to invest in being a good storyteller." After dozens of investor meetings, Antani said he mastered his pitch and received two term sheets , one of which he chose for Horizon3's $3.5 million seed round — the venture-capital firm SignalFire. (The company's latest raise was co-led by NightDragon and NEA.) Today, Horizon3 is far larger than the small team Antani started with, made up of former intelligence, special operations, and enterprise software veterans — mostly people he knew through his past work. The company, one of the earliest companies to bring the concept of an AI hacker to market, has about 7,000 customers globally and 550 employees. Antani said the experience he gained across different companies, roles, and environments made that possible. "You don't want to learn how to deal with HR issues for the first time as a founder," he said. "You want to have learned that stuff ahead of time." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Erin Piacenti, killed in Times Square stabbing, was a 'superstar' at Bank of America known for mentoring junior teammates
items.summary: Erin Piacenti was known for mentoring younger employees. Bank of America Erin Piacenti, who was killed in Times Square on Monday, was known as a mentor at Bank of America. Colleagues remembered her not only for her sharp legal mind, but love of books, Disney, and family. Piacenti's boss remembers describing her as a 'superstar' to senior management before her death. When Erin Piacenti walked into Bank of America on Monday after five months on maternity leave, she found pink daisies sitting on her desk. Welcome signs were strung around the office she shared with a few teammates. Piacenti showed them photos of Madison, her newborn daughter, before settling in to read case law. That afternoon, Piacenti was fatally stabbed in Times Square in what police described as an unprovoked attack. She was 32. Though Piacenti only started as a vice president in the firm's Americas Business Selection and Conflicts group around 18 months ago, she'd already made an impact on the small team. Hallie Ziesmer, the head of the roughly 20-person group, described Piacenti as a "superstar" in conversations with senior management before her death, and remembers interviewing Piacenti at the end of 2024. "It was probably one of the shortest interviews, because I think within three minutes I wanted to hire her," Ziesmer, who was Piacenti's direct boss, said on Friday. "She was obviously very intelligent, very capable. She was polished but down-to-earth." Piacenti was attacked by Pamela Cisneros, 49, who also injured another victim before officers shot her and killed her at the scene. There's been a wave of support on and beyond Wall Street since the event, and a GoFundMe to help her daughter has raised more than $800,000. Many Bank of America employees have contributed, a spokesperson for the bank said. Before joining Bank of America, Piacenti worked at the law firm Davis Polk for more than three years, focusing on mergers and acquisitions for part of that time. She started her career as a buyer at Bloomingdale's and graduated magna cum laude from Fordham Law. Piacenti had a niche focus at the bank, helping investment bankers prepare disclosure documents for companies gearing up for an M&A transaction and clients navigate a thicket of regulations. A colleague remembers her as resourceful, always finding creative solutions on her own. Piacenti would mentor more junior teammates who didn't have the same legal expertise, Ziesmer said. Many of them have spent time in Ziesmer's office this week, remembering how detailed and caring Piacenti was with her help. One junior employee who sat across from Piacenti said in an email that she reviewed much of their work, and had offered personal advice on top of professional tips during their occasional coffees. "She could have, on some days, left the office to be home, but she would spend time with juniors. She wanted them to understand and share a passion for what she was doing. She really enjoyed it," Ziesmer said. Piacenti would often talk about visiting her four younger siblings, or books, or Disney. When the team attended a cooking class last year, the same colleague who admired Piacenti's resourcefulness said she made the best dish (and helped save them, an inadequate chef). When another colleague ran into her on the Q train one morning, she was thrilled to introduce them to her husband, Frank, whom she talked about all the time. Around the holidays, Piacenti brought dozens of cookies into the office after she and Frank hosted the family's Christmas cookie party at their new home in New Jersey. Ziesmer says the team now plans to bring in cookies every year. Read the original article on Business Insider

Hallie Ziesmer, the head of the roughly 20-person group, described Piacenti as a "superstar" in conversations with senior management before her death, and remembers interviewing Piacenti at the end of 2024.

"It was probably one of the shortest interviews, because I think within three minutes I wanted to hire her," Ziesmer, who was Piacenti's direct boss, said on Friday. "She was obviously very intelligent, very capable. She was polished but down-to-earth."

Piacenti was attacked by Pamela Cisneros, 49, who also injured another victim before officers shot her and killed her at the scene.

There's been a wave of support on and beyond Wall Street since the event, and a GoFundMe to help her daughter has raised more than $800,000. Many Bank of America employees have contributed, a spokesperson for the bank said.

Before joining Bank of America, Piacenti worked at the law firm Davis Polk for more than three years, focusing on mergers and acquisitions for part of that time. She started her career as a buyer at Bloomingdale's and graduated magna cum laude from Fordham Law. Piacenti had a niche focus at the bank, helping investment bankers prepare disclosure documents for companies gearing up for an M&A transaction and clients navigate a thicket of regulations. A colleague remembers her as resourceful, always finding creative solutions on her own.

Piacenti would mentor more junior teammates who didn't have the same legal expertise, Ziesmer said. Many of them have spent time in Ziesmer's office this week, remembering how detailed and caring Piacenti was with her help. One junior employee who sat across from Piacenti said in an email that she reviewed much of their work, and had offered personal advice on top of professional tips during their occasional coffees.

"She could have, on some days, left the office to be home, but she would spend time with juniors. She wanted them to understand and share a passion for what she was doing. She really enjoyed it," Ziesmer said.

Piacenti would often talk about visiting her four younger siblings, or books, or Disney. When the team attended a cooking class last year, the same colleague who admired Piacenti's resourcefulness said she made the best dish (and helped save them, an inadequate chef). When another colleague ran into her on the Q train one morning, she was thrilled to introduce them to her husband, Frank, whom she talked about all the time.

Around the holidays, Piacenti brought dozens of cookies into the office after she and Frank hosted the family's Christmas cookie party at their new home in New Jersey.

Ziesmer says the team now plans to bring in cookies every year.

items.title: Toyota spent years moving slowly on EVs. I drove its new, affordable C-HR to see whether the wait paid off.
items.summary: Toyota took its time developing EVs. Was the C-HR worth the wait? Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Toyota wasn't a big player in the early-2020s all-electric game. It only launched one EV: the bZ4X. Suddenly, there's an influx of Toyota EVs for 2026, when competitors are leaving the market. I drove a new entrant to see if it works — and I think I'm in love. Let's go back to 2023. GM is rolling out a dozen EVs , Ford has borrowed the iconic F-150 and Mustang nameplates for all-electric vehicles, Polestar looks like a potential up-and-comer… And Toyota — long heralded as one of the more environmentally conscious automakers after the runaway success of the Prius hybrid — isn't really competing. Its single EV, the bZ4X, is a little weird-looking, charges slowly, and won't reach 300 miles on a full battery. Toyota's slow approach surprised industry watchers. Environmentalists blew up my phone at the time, complaining that the world's largest automaker was leaning heavily on hybrids that still got most of their power by burning dinosaur juice. Fast-forward three years. The industry's rosier EV predictions have succumbed to billion-dollar write-downs , a big graveyard of discontinued models , and Polestar's removal from the US market. Simultaneously, and almost inexplicably, Toyota's consumer EV lineup in 2026, fresh off a partnership with Subaru, has more nameplates than Tesla. That reversal is what made me particularly curious about the new C-HR. Handsome. Efficient. Kinda… super sporty? The C-HR is more of a looker than its bigger sibling. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider I drove about 200 miles through New York City traffic and New Jersey's highways in a 2026 Toyota C-HR XSE. And man, oh man, did I like my time in the driver's seat. Let's start with pricing. Starting at $37,080, the C-HR isn't Toyota's most affordable EV — that distinction goes to the bigger, $34,980 bZ . The C-HR is, however, the cheapest way to get into an all-wheel-drive Toyota EV. AWD comes standard on the base $37,080 C-HR, while it's a $5,000 upgrade on the bZ. My tester, with two-tone exterior paint, oomph-ier speakers, and some other goodies, topped out at $43,429. The car was wildly efficient. The EPA says the XSE can squeeze 273 miles from a full battery. I would have easily outperformed that during my week. I grabbed the EV with its battery at 89%, and after driving about 170 miles without charging, it never dropped below 40%. That suggests I would have gotten around 400 miles on a charge. On several drives, the car reported efficiency in the high-5s and low-6s in miles per kilowatt-hour. Those numbers, if true and consistent, are phenomenal. It reminded me of my time in Lucid's cars , a high-end EV maker practically obsessed with engineering every possible mile from a battery. The C-HR's interior was comfy and airy. Its storage was a little cramped, though. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Efficient is not a synonym for boring, and the C-HR makes that super clear. Toyota says the car can jump from a standing start to 60 mph in 4.9 seconds, which would make it the third-quickest car in Toyota's lineup, matching the time of the sport-oriented GR Corolla. Once it merged onto the highway, though, it acted more Toyota-like: composed, comfortable, and whisper-quiet. A Tesla Model Y owner joined me for about two hours, riding mostly in the back seat. They entered the C-HR deeply skeptical that an EV from a legacy automaker could hold a candle to their Tesla — and also walked away impressed with the airy interior and back-seat comfort. Lastly, aesthetics. I think the C-HR looks like it's about to pounce, even when parked. Its smoothed-out edges make it easier on the eyes than Toyota's larger bZ, without falling into the look-at-me-I'm-a-weird-EV styling trap that has befallen plenty of battery-powered cars. The C-HR's curved roofline makes it look like it's about to pounce. It's also a headache for tall backseat passengers. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider My demerits list was small, though potentially substantial for some buyers. There's no glovebox, cramping front-seat storage. My Model Y-owning passenger is about 5-foot-8 and had plenty of headroom in the back, but anyone who regularly lugs tall adults around may have to do some cramming. The trunk is smaller than the bZ's, there's no frunk, and the infotainment occasionally lagged while the car booted up. Still, by the end of the week, I did something I've rarely done after reviewing around 75 cars in my career: I imagined my own life with the C-HR. I was genuinely sad to see the car go. That's not common. Was it worth the wait? Toyota's C-HR smooths the jagged edges found in other modern EVs. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Showing up late did have advantages. The biggest is charging: The C-HR comes standard with a NACS charging port, the widely accepted charging standard developed by Tesla. That lets Toyota skip some of the awkward charging port transitions other automakers have had to navigate. It also helps Toyota avoid some of the costly EV bets that led rivals to their billion-dollar write-downs. The C-HR, like all of Toyota's other EVs, was jointly developed with Subaru, allowing the companies to share development costs in a period of auto industry decluttering . Most of what makes the C-HR so good feels very Toyota: strong efficiency, a comfortable ride, solid initial quality, and an easy-to-live-with interior. Those are not new competencies for the company. The wait paid off with a great EV. Did Toyota need to wait this long to build it? Maybe not. I'm still glad we got here. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Toyota took its time developing EVs. Was the C-HR worth the wait?

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

  • Toyota wasn't a big player in the early-2020s all-electric game. It only launched one EV: the bZ4X.
  • Suddenly, there's an influx of Toyota EVs for 2026, when competitors are leaving the market.
  • I drove a new entrant to see if it works — and I think I'm in love.

Let's go back to 2023. GM is rolling out a dozen EVs, Ford has borrowed the iconic F-150 and Mustang nameplates for all-electric vehicles, Polestar looks like a potential up-and-comer…

And Toyota — long heralded as one of the more environmentally conscious automakers after the runaway success of the Prius hybrid — isn't really competing. Its single EV, the bZ4X, is a little weird-looking, charges slowly, and won't reach 300 miles on a full battery.

Toyota's slow approach surprised industry watchers. Environmentalists blew up my phone at the time, complaining that the world's largest automaker was leaning heavily on hybrids that still got most of their power by burning dinosaur juice.

Fast-forward three years. The industry's rosier EV predictions have succumbed to billion-dollar write-downs, a big graveyard of discontinued models, and Polestar's removal from the US market.

Simultaneously, and almost inexplicably, Toyota's consumer EV lineup in 2026, fresh off a partnership with Subaru, has more nameplates than Tesla.

That reversal is what made me particularly curious about the new C-HR.

Handsome. Efficient. Kinda… super sporty?The C-HR is more of a looker than its bigger sibling.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

I drove about 200 miles through New York City traffic and New Jersey's highways in a 2026 Toyota C-HR XSE. And man, oh man, did I like my time in the driver's seat.

Let's start with pricing. Starting at $37,080, the C-HR isn't Toyota's most affordable EV — that distinction goes to the bigger, $34,980 bZ.

The C-HR is, however, the cheapest way to get into an all-wheel-drive Toyota EV. AWD comes standard on the base $37,080 C-HR, while it's a $5,000 upgrade on the bZ. My tester, with two-tone exterior paint, oomph-ier speakers, and some other goodies, topped out at $43,429.

The car was wildly efficient. The EPA says the XSE can squeeze 273 miles from a full battery.

I would have easily outperformed that during my week. I grabbed the EV with its battery at 89%, and after driving about 170 miles without charging, it never dropped below 40%. That suggests I would have gotten around 400 miles on a charge.

On several drives, the car reported efficiency in the high-5s and low-6s in miles per kilowatt-hour. Those numbers, if true and consistent, are phenomenal. It reminded me of my time in Lucid's cars, a high-end EV maker practically obsessed with engineering every possible mile from a battery.

The C-HR's interior was comfy and airy. Its storage was a little cramped, though.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

Efficient is not a synonym for boring, and the C-HR makes that super clear. Toyota says the car can jump from a standing start to 60 mph in 4.9 seconds, which would make it the third-quickest car in Toyota's lineup, matching the time of the sport-oriented GR Corolla.

Once it merged onto the highway, though, it acted more Toyota-like: composed, comfortable, and whisper-quiet.

A Tesla Model Y owner joined me for about two hours, riding mostly in the back seat.

They entered the C-HR deeply skeptical that an EV from a legacy automaker could hold a candle to their Tesla — and also walked away impressed with the airy interior and back-seat comfort.

Lastly, aesthetics. I think the C-HR looks like it's about to pounce, even when parked. Its smoothed-out edges make it easier on the eyes than Toyota's larger bZ, without falling into the look-at-me-I'm-a-weird-EV styling trap that has befallen plenty of battery-powered cars.

The C-HR's curved roofline makes it look like it's about to pounce. It's also a headache for tall backseat passengers.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

My demerits list was small, though potentially substantial for some buyers. There's no glovebox, cramping front-seat storage. My Model Y-owning passenger is about 5-foot-8 and had plenty of headroom in the back, but anyone who regularly lugs tall adults around may have to do some cramming. The trunk is smaller than the bZ's, there's no frunk, and the infotainment occasionally lagged while the car booted up.

Still, by the end of the week, I did something I've rarely done after reviewing around 75 cars in my career: I imagined my own life with the C-HR.

I was genuinely sad to see the car go. That's not common.

Was it worth the wait?Toyota's C-HR smooths the jagged edges found in other modern EVs.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

Showing up late did have advantages.

The biggest is charging: The C-HR comes standard with a NACS charging port, the widely accepted charging standard developed by Tesla. That lets Toyota skip some of the awkward charging port transitions other automakers have had to navigate.

It also helps Toyota avoid some of the costly EV bets that led rivals to their billion-dollar write-downs. The C-HR, like all of Toyota's other EVs, was jointly developed with Subaru, allowing the companies to share development costs in a period of auto industry decluttering.

Most of what makes the C-HR so good feels very Toyota: strong efficiency, a comfortable ride, solid initial quality, and an easy-to-live-with interior. Those are not new competencies for the company.

The wait paid off with a great EV.

Did Toyota need to wait this long to build it? Maybe not. I'm still glad we got here.

items.title: Uber says it can replace car ownership. My used Toyota Yaris proved its point.
items.summary: I bought a used car. It was much more expensive than using Uber or Lyft. Alex Bitter/BI I bought a used car one year ago and compared the costs with using Uber and Lyft. The car was much more expensive, even though I made choices to save money. It shows why Uber says that its service competes with car ownership. No one had ever been this excited about a used Toyota Yaris. That was my thought as my wife and I picked up the keys to the car we found on Facebook Marketplace one morning in August 2025. For the first time in seven years of living in the Washington, DC area, we were car owners. It was also a rebuke of sorts for one of the companies I write about most often. For years, Uber executives have said that the company's gig-worker drivers — and, increasingly, the self-driving cars on its app — compete with car ownership. Uber President Andrew MacDonald told a podcast last month that the rising cost of a new car makes owning one a worse deal than several years ago. And CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said last year that the rise of robotaxis will reduce car ownership over the next two decades, making driving a car yourself look "something like horseback riding." So, did I make a horrible mistake spending just over $6,000 on a used sub-compact car that's effectively the next draft horse? Last month, one year after buying my Yaris, I decided to add up all my expenses and compare them with the previous year, when I was car-free and relied on Uber, Lyft, and public transportation. Your milage my vary. Your own calculation will depend on where you live, the cost of your car, how fast it depreciates, and the current price of gas (or charging, if you drive an EV). My results showed that Uber might have a point. The costs of a Toyota Yaris add up My wife and I decided we wanted a car last summer when we realized that parking at our apartment complex was free. Owning a car never made sense to us in Washington. DC is one of about a dozen US cities with a rapid transit system, and a parking spot can cost up to $300 a month. Plus, wait times for rides on Uber and Lyft are rarely more than a few minutes. Parking is just one of the costs of owning a car these days. The average sticker price of a new car is above $50,000, according to Kelly Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand that tracks car prices. Used cars , while more affordable, have become more expensive, too. There's also maintenance, insurance, and, for many of us, the elevated price of gas. When my wife and I found our used Toyota Yaris L — that's "L" meaning the lowest-trim model — we thought that we were being as thrifty as possible. We could buy the car without a loan. And my research suggested that, even when it needed repairs, they wouldn't be that expensive on a small, simple vehicle. If any car had a chance of rivaling the cost of Uber, this was it. But it didn't. After buying the car for $6,000, one year of car ownership cost us another $5,000. That's more than three times as much as the $1,600 we spent on ride-hailing trips and rental cars in the year before we bought the car. Some of the expenses were optional, like $250 to have my transmission fluid drained and replaced as a preventative maintenance measure. But most of those costs were the basics: Oil changes, gas, registration fees, insurance, and tolls. I also didn't quit using Uber or Lyft. I took rides to plenty of weekend bar hangs with friends, either because parking was a hassle or because I wanted to drink. Suddenly, free parking started to lose its shine. Our little sub-compact was more expensive than I had expected. Maybe, though, there's more to it. 'Ready to be driven at a moment's notice' I'm merely the latest person to compare whether owning a car makes sense in the era of ride-hailing apps. Even Sam Altman made the comparison in a blog post back in 2014. His conclusion: Using Uber was cheaper than driving his Tesla Roadster — at least, back when the millennial life subsidy made fares on the app cheaper than they are today. Doing a strict cost comparison isn't how most of us think about car ownership, though, according to David Keith, associate professor of strategy at the Melbourne Business School in Australia. Keith is one of the authors of a 2021 study that asked drivers from major US cities how much they would need to be paid annually to give up their car. The exact number — $11,197 on average — wasn't as interesting as why people said that they valued owning a car. More than half of that amount, Keith and colleagues found, was "non-use value," which includes having the option to take a car whenever you want, and a perceived status boost from owning a car. In other words, drivers are okay if their car sits unused most of the time. "I can walk outside, and there's this box of metal sitting there on the street, ready to be driven at a moment's notice," he said. I knew exactly what he meant. For weeks after buying my car, I had to change how I thought about transportation. Questions like "How much are Uber rides?" and "Is my destination accessible by Metro?" were replaced by a single statement: "Just drive there now, stupid!" There were also places I would never have visited without a car: For example, Fredericksburg, Virginia, for a day of antiquing, or rural Maryland to search the site of a Civil War camp with my metal detector. Being able to hop in a car whenever you want feels great. Those are trips that would have been difficult or impossible with Uber, and they're the main reason that my wife and I plan to keep our car, extra costs and all. Recreating that freedom with modes of transportation that you don't own is an important aspect of reducing car ownership in the US, Keith told me. Some places have tried it. A company called MaaS Global — that's "Mobility as a service" — operated an app called Whim, which offered taxi rides, bike shares, and public transit as a bundle for a monthly subscription. Whim operated in several European cities, including Helsinki and Vienna, before MaaS Global filed for bankruptcy in 2024 and ceased operations. Meanwhile, in the US, car ownership has stayed steady over the last couple of decades, even as alternatives from Uber and Lyft to local bike-sharing programs grow. "All of these things are fantastic, but none of them have really led to there being fewer cars in cities," Keith said. Do you have a story idea about Uber? I bought a used car. It was much more expensive than using Uber or Lyft.

Alex Bitter/BI

  • I bought a used car one year ago and compared the costs with using Uber and Lyft.
  • The car was much more expensive, even though I made choices to save money.
  • It shows why Uber says that its service competes with car ownership.

No one had ever been this excited about a used Toyota Yaris.

That was my thought as my wife and I picked up the keys to the car we found on Facebook Marketplace one morning in August 2025. For the first time in seven years of living in the Washington, DC area, we were car owners.

It was also a rebuke of sorts for one of the companies I write about most often. For years, Uber executives have said that the company's gig-worker drivers — and, increasingly, the self-driving cars on its app — compete with car ownership.

Uber President Andrew MacDonald told a podcast last month that the rising cost of a new car makes owning one a worse deal than several years ago. And CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said last year that the rise of robotaxis will reduce car ownership over the next two decades, making driving a car yourself look "something like horseback riding."

So, did I make a horrible mistake spending just over $6,000 on a used sub-compact car that's effectively the next draft horse?

Last month, one year after buying my Yaris, I decided to add up all my expenses and compare them with the previous year, when I was car-free and relied on Uber, Lyft, and public transportation.

Your milage my vary. Your own calculation will depend on where you live, the cost of your car, how fast it depreciates, and the current price of gas (or charging, if you drive an EV).

My results showed that Uber might have a point.

The costs of a Toyota Yaris add up

My wife and I decided we wanted a car last summer when we realized that parking at our apartment complex was free.

Owning a car never made sense to us in Washington. DC is one of about a dozen US cities with a rapid transit system, and a parking spot can cost up to $300 a month. Plus, wait times for rides on Uber and Lyft are rarely more than a few minutes.

Parking is just one of the costs of owning a car these days. The average sticker price of a new car is above $50,000, according to Kelly Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand that tracks car prices. Used cars, while more affordable, have become more expensive, too. There's also maintenance, insurance, and, for many of us, the elevated price of gas.

When my wife and I found our used Toyota Yaris L — that's "L" meaning the lowest-trim model — we thought that we were being as thrifty as possible. We could buy the car without a loan. And my research suggested that, even when it needed repairs, they wouldn't be that expensive on a small, simple vehicle. If any car had a chance of rivaling the cost of Uber, this was it.

But it didn't.

After buying the car for $6,000, one year of car ownership cost us another $5,000.

That's more than three times as much as the $1,600 we spent on ride-hailing trips and rental cars in the year before we bought the car.

Some of the expenses were optional, like $250 to have my transmission fluid drained and replaced as a preventative maintenance measure. But most of those costs were the basics: Oil changes, gas, registration fees, insurance, and tolls.

I also didn't quit using Uber or Lyft. I took rides to plenty of weekend bar hangs with friends, either because parking was a hassle or because I wanted to drink.

Suddenly, free parking started to lose its shine. Our little sub-compact was more expensive than I had expected.

Maybe, though, there's more to it.

'Ready to be driven at a moment's notice'

I'm merely the latest person to compare whether owning a car makes sense in the era of ride-hailing apps. Even Sam Altman made the comparison in a blog post back in 2014.

His conclusion: Using Uber was cheaper than driving his Tesla Roadster — at least, back when the millennial life subsidy made fares on the app cheaper than they are today.

Doing a strict cost comparison isn't how most of us think about car ownership, though, according to David Keith, associate professor of strategy at the Melbourne Business School in Australia.

Keith is one of the authors of a 2021 study that asked drivers from major US cities how much they would need to be paid annually to give up their car.

The exact number — $11,197 on average — wasn't as interesting as why people said that they valued owning a car. More than half of that amount, Keith and colleagues found, was "non-use value," which includes having the option to take a car whenever you want, and a perceived status boost from owning a car.

In other words, drivers are okay if their car sits unused most of the time. "I can walk outside, and there's this box of metal sitting there on the street, ready to be driven at a moment's notice," he said.

I knew exactly what he meant.

For weeks after buying my car, I had to change how I thought about transportation. Questions like "How much are Uber rides?" and "Is my destination accessible by Metro?" were replaced by a single statement: "Just drive there now, stupid!"

There were also places I would never have visited without a car: For example, Fredericksburg, Virginia, for a day of antiquing, or rural Maryland to search the site of a Civil War camp with my metal detector. Being able to hop in a car whenever you want feels great. Those are trips that would have been difficult or impossible with Uber, and they're the main reason that my wife and I plan to keep our car, extra costs and all.

Recreating that freedom with modes of transportation that you don't own is an important aspect of reducing car ownership in the US, Keith told me.

Some places have tried it. A company called MaaS Global — that's "Mobility as a service" — operated an app called Whim, which offered taxi rides, bike shares, and public transit as a bundle for a monthly subscription. Whim operated in several European cities, including Helsinki and Vienna, before MaaS Global filed for bankruptcy in 2024 and ceased operations.

Meanwhile, in the US, car ownership has stayed steady over the last couple of decades, even as alternatives from Uber and Lyft to local bike-sharing programs grow.

"All of these things are fantastic, but none of them have really led to there being fewer cars in cities," Keith said.

items.title: One runner spent $40,000, another took a second job. Marathoners are making big sacrifices to chase medals worldwide.
items.summary: David Boyce, who takes runcations, competing in the London Marathon in 2024. Courtesy of David Boyce When some people travel, they collect fridge magnets or shot glasses. Eugen Godun collects marathon medals. Last March, the 34-year-old software developer earned the coveted Six Star medal for running the Boston, Chicago, New York City , London, Berlin, and Tokyo marathons, known as the original World Marathon Majors. When Godun crossed the finish line in Japan, he burst into tears, overcome by a mixture of pride, happiness, and pure exhaustion. Godun started running in 2014 and completed his first international marathon in Poland the following year, shaving an hour off his previous time of 4 hours and 6 minutes. Over the past decade, his pursuit of medals and faster finishes has taken him from his home in Kyiv to eight countries across Europe, the US, and Asia. For amateur runners like Godun, destination races kill several birds with one stone: a trip abroad, a major athletic achievement , and some serious bragging rights. Godun is particularly proud to be one of only 60 Ukrainians recorded as having received a Six Star medal. For all their rewards, international marathons demand plenty in return: vacation days, family time, and money. In 11 years, Godun said he has spent roughly $40,000 on international marathon trips, or $5,000 a race on average. Godun sometimes wonders where he'd be financially if he'd saved the money instead. "Maybe if I switched these marathons for saving money, I'd be able to buy my own apartment,” he said. Even so, he thinks it was worth it. "I like to spend my money on experiences, not on things," Godun added. Godun received his Six Star medal after running the Tokyo Marathon in 2025. Courtesy of Eugen Godun Have you taken on a second job, gone into debt, or found an unusual way to make the numbers work to pursue a passion? Business Insider wants to hear about the trade-offs you've made for a hobby. Contact this reporter at jzitser@businessinsider.com . The pursuit of far-flung finish lines Running’s pandemic-era boom shows little sign of fading, and Americans are prioritizing fitness and experience-led travel . More than 52.3 million Americans went road-running in 2025, up more than a million from 2024, according to the Outdoor Industry Association's 2026 Running Report, which is based on data from the Physical Activity Council. In KPMG's summer 2026 consumer survey, half of respondents named physical fitness as their top wellness priority, while 54% of those planning to travel more were seeking a specific experience or event. Destination marathons combine the two. Godun has plenty of company in the expensive pursuit of far-flung finish lines. Demand for marathon spots has grown in recent years, with international competitors accounting for an increasing share of participants, according to data shared with Business Insider by five of the now-seven World Marathon Majors, the global series of marathon races. Godun ran the New York City Marathon in 2019. Courtesy of Eugen Godun Since 2023, international applications for the London Marathon have almost tripled, from 89,108 in 2023 to 258,502 in 2026, when the race drew 854,452 applicants overall. The Boston Marathon’s share of international runners has risen from about a quarter of the field in 2023 to roughly a third of the 30,000 participants in each of the past three years. The Sydney Marathon has seen even more dramatic international growth. The number of overseas finishers jumped from 260 in 2022 to more than 13,500 of a total 32,963 runners in 2025, when it became the seventh World Marathon Major. “People like a challenge, particularly one that is tough but achievable, and completing the six, or now seven, race series has become the ultimate running challenge,” Steven Seaton, the founder of the UK-based sports tourism firm 2:09 Events, said. “The fact that the races are hard and increasingly expensive to enter only seems to fuel greater demand.” The cost for international competitors entering the World Marathon Majors ranges from about $237 for Sydney to $333 for New York, before accounting for flights, hotels, food, and other costs. Godun, for example, has tried to cut costs by staying with friends, where possible, and drawn a line on what he’s willing to spend. He gave up a spot in the 2026 Sydney Marathon because he couldn't justify spending thousands of dollars on flights. He said he has since started setting aside about $1,000 a month, or about 20% of his monthly income, to avoid ruling out future races on cost alone. Godun has found himself working harder at his job, too. “I need to earn more money to be able to do this,” he said. A second job to keep chasing marathon medals David Boyce, 59, is so committed to running international marathons that he took on a part-time job lecturing at a local university three years ago to, in his words, “feed my addiction.” The extra income has helped the Canadian government employee pay for a coach, enter races farther afield, and spend longer abroad exploring the destinations. In the lead-up to a marathon, Boyce prioritizes rest, saving the indulgences for later. “Then you can do all the things that you want to do, like have a beer, have a decadent meal, or things like that,” Boyce said. Boyce ran the Boston Marathon in 2022. Courtesy of David Boyce In his early 40s, Boyce couldn’t have imagined organizing his vacations around marathons. items.title: I resigned and couldn't find a job. I lived with family, lost my storage unit, and relied on government assistance.
items.summary: Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her deputy director role. Kymberly McClain Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her nonprofit role. She eventually deleted her LinkedIn account out of frustration and relied on government assistance. McClain shared how she navigated her long job search and eventually found a call center job. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kymberly McClain, a 45-year-old who lives in Las Vegas. She previously worked at a small nonprofit until resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Two years ago, I was working as a deputy director at a small nonprofit in California focused on providing resources for the homeless population. After some leadership changes, I didn't feel like I had the support I needed. In August 2024, I resigned. When I started looking for a new job , I was so confident. I'd gained experience and felt like I'd parted ways on good terms, even getting a letter of recommendation. I thought I was going to slide into another role. Instead, I struggled to find work for nearly two years. I started applying for jobs I never expected to consider When I started looking, I was applying for deputy director, program manager, case manager, and other social service roles. I used LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, CareerBuilder, and other job sites. I sought out résumé help because I had been out of the job market for a few years and didn't know what had changed. September, October, November, and December went by, and nothing happened. As the search continued, I started broadening the scope of the types of jobs I was applying for. I went from thinking I could easily land another deputy director job to applying for retail jobs at places like Burlington Coat Factory. I was willing to take anything. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I eventually deleted LinkedIn out of frustration LinkedIn was probably the platform I used most during the first six months of my search. I went to LinkedIn training sessions about how to get a job and read up on interview tips. At one point, I was applying to multiple jobs a day and changing my résumé for each one. I would research the company and position before applying. But I wasn't having any luck. I remember seeing comments from other people on LinkedIn asking whether anyone else was having trouble finding a job or getting employers to respond. As the rejections piled up, I started questioning everything. Was it my race? My age ? My lack of a college education? I even wondered whether I was on somebody's list of people not to hire. I had never imagined that I would be without a job for this long. After about a year of searching, I was exhausted by the rejection. I started pulling back from my job search and eventually deleted my LinkedIn account out of frustration. I thought, What's the point? My long job search created financial challenges My job search took a toll on my finances, and I had to apply for government assistance . For a while, I went back and forth between staying with a friend in California and with family in Las Vegas while I tried to figure things out. Eventually, I moved in with my family members in Las Vegas. Eventually, I felt like I needed to contribute financially to the household. I had to choose between helping my family and paying for the storage unit I'd stored my belongings in when I moved, so I gave up the unit and lost the belongings in it. When I wasn't looking for work , I focused more of my time on a nonprofit I'd founded years earlier, based partly on my own experiences navigating the social services system. It helps people experiencing homelessness and domestic violence survivors navigate housing and other resources. It wasn't generating income, but I needed to feel like I was doing something productive. Sometimes rejection is redirection Earlier this year, I gave the job market another try. I applied for several healthcare billing roles , but I was rejected from all of them. Then, my daughter sent me a link to a remote customer-service job. I completed an assessment, went through the process, and got a yes. It's a full-time customer-service call center job . It pays significantly less than I made in my prior role, but after being out of work for so long, I'm just excited somebody said yes. When I got the offer, I thought, Okay, I'm not blackballed from the job market. I'm still not sure what the future holds, but I plan to keep working on my nonprofit while I work this new job. My advice to other job seekers is to have faith in closed doors. Sometimes rejection is redirection, and sometimes it's the push you need to build something of your own. Do you have a story to share? This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kymberly McClain, a 45-year-old who lives in Las Vegas. She previously worked at a small nonprofit until resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Two years ago, I was working as a deputy director at a small nonprofit in California focused on providing resources for the homeless population.

After some leadership changes, I didn't feel like I had the support I needed. In August 2024, I resigned.

When I started looking for a new job, I was so confident. I'd gained experience and felt like I'd parted ways on good terms, even getting a letter of recommendation.

I thought I was going to slide into another role. Instead, I struggled to find work for nearly two years.

I started applying for jobs I never expected to consider

When I started looking, I was applying for deputy director, program manager, case manager, and other social service roles.

I used LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, CareerBuilder, and other job sites. I sought out résumé help because I had been out of the job market for a few years and didn't know what had changed.

September, October, November, and December went by, and nothing happened.

As the search continued, I started broadening the scope of the types of jobs I was applying for. I went from thinking I could easily land another deputy director job to applying for retail jobs at places like Burlington Coat Factory. I was willing to take anything.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

I eventually deleted LinkedIn out of frustration

LinkedIn was probably the platform I used most during the first six months of my search.

I went to LinkedIn training sessions about how to get a job and read up on interview tips. At one point, I was applying to multiple jobs a day and changing my résumé for each one. I would research the company and position before applying.

But I wasn't having any luck. I remember seeing comments from other people on LinkedIn asking whether anyone else was having trouble finding a job or getting employers to respond.

As the rejections piled up, I started questioning everything. Was it my race? My age? My lack of a college education? I even wondered whether I was on somebody's list of people not to hire. I had never imagined that I would be without a job for this long.

After about a year of searching, I was exhausted by the rejection. I started pulling back from my job search and eventually deleted my LinkedIn account out of frustration. I thought, What's the point?

My long job search created financial challenges

My job search took a toll on my finances, and I had to apply for government assistance. For a while, I went back and forth between staying with a friend in California and with family in Las Vegas while I tried to figure things out. Eventually, I moved in with my family members in Las Vegas.

Eventually, I felt like I needed to contribute financially to the household. I had to choose between helping my family and paying for the storage unit I'd stored my belongings in when I moved, so I gave up the unit and lost the belongings in it.

When I wasn't looking for work, I focused more of my time on a nonprofit I'd founded years earlier, based partly on my own experiences navigating the social services system. It helps people experiencing homelessness and domestic violence survivors navigate housing and other resources.

It wasn't generating income, but I needed to feel like I was doing something productive.

Sometimes rejection is redirection

Earlier this year, I gave the job market another try. I applied for several healthcare billing roles, but I was rejected from all of them.

Then, my daughter sent me a link to a remote customer-service job. I completed an assessment, went through the process, and got a yes.

It's a full-time customer-service call center job. It pays significantly less than I made in my prior role, but after being out of work for so long, I'm just excited somebody said yes. When I got the offer, I thought, Okay, I'm not blackballed from the job market.

I'm still not sure what the future holds, but I plan to keep working on my nonprofit while I work this new job.

My advice to other job seekers is to have faith in closed doors. Sometimes rejection is redirection, and sometimes it's the push you need to build something of your own.

items.title: Sam Altman says he's 'a mega Apple fan boy' and is sad they are suing OpenAI
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman looks past then-Apple CEO Tim Cook during a dinner for tech leaders at the White House in September 2025. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is a self-described "mega Apple fanboy." Altman said he was "very sad" to see Apple sue OpenAI. The legal fight illustrates how frayed the relationship between the two companies has become. Sam Altman 's love for Apple is being tested by that pesky detail: the Cupertino tech giant's lawsuit against OpenAI. "I'm like a mega Apple fanboy, and I was very sad about that," Altman told tech journalist Alex Heath during a recent interview. In July, Apple sued OpenAI , accusing the ChatGPT creator of a "coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal Apple's closely held secrets. OpenAI has said it has "no interest in other companies' trade secrets" and that the lawsuit doesn't live up to Apple's "reputation for obsessing over the smallest details." Altman said when he first heard about the suit, he thought something had gone significantly wrong. "When I first heard about it, I was like, 'Man, this sounds egregious. Someone must have done something badly,'" Altman said. "We don't want any company's IP, and we certainly don't want people who are going to take a company's IP and bring it to us." Altman is barely mentioned in Apple's initial 40-page complaint, which, in addition to various corporate entities, directly named only two OpenAI employees, Chang Liu and Tang Tan , both of whom formerly worked for Apple, as defendants. Apple's suit said Liu and Tan took or retained confidential information when they left the company and, in some instances, asked current Apple employees about unannounced products. The lawsuit marks a dramatic turn from what had once been a major partnership. In June 2024, Altman went to Cupertino to announce that Apple would integrate ChatGPT across its products. Their cooperation has frayed as OpenAI has entered the consumer space Apple has long dominated. Less than a year after speaking at Apple's Worldwide Developer Conference, Altman and iPhone designer Jony Ive announced that they had been collaborating for years and that OpenAI would acquire Ive's startup IO for nearly $6.5 billion. As part of the legal battle, Apple requested a preliminary injunction, which could potentially delay OpenAI's plans. In response, OpenAI said Apple is trying to delay OpenAI's hardware "because it fears OpenAI's product might reduce demand for Apple's." The Apple of his eye Altman is seen at the 2024 Apple Worldwide Developers Conference Nic Coury/AFP via Getty Images Altman's love for Apple is well documented. In 2008, he demoed Loopt, the location-based social networking app he cofounded, at Apple's Worldwide Developer Conference. Altman said getting up onstage required Apple CEO Steve Jobs' approval. Looking back on the experience, he called it "a career highlight" and said it was "the only time in business" he felt that much anxiety. "It was like Steve Jobs, you know," Altman said in 2015, recalling how he grew up viewing Jobs as an iconic figure. Altman said growing up, his first computer was a Macintosh LC II . In 2024, he told Bill Gates that he still owns it and it still works. When Altman announced his partnership with Ive, he cited his hope to bring "some of the delight, wonder and creative spirit that I first felt using an Apple Computer 30 years ago." Speaking with Ive and Laurene Powell Jobs last year, Altman declared the iPhone "the crowning achievement of consumer products" during an onstage interview last November. Altman, who does not own a stake in OpenAI, built his fortune largely through investments in companies including Stripe and Reddit. His grandma gave him what may have been one of his first tech investments. In a 2016 interview, he conducted with his brother Jack, the pair recalled how, for their birthdays, their grandma gave them equal shares in companies she thought they would like. Jack was given Applebee's, while Sam received Apple. "I still have those Apple shares marked in my brokerage account as 'Grandma's birthday Apple shares,' Sam Altman said, adding, "I'm going to keep them." Read the original article on Business Insider

Mike Windle/Getty Images for StarClub Bernhard Fritsch rubbed elbows with stars and owned a McLaren. Now he's a convicted fraudster, a fugitive, and a top target of the FBI. A $150,000 bounty, a severed ankle monitor, escape from US authorities, and an arrest in Mexico — the Bernhard Fritsch file reads like a Hollywood script. On Thursday, the FBI added the 65-year-old German to its "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list . Fritsch studied audio engineering in Berlin in the 1980s before moving to New York in the 1990s. With his company MCY, he wanted to sell music over the internet — sort of a precursor to the streaming giant Spotify at an early stage of the dot-com economy. He told a reporter from the German Manager Magazin in 2000 that he had already won over Michael Jackson, Paul McCartney, Luciano Pavarotti, and the Backstreet Boys to his idea. "You wouldn't believe who's already walked through that door," he said at the time. He had met Michael Jackson in Munich the previous year. Michael Jackson and Bernhard Fritsch at a charity event. Peter Bischoff/Getty Images Sometime in the early 2010s, Fritsch relocated from New York to Santa Monica, California, where he founded the company StarClub. Its app, StarSite, was meant to help celebrities and influencers monetize their reach through advertising. Between 2014 and 2017, according to federal officials, Fritsch raised between $20 million and $30 million from investors. To raise that much, Fritsch apparently relied on prominent connections. In California, he was seen as a skilled operator behind the scenes, Los Angeles Magazine reported. While spending time in Germany, the Bavarian had cultivated ties to the world of celebrities, too: Photos show him with three-time Wimbledon-winner Boris Becker — who in 2022 was sentenced to prison in the UK for tax evasion — and in 2016, Fritsch walked the red carpet with actor Wesley Snipes at Bertelsmann's summer party in Berlin. He also courted proximity to show business in the U.S. In 2014, for example, he had actor Tyrese Gibson (best known from the "Fast & Furious" movies) host a private StarClub party for him. Singer Enrique Iglesias was also linked to the project, and actresses Caitlin O'Connor and Elise Neal appeared at promotional events. According to the website Courthouse News, one investor later claimed in a lawsuit that Fritsch owed him $750,000 for arranging contacts with Jessica Simpson. Tyrese Gibson and Bernhard Fritsch attend a StarClub party in 2014. Mike Windle/Getty Images for StarClub In 2017, Fritsch was criminally charged by federal prosecutors who alleged he made false statements to investors about the app, claiming his company would strike deals with major media companies like Disney and that acquisition offers were forthcoming. At least $7.3 million of investor money is alleged to have ended up in his personal accounts instead — funding a McLaren, a Rolls-Royce, a yacht, and a mortgage on his villa near the popular Carbon Beach in Malibu. In April last year, after a nine-day trial, a jury found him guilty on one of two counts of wire fraud, a verdict for which he could have faced up to 20 years in prison. And then, suddenly, Fritsch was gone. In June 2025, according to the FBI, he cut off his court-ordered ankle monitor and fled to Mexico. This is particularly striking given that his attorney, Kirk Schenck, had argued there was no flight risk, since Fritsch would be leaving his two children behind. According to Mexican authorities, the entrepreneur turned up, of all places, in the state of Sinaloa — considered a stronghold of Mexico's powerful drug cartels. An arrest warrant from Los Angeles followed, and American officials alerted Mexican police. In September of last year, Mexican authorities caught him — allegedly carrying forged documents. After his arrest, Mexican police released him on the condition that he check in at the station every two weeks. Authorities say Fritsch used the opportunity to travel to Mexico City, where in early October he boarded a Lufthansa flight to Munich. The FBI believes he has been in Bavaria ever since. In his absence, a federal judge in Los Angeles sentenced him in absentia to 15 years in prison, a $35,000 fine, and nearly $26.8 million in restitution. Fritsch need not fear extradition. Article 16 of Germany's constitutional Law forbids the extradition of German citizens. So as long as he doesn't leave the country, no US arrest warrant can reach him. The FBI put Fritsch on its list of most-wanted fraudsters. FBI Fritsch's partner, former actress Lucy Weist, pleaded guilty in June of this year to being an accessory after the fact, and she now faces up to five years in prison. FBI Director Kash Patel in June launched the "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list as a counterpart to the classic most-wanted list — this one for white-collar criminals. The goal, Patel said, is to hold "the worst of the worst" accountable. Patrick Grandy, the FBI agent leading the investigation in Los Angeles, describes California as especially fertile ground for fraudsters — and has made clear that the hunt for Fritsch continues. The feds have put up a $150,000 bounty. A request for comment sent to Fritsch via his Instagram profile was not answered. Since his post about the mountain walk in April, Fritsch hasn't uploaded anything new to his profile. He does seem to have been indulging in old memories from time to time. He has captioned several posts "Throwback": One, a photo from 1999 showing him with Michael Jackson, another from 2001 showing him shaking hands with Pope John Paul II at the Vatican. On a sunny day in April, visits a hilltop near Lake Starnberg in Germany. After a hike against the backdrop of the Bavarian mountain panorama, he treats himself to a slice of cake with vanilla ice cream at the Forsthaus Ilkahöhe, a popular hikers' inn. Later, he uploads photos of the outing to Instagram, gushing over the view of the snowy Zugspitze mountain.

Does someone who is on the run and wanted by the American federal police post something like that? It is, by far, not the only question raised by this bizarre case. A $150,000 bounty, a severed ankle monitor, escape from US authorities, and an arrest in Mexico — the Bernhard Fritsch file reads like a Hollywood script.

On Thursday, the FBI added the 65-year-old German to its "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list.

Fritsch studied audio engineering in Berlin in the 1980s before moving to New York in the 1990s. With his company MCY, he wanted to sell music over the internet — sort of a precursor to the streaming giant Spotify at an early stage of the dot-com economy.

He told a reporter from the German Manager Magazin in 2000 that he had already won over Michael Jackson, Paul McCartney, Luciano Pavarotti, and the Backstreet Boys to his idea. "You wouldn't believe who's already walked through that door," he said at the time. He had met Michael Jackson in Munich the previous year.

Michael Jackson and Bernhard Fritsch at a charity event.

Peter Bischoff/Getty Images

Sometime in the early 2010s, Fritsch relocated from New York to Santa Monica, California, where he founded the company StarClub. Its app, StarSite, was meant to help celebrities and influencers monetize their reach through advertising.

Between 2014 and 2017, according to federal officials, Fritsch raised between $20 million and $30 million from investors. To raise that much, Fritsch apparently relied on prominent connections. In California, he was seen as a skilled operator behind the scenes, Los Angeles Magazine reported.

While spending time in Germany, the Bavarian had cultivated ties to the world of celebrities, too: Photos show him with three-time Wimbledon-winner Boris Becker — who in 2022 was sentenced to prison in the UK for tax evasion — and in 2016, Fritsch walked the red carpet with actor Wesley Snipes at Bertelsmann's summer party in Berlin.

Singer Enrique Iglesias was also linked to the project, and actresses Caitlin O'Connor and Elise Neal appeared at promotional events. According to the website Courthouse News, one investor later claimed in a lawsuit that Fritsch owed him $750,000 for arranging contacts with Jessica Simpson.

Tyrese Gibson and Bernhard Fritsch attend a StarClub party in 2014.

Mike Windle/Getty Images for StarClub

In 2017, Fritsch was criminally charged by federal prosecutors who alleged he made false statements to investors about the app, claiming his company would strike deals with major media companies like Disney and that acquisition offers were forthcoming.

The goal, Patel said, is to hold "the worst of the worst" accountable. The feds have put up a $150,000 bounty.

Since his post about the mountain walk in April, Fritsch hasn't uploaded anything new to his profile. He does seem to have been indulging in old memories from time to time.
